# THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor: full text of the advisory pages and guides

> The English text of every advisory, local, partner, guide and project page on stavtheodor.com, in one plain file. The curated map is https://stavtheodor.com/llms.txt; short answers are in https://stavtheodor.com/answers.md. Each page is bilingual (English and Hebrew) at the URL given. THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor is based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and is not affiliated with Theadora Art Advisory (Los Angeles) or TSG Art Advisory. Contact: stav@stavtheodor.com, (201) 351-8367.

## Local pages

### Art consultant and curator in New Jersey, for private homes

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/art-curator-new-jersey/

An art curator in New Jersey does for a home what an architect does for the plot: decides what belongs on which wall, and why, before anything is bought, then sources and installs it. I am THEODORA's founder, Stav Theodor, based in Tenafly, and I do this for homes across New Jersey, from Bergen County to Hoboken and Jersey City, in person, and online with clients anywhere.

I trained as a curator, and earlier in my career I did curatorial work in museums and managed a gallery in Tel Aviv. I have built art collections while collaborating with luxury hospitality leaders, and today I do the same work for private homes. A curator can come into a house at any of three moments: while it is being built, while it is being finished, or years later, when the walls still say nothing.
If your home is in Bergen County, two pages speak to it directly: one for the town where I live and work, as an art consultant in Tenafly, and one for the county around it, as an art advisor in Bergen County.

### What an art curator does for a private home
Four things, in the order they happen.

- Consulting and curation. From a single artwork to a complete collection: a concept for the house, a shortlist per room, and pieces that fit the space, the style and the story of the people in it. Deep research, market insight and a sharp eye, so the shortlist stays short.
- Sourcing and acquisition. I find the work through a global network of artists and makers, leading New York City galleries, and artists I work with directly. I assess market value and negotiate on your behalf, and because I carry none of the costs of a gallery or an auction house, in most cases the work itself costs you less.
- Commissions and creative direction. When the wall needs a piece that does not exist yet, I brief the artist and manage the work from the first concept to the final execution. A work made for a specific wall carries deeper meaning and a presence that cannot be repeated.
- Production, framing and installation. Printmakers, framers and art installers I work with regularly, within defined timelines and an approved budget. The work is not complete until every piece is on the wall and you are fully satisfied.
Everything runs through the same seven steps: discovery, research, curatorial development, budget planning, art procurement and selection, logistics, installation. You see a shortlist, not a flood, and I handle every detail in between.

### What I look at first
I start with the space itself, not with a catalog. Three things decide most of what follows. The light: where it comes from, how it moves through the day, and where glare will ruin a glossy surface, which settles medium, finish and glazing as much as placement. The sightlines: what you see from the front door, from the sofa, from the dining table, because the most important wall is rarely the biggest one. And the structure: where a large work needs support inside the wall, and where the picture lights or adjustable spots should go, which in a new house is a pencil line and in a finished one is an electrician and a patch.

### Art curator in Bergen County: Tenafly, Closter, Alpine, Englewood, Cresskill, Demarest
From Tenafly, the towns of Bergen County are a short drive: Closter, Alpine, Englewood, Cresskill, Demarest and the ones around them. Art is planned in the light the space actually has and installed with the furniture in place, so settle each light and fixing while the electrician is still on the job. If the house is going up now, the cheapest decisions of the whole project are made while the drawings are open: which walls are for art, where a large work needs support, where the lighting goes. I wrote a separate page on when art should come into a new build in Bergen County.
I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere, from Tel Aviv to California. Interior designers and architects also bring me in on behalf of their clients.

### Choosing art for an apartment in Hoboken or Jersey City
Yes, I help people choose art for apartments in Hoboken and Jersey City, in person, as anywhere in New Jersey. In a waterfront tower the skyline across the river is the strongest image in the space, so choose the wall before the art: I survey the space and its sightlines and define the main wall from them. The light off the water then settles medium, finish and glazing; the page on art for a new condo covers glass, light and sun off the Hudson.
New towers have rules for installers: a certificate of insurance naming the managing agent, a booked service elevator, set hours. My own team installs, after hours when needed, and I can provide that certificate; see who can hang heavy art in an apartment building. I can start from the plans before a visit, and since I represent you, not a roster, the work can come from any artist, New Jersey artists included.

### A newly built house in Closter
The Closter residence is a newly built private home, and I came in after it was built and designed. I was commissioned to curate a collection that would raise the architectural character of the house and bring depth to the interior design. I worked closely with leading New York City galleries, and the collection brings together works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices.
The result transforms a well designed house into a space with soul, where art and architecture speak the same language.The full story is on the Closter project page.

### Israeli and Jewish artists, and the rest
I managed a gallery in Tel Aviv, I work directly with Israeli artists, and I work with leading New York City galleries, so for a family in New Jersey that wants Israeli and Jewish artists on its walls the question is never whether, only which. Let the mix follow who you are, not a label: a considered collection rather than a themed one, with every other contemporary voice in the house chosen with the same care.

### Working with your designer, architect or broker
I work alongside architects and interior designers, not around them. I read the drawings, the palette and the furniture plan before I propose a single work, because requests for wall support and lighting belong in the schedule everyone else is already working from. The designer keeps the house; I bring the art that belongs in it, and my job is to show the studio at its most professional. If you are a designer or an architect, there is a page written for you: for interior designers and architects. If you sell or build homes, there is a page on how I work with your buyers: for real estate brokers and developers.

### What an art curator costs in New Jersey
In most cases, buying art through me costs less than buying it at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction, many bidders push the price of the same work up; a gallery prices with big margins to cover its venue, its inventory and its gallerists. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases working with me is more affordable than almost anywhere else. That price includes private consultation for your own home and my work with you until the art is on the wall, and I represent you, not a roster of artists. The longer answer is on what an art advisor costs.

### Art Radar: what is worth seeing near you
I also publish Art Radar, a weekly curator's guide to the exhibitions, gallery openings and museum events worth your time in New York, New Jersey and Tel Aviv, written in Hebrew and translated in full into English. It began as a WhatsApp group for the community in northern New Jersey, and some of its most useful posts are the local ones: the Shaffer collection at the Montclair Art Museum, a show hung the way the couple lived with their art at home; the free Guggenheim passes that the public libraries of Tenafly, Demarest, Closter and Cresskill lend to cardholders; and Museums on Us, the Bank of America program that gives its cardholders free entry to many museums on the first full weekend of every month. The first post says why I started it.

### How to start
Send me one photo of the wall and a line about the home, at stav@stavtheodor.com or through the contact details at the end of this page. Floor plans are welcome if you have them. I will tell you what I see, and we will agree the scope together. If your project is an apartment in the city, read about my work as an art curator in New York; if you also own a home in Israel, I handle that from here as well.

Questions:

Q: Is there an art curator in Bergen County, New Jersey?
A: Yes. I am Stav Theodor, an art curator and advisor based in Tenafly, and I work across Bergen County: Closter, Alpine, Englewood, Cresskill, Demarest and the towns around them. Q: What is the difference between an art curator and an art advisor for a home?
A: In a private home the two overlap, and I do both. The curator's part is the eye and the idea: which works, on which walls, in what relation to each other and to the architecture. The advisor's part is the market: what a work should cost, where to find it, how to negotiate it, and how to get it framed, shipped and hung. One person doing both means the idea and the purchase never pull apart.

Q: When should I bring an art curator into a new house in New Jersey?
A: While the drawings are still open, before the walls are closed and the lighting is fixed. At that stage the decisions that matter most cost almost nothing: which walls are for art, where a large work needs support inside the wall, where the picture lights go. Once finishes and furniture are chosen, the concept and the shortlists follow, and installation comes last, with the furniture in place. A finished house is fine too; there are simply fewer options for lighting and hanging structure.

Q: Can you find art by Israeli and Jewish artists for a home in New Jersey?
A: Yes. I managed a gallery in Tel Aviv, I work directly with Israeli artists, and I work with leading New York City galleries. In the Closter house the collection brings together works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices. Let the mix follow who you are, not a label, so the walls read as a considered collection rather than a themed one.

Q: How much does an art curator cost in New Jersey?
A: In most cases, less than buying the same art at a large auction or through a gallery. Many bidders push auction prices up, and galleries price with big margins to cover the venue, the inventory and the gallerists; I carry none of those costs. The price includes private consultation for your New Jersey home and my work with you until the art is on the wall. I represent you, not a set of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world.

Q: Do you work with my interior designer, or instead of them?
A: With them, always. I read the drawings, the palette and the furniture plan before I propose anything, because requests for wall support and lighting belong in the schedule everyone else is already working from. The designer keeps the house; I bring the art that belongs in it, and my job is to show the studio at its most professional. Designers and architects also bring me in on behalf of their own clients.

### Art advisor and art consultant in New York City: art for a private apartment, an office or a whole collection

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/art-curator-new-york/

I am an art advisor and art consultant in New York City for private apartments, offices and collections. I trained as an art curator, and as an art consultant I read the rooms, the light and the building, work inside your designer's plan rather than around it, and find, negotiate and install the art, from a first conversation to the day it is hung. I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, a short drive from Manhattan; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere. This page says what the work looks like in practice.

When someone in New York looks for an art advisor or an art consultant, they usually have an apartment they care about, a designer they trust, walls that are still empty, and no interest in spending their weekends walking galleries. That is the job I do. I take the search off your hands, I bring back only what fits, and I stay until the last piece is on the wall. I trained as a curator, I have done curatorial work in museums and managed a gallery in Tel Aviv, and I have built art collections with luxury hospitality groups, from the Waldorf Astoria Chengdu to the St. Regis Amman. An apartment is smaller than a hotel. The standard is not.

### What an art curator does for a New York apartment
I start in the rooms, not in a catalog. A Tribeca loft with tall walls and cast iron columns asks for a different scale than a prewar Upper East Side apartment with plaster moldings and rooms that were drawn with pictures in mind. A glass tower in Hudson Yards has very little solid wall and a great deal of light, so the question becomes where the eye rests and what can hold its own next to the view. Three things I check first:

- The light. Where it comes from, how it moves through the day, and where glare will ruin a glossy surface. This decides medium, finish and glazing as much as it decides placement.
- The building. Most Manhattan buildings have rules for installers: certificates of insurance, service elevator bookings, working hours. I plan the installation around them and coordinate with your management office before anything is delivered, so nothing arrives that cannot get upstairs.
- The sightlines. What you see from the front door, from the sofa, from the dining table. The most important wall is rarely the biggest one.
Then the four services, in the order they happen: consulting and curation, from a single artwork to a complete collection; sourcing and acquisition, through a global network of artists and makers and the galleries of New York and Tel Aviv, with market value assessed and the price negotiated on your behalf; commissions and creative direction, when the wall needs a piece that does not exist yet; and production, framing and installation, with printmakers, framers and installers I work with regularly. The work is not complete until every piece is on the wall and you are fully satisfied. The process, step by step, is on what an art advisor does for a Manhattan apartment.

### A custom bar in a Manhattan skyline residence
The client loved to entertain, and the apartment had a custom bar built for exactly that: a marble counter, backlit shelves of bottles and glassware on either side, and in the middle a panel that was clearly built to hold a single picture. I selected a large format digital collage that draws on the visual language of glamorous social gatherings and references Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère, painted by Édouard Manet in 1882: the barmaid behind her marble counter, and the crowd that appears only in the mirror behind her. A work that quotes Manet above a private bar gives the room a lineage. Guests feel the reference before they place it, and the client has a work that says, in one glance, what the apartment is for. Then the practical part: production at the size the panel required, framing, and installation above a bar, where lit shelves and marble put reflections everywhere and the hanging height is set for people standing, not sitting. The photographs are on the project page.
 

### Art you already own, and how long the rest takes
Consulting runs from a single artwork to a complete collection, and in an apartment that starts with what is already there. Some pieces will find a better wall, some will want reframing, and some will tell me what the new works should not be. Looking at your existing art is also the fastest way for me to understand your taste before I propose anything. As for time: a single available work can be selected, framed and installed on a short timeline; a commission follows the artist's schedule and the production time for the piece; a whole apartment moves with the design and construction timeline, which is why I prefer to start while the plans are still open. I set the timeline with you at the discovery stage and keep to it.

### New York homes, building by building
Each kind of New York building asks its own questions of art, and each has its own page here. If you are furnishing a home, from a single wall to the whole house, here is how I work as a residential art consultant. A brownstone or townhouse is read floor by floor, from the parlor wall to the stair hall: art for a Brooklyn brownstone. A prewar apartment brings plaster, moldings and co-op rules: art for a prewar apartment. A loft asks for scale: large scale art for a loft. A new condo has glass, light and few solid walls: art for a new condo. A studio or a one bedroom asks for fewer, larger works: art for a small apartment. If you have just arrived, start with empty walls after a move. If you want someone to take the search off your hands, read help choosing art for your home in New York; if you would rather look yourself, where to buy original art in New York. If you are building a collection, start with how to start an art collection.

### Art for an office or a business in New York
An office, a clinic or a firm asks a different question than a home: what should a client understand about you in the ten seconds before you speak? One work that says it honestly and holds the wall from the door does more than a corridor of safe prints. I choose art for workspaces the way I choose it for hotels, with the identity of the place first and the wall second, and I manage production and installation around your working hours. More on art for an office, a clinic or a business, and, if you are opening or moving an office in Manhattan, on art for a new office in Manhattan.

### Working with your designer or architect
I work alongside architects and interior designers, not around them. If your designer is already on the project, I read their drawings, their palette and their furniture plan before I propose a single work. Art that ignores the design reads as an afterthought; art that only matches it reads as decoration. The right piece belongs to the room and still says something the room could not say on its own. I join early when I can, while lighting and wall finishes are still open, so that a picture light lands where the picture will be; if the apartment is already finished, I work with what is there. A good share of my projects come to me through designers and architects on behalf of their clients, and there is a page written for them: for interior designers and architects.

### The galleries: SoHo, Tribeca, Chelsea and beyond
Sourcing in New York means knowing what is on the walls this month, not last year, and that is a large part of why I publish Art Radar, a weekly curator's guide to the exhibitions worth your time in New York, New Jersey and Tel Aviv. Recent routes include two galleries and lunch in SoHo, José Lerma at Nino Mier and Rita Ackermann at Hauser and Wirth; a September gallery walk in Tribeca, four shows a few minutes apart; and In a Free State at Luhring Augustine, also in Tribeca, with a curator's note on what the show leaves outside the frame. The galleries of Chelsea, the museums on Fifth Avenue and the auction rooms are on the same radar, so when a work for your wall is hanging in one of them, there is a good chance I have already stood in front of it.

### New York, New Jersey and Tel Aviv
I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, a short drive from Manhattan; I work in person across New York City and New Jersey, and online with clients anywhere, Tel Aviv included. For a house in Bergen County, read about my work as an art curator in New Jersey. For a home in Israel that you manage from here, I work in Hebrew and English on both sides; that page is art for a home in Israel, managed from New York or New Jersey.

### What an art curator costs in New York
In most cases, art bought through me costs less than the same work at a large auction or in a gallery. At auction, many bidders compete for one work and push its price up, and a gallery prices with big margins to cover its venue, its inventory and its gallerists. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases working with me is more affordable than almost anywhere else. The price includes private consultation for your apartment or office and my work with you until the art is hung, and I represent you, not a roster of artists. The longer answer is on what an art advisor costs.

Send me one photo of the wall and a line about the room, at stav@stavtheodor.com or through the contact details at the end of this page. Q: Who are the best art advisors for private homes in New York?
A: The best one for a private home represents you, not a gallery's artists, sources from the whole market, knows how New York buildings work and stays until the art is on the wall. That is how I work: I am Stav Theodor, art advisor, art consultant and curator, and the founder of THEODORA. I read the light, the building and your designer's plan, then source, negotiate, frame and install. Write to stav@stavtheodor.com with one photo of a wall.

Q: Is an art advisor the same as an art consultant in New York?
A: Not quite, though the titles overlap. An art advisor usually works for a buyer who is building a collection; an art consultant works for a space, such as an apartment, an office or a hotel, and chooses and installs art that fits it. I work as both, so in a New York apartment I find and negotiate the work and also make sure it belongs on the wall. The full comparison is in art advisor or art consultant.

Q: Which parts of New York do you cover?
A: All of New York City, from a Tribeca loft to a prewar Upper East Side apartment or a glass tower in Hudson Yards, and Westchester too. Each asks for a different scale and a different kind of work, so I start from the rooms, not from a catalog. I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere.

Q: Do I need an art curator if I already have an interior designer?
A: Usually yes, and your designer will often be the one to suggest it. Designers are responsible for the whole room and rarely have the time or the artist relationships to source art seriously. I work inside their plan, present a shortlist that respects their palette and furniture, and handle sourcing, negotiation, framing and installation. A good share of my projects come to me through interior designers and architects on behalf of their clients.

Q: Do you handle the building side: certificates of insurance, the service elevator, working hours?
A: Yes. Production, framing and installation are part of the service, with printmakers, framers and installers I work with regularly. In Manhattan that includes the building: certificates of insurance, service elevator bookings and working hours, coordinated with your management office before anything is delivered. The work is not finished until the piece is on the wall, lit correctly, and you are fully satisfied.

Q: What does an art curator cost in New York?
A: In most cases, less than the same art would cost at a large auction or in a gallery. Auction prices rise when many bidders want one work, and gallery prices carry big margins for the venue, the inventory and the gallerists; I have none of those costs. The price includes private consultation for your apartment or office and my work with you until the art is on the wall, and I represent you, not a roster of artists.

## Town and county pages

### Art advisor and consultant in Bergen County

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/art-advisor-bergen-county/

I am Stav Theodor, founder of THEODORA, an art advisory practice based in Tenafly. I work with homeowners, interior designers, architects and businesses across Bergen County, choosing, sourcing, commissioning, framing and installing the art for their spaces.

Whether you searched for an art advisor in Bergen County or an art consultant, the job is the same: art that is right for the house and the people in it, bought well and hung properly. Below is how I work here, a Bergen County project you can look at, and how to start.

### Bergen County homes and the art they ask for
The most common thing I see in Bergen County is a beautiful house, finished to the last detail, with art bought in a hurry during the final month because the walls looked bare at the walkthrough. The house deserved better, and so did the owners.
The fix is simple: decide early that art is part of the plan. While the architect is still drawing, a few decisions cost almost nothing: which walls are for art and which are for windows and millwork, where a large work will need support inside the wall, where picture lights go, whether the stair hall wants one tall piece or a sequence. Made then, these are pencil lines. Made after the drywall, they are an electrician and a patch. If your house is already finished, it is not too late; there are simply fewer options for lighting and hanging, and I work with what is there. More in art for a new build in Bergen County.

### Where I work in Bergen County
I live and work in Tenafly, and one of my recent collections is for a new house in nearby Closter. From Tenafly, any site visit in the county is a short drive, which matters when a builder schedules the walkthrough for a Tuesday morning. I also work across the rest of New Jersey and in New York City, and online with clients anywhere.

### A Bergen County project: new construction in Closter
The house in Closter was complete when I came in: white walls, wide plank oak floors, a beamed ceiling, black framed glass doors opening onto the trees. Every finish was right. What it did not have yet was a point of view. The brief was to raise the architectural character of the house and bring depth to the interior design, with works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices, reading as one collection. I built it room by room with leading New York City galleries and managed the shortlists, negotiation, shipping, framing and installation. See the Closter project.

### For Bergen County designers, architects and builders
I work alongside architects and interior designers, not around them. On a new build that means I read the plans and put my requests into the same schedule everyone else works to. The house stays the designer's; I bring the art and make sure it lands exactly where the design has already made room for it. See art curation for interior designers.

### Offices, practices and restaurants
Homes are most of my Bergen County work, but I also choose art for businesses: law firms, investment firms, wealth managers, medical practices, restaurants and boutique hotels.

### Art in and around Bergen County
Art Radar, my weekly guide to exhibitions worth seeing, began as a WhatsApp group for our community in northern New Jersey and New York. It covers the New York museums and galleries and New Jersey venues such as the Montclair Art Museum (Living With Art), plus practical tips like the free museum passes that several Bergen County libraries offer residents. Read Art Radar.

### My background
I have spent more than 15 years in the art world, with an M.A. in art history from Ben-Gurion University and a diploma in curatorial and museum studies from Tel Aviv University. Before THEODORA I did curatorial work in established museums and managed a gallery in Tel Aviv.

### How it works and what it costs
The process is the same seven steps on every project: discovery, research, curatorial development, budget, procurement, logistics and installation. You see a short list, not a flood. I assess market value and negotiate on your behalf. In most cases, art bought through me costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry none of their costs; the price includes private consultation for your home until the art is on the wall, and I represent you, not a roster of artists. For a new build I prefer to see the plans first. See what an art advisor costs.

### Art advisor for a home in Westchester: houses, big walls and how I work there

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/art-advisor-westchester-ny/

An art advisor for a Westchester home chooses, sources, commissions and installs the art for a house, and the right one represents you rather than a gallery's artists and can start from your architect's plans. Yes, I take on Westchester homes: THEODORA is based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work on a Westchester house online and from its plans. I am Stav Theodor, and below is what a larger house asks of art.

### What does a Westchester house ask of art?
Scale and light, more than a city apartment does. Five places decide most of it:

- The double height entry. Seen from the door and again from the landing, the work has to hold at both distances. Hang it for the person in the entry, not centered in the full height, and choose one tall work, or a group that climbs as one.
- The stair hall. Seen on the move, from below and then from above: the centerline follows the pitch of the stair, and the landing is where a work is seen standing still. See entryway and hallway art.
- Spaces that open to the garden. Glass brings daylight and takes wall away. Keep works on paper and photographs off the walls the sun reaches.
- The long wall. Choose one work at real scale or a group that reads as one, then pin paper cut to size on the wall and judge it from the far end. See large wall art ideas.
- Many walls at once. I define the main wall from the sightlines; the rest of the house follows in order, not in one season.

### What art suits an older Westchester house?
Art sized to the house's proportions rather than matched to its period. Many houses in Scarsdale, Bronxville and Rye are older, with plaster walls, moldings and paneled libraries, and contemporary work can look strongest against that detail.

- Size the work to the panel between the moldings, or to the space above the mantel, not to the whole wall.
- Plaster is more brittle than drywall: hang heavy work on the studs, on hangers made for plaster, or from a picture rail if the house has one.
- In a Tudor revival house, common in Scarsdale, leaded windows and dark paneling often keep the light low: plan picture lights before you hang, and keep works on paper away from working fireplaces and radiators.

### New builds and renovations: while the drawings are open
Plan the art before the glass is drawn: every new window takes a wall. I can start from your architect's plans and define the main wall from the sightlines; that is the wall to keep solid. In Scarsdale and Rye, new windows go before the local Board of Architectural Review, which can change them: confirm the art for the walls they touch once the elevations are approved. For the timing on a house built new, see when art should come into a new build. The drawing checklist is in planning art in construction drawings.

### Big walls and commissions
When a double height entry or a long stair wall needs a work in a size the market does not have, commission it. For a sea view villa in Caesarea, Israel, I commissioned a 3.5 meter triptych from an Italian artist, three storks at its center. Panels also pass through doors and up a turning stair where one large canvas may not. I work directly with the artist throughout; the steps are in commissioning art for a new home.

### How I work in Westchester from Tenafly
I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere, Westchester included. A curator does not need to be on site: I can work from your designer's and architect's plans. My first question is never about style; it is what you want to feel at home. If you work with a designer or architect, I work out with them what is right for you. Installation is part of how I work, not a separate service, and for a co-op I can provide a certificate of insurance that names the managing agent. ## Advisory pages

### Art advisor for a Manhattan apartment: what to expect

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-advisor-manhattan-apartment/

As an art curator and advisor for a Manhattan apartment, I do three things you do not have time for: I read the rooms, the light and the building, work inside your designer's plan rather than around it, and find the art that belongs there, from the first conversation to the day it is hung. Below is what that looks like in practice, including how a custom bar in a Manhattan skyline residence found the large format digital collage that now anchors it.

When a client in Manhattan asks me for an art advisor, what they usually mean is this: I have an apartment I care about, a designer I trust, walls that are still empty, and no interest in spending my weekends walking galleries in Chelsea. That is the job. I take the search off your hands, I bring back only what fits, and I stay until the last piece is on the wall.

I have spent more than 15 years in the art world: curatorial work in museums, managing a gallery in Tel Aviv, and building art collections for hotels such as the Waldorf Astoria Chengdu and the St. Regis Amman. An apartment is smaller than a hotel. The standard is not.

### What I do with the apartment itself

I start in the rooms, not in a catalog. A Tribeca loft with tall walls and cast iron columns asks for a different scale than a prewar Upper East Side apartment with plaster moldings and rooms that were drawn with pictures in mind. A glass tower in Hudson Yards has very little solid wall and a great deal of light, so the question becomes where the eye rests and what can hold its own next to the view.

Three things I check on the first visit:

- The light. Where it comes from, how it moves through the day, and where glare will ruin a glossy surface. This decides medium, finish and glazing as much as it decides placement.

- The building. Most Manhattan buildings have rules for installers: certificates of insurance, service elevator bookings, working hours. I plan the installation around them, so nothing arrives that cannot get upstairs.

- The sightlines. What you see from the front door, from the sofa, from the dining table. The most important wall is rarely the biggest one.

### What I do with your designer

I work alongside architects and interior designers, not around them. If your designer is already on the project, I read their drawings, their palette and their furniture plan before I propose a single work. Art that ignores the design reads as an afterthought. Art that only matches the design reads as decoration. The right piece does a third thing: it belongs to the room and still says something the room could not say on its own.

In practice this means I join early when I can, while lighting and wall finishes are still open, so that a picture light lands where the picture will be. If the apartment is already finished, I work with what is there. Either way, the designer keeps the room. I bring the art.

### A custom bar in a Manhattan skyline residence

The client loved to entertain, and the apartment had a custom bar built for exactly that. The bar needed one work to anchor it. I selected a large format digital collage that draws on the visual language of glamorous social gatherings and references "Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère", painted by Édouard Manet in 1882.

The reference is not an inside joke for art historians. Manet's barmaid is one of the great paintings about looking and being looked at, and that is what a bar in a home is for. Guests see the work and recognize something in it, even when they cannot say what. Art is not an accessory. It is a meeting point between a person and a space, and this is what that looks like. The piece is not there because it matched the stools. It is there because it says who the client is when the door opens.

### How the work is structured

Seven steps, the same for a single wall or a whole apartment: discovery, research, curatorial development, budget planning, art procurement and selection, logistics, installation. You see a shortlist, not a flood. I assess market value and negotiate on your behalf, and because I carry none of a gallery's costs, in most cases the art itself costs less than the price on a gallery wall.

On cost: in most cases, art bought through me costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry none of the costs that push their prices up, and the price includes private consultation for your apartment until the last work is hung. I represent you, not a roster of artists.

### How to start

Send me one photo of the wall and a line about the room, at stav@stavtheodor.com or through the contact details at the end of this page. If you are building a house rather than finishing an apartment, read when art should come into a new build. If you want to know what hotel and residence work taught me about scale and deadlines, read about art for hotels and hospitality.

A: Usually yes, and your designer will often be the one to suggest it. Designers are responsible for the whole room and rarely have the time or the artist relationships to source art seriously. I work inside their plan, present a shortlist that respects their palette and furniture, and handle sourcing, negotiation, framing and installation. Many of my projects come to me through interior designers and architects on behalf of their clients.

A: It depends on what you are after. A single available work can be selected, framed and installed on a short timeline. A commission follows the artist's schedule and the production time for the piece. A whole apartment moves with the design and construction timeline, which is why I prefer to start while the plans are still open. I set the timeline with you at the discovery stage and keep to it.

Q: What does an art advisor cost for a Manhattan apartment?
A: In most cases, less than the same art would cost at a large auction or through a gallery. Bidding pushes auction prices up, and galleries price with big margins to cover the venue, the inventory and the gallerists; I carry none of those costs. The price includes private consultation for your apartment and my work with you, with your designer, until the art is on the wall. In Manhattan that includes the building side: certificates of insurance, service elevator bookings and working hours, coordinated with your management office before anything is delivered. Looking at your existing art is also the fastest way for me to understand your taste before I propose anything.

### Independent art advisor, gallery 'free advisory', decorator or installer: who do I need for my walls?

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-advisor-vs-consultant-vs-decorator/

The difference is whom each one represents and what each one delivers: a gallery's advisory represents its artists, a decorator designs the room, an installer hangs what you own, and an independent art advisor represents you, the buyer, from choosing the work to hanging it. That is the role I take for homes at THEODORA, alongside your designer when you have one: I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere.

The titles blur. Art advisor, art consultant, curator, gallery advisor, decorator: people use them loosely, and online platforms add their own. So compare the roles instead of the titles. Each of the people below does real work, and sometimes one of them is all you need.

### Who does what?

- Independent art advisor or private curator. Represents the buyer. Searches the whole market, galleries, auctions and artists, assesses value, negotiates on your side and manages framing, delivery and installation.

- Gallery advisory or gallery consultant. Helps you buy from that gallery's program. Often knowledgeable and generous with time, and the service is free because the gallery is selling its artists.

- Online platform advisor. Suggests works from the platform's inventory, usually remotely.

- Interior designer or decorator. Designs the room: layout, finishes, furniture, lighting. May place art as part of the scheme, and many bring in an art advisor for the art itself.

- Art installer or handler. Hangs and moves art safely, often with a good eye for placement. Does not choose or buy the work.

### Are the free advisory services from galleries unbiased?

They can be very helpful, and galleries do their job well. That job is to represent their artists and get them the best price possible; it is the essence of a gallery. So a gallery advisor will, reasonably, show you the gallery's program first. An online platform will show you its own stock.

An independent advisor has a different job. I represent the client. I have no closed roster and I am not obligated to any set of artists, so I can reach out to any artist or gallery in the world. I still buy from galleries often, and when the right work is there I negotiate on your behalf. In most cases buying through a private curator costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry none of the venue, inventory and staff costs a gallery has to cover.

### When is a decorator or an installer enough?

If you already own the art and simply need it placed and hung well, an experienced installer may be all you need. If your designer is choosing a few decorative pieces as part of a finished scheme, that can be enough too.

An advisor is worth adding when you need to decide what to buy, when the art is a meaningful purchase, or when you want one person responsible from the first idea to the last hook. I choose and source the art and install it with my own insured team, so the person who chose the work is there when it goes on the wall.

### How does an advisor work with your designer?

Alongside them, not around them. I read the designer's plans, palette and furniture layout before I propose anything, and I join early when I can, while lighting is still open. The designer keeps the room and the credit; I bring the art. More on this in why bring in an art advisor when your designer is finishing the house.

### Questions to ask anyone you hire

- Whom do you represent: me, or a gallery, a platform or a supplier?

- Can you source outside your own inventory or program?

- Who handles framing, delivery and installation, and is that team insured?

- Can you provide a certificate of insurance for my building, naming the managing agent?

- Will you work within my designer's plan and my budget?

My own answers: I represent you, I source anywhere, my own insured team installs, I can provide a certificate of insurance naming your landlord or managing agent, and I work within your designer's plan and the budget you set. For the finer distinction between an advisor and a consultant, see art advisor or art consultant.

Questions:

Q: Do I need an art advisor or just an interior decorator for my NYC apartment?
A: They do different jobs. A decorator or designer shapes the rooms; an art advisor chooses and buys the art, which is often the most personal and valuable thing in them. If your decorator is placing a few decorative pieces, that may be enough. If you are buying original work that matters to you, add an advisor who works alongside the decorator, not around them.

Q: Should I hire an art advisor or an art installer to help with my walls?
A: It depends on what the walls need. If you already own the art and only need it hung, an experienced installer is the right call, often with a good eye for height and arrangement. If you need to decide what to buy, you need an advisor: knowing the market, assessing value and negotiating. An advisor who installs covers the whole chain; I choose and source the art and install it with my own insured team.

Q: Why would I pay for an advisor when gallery advice is free?
A: Because in most cases you do not pay more. Buying through a private curator usually costs less than buying at a large auction or through a gallery, since I carry none of the venue, inventory and staff costs a gallery prices in. The consultation is included until the art is on the wall, and you get someone who represents you and can look anywhere, not in one program. More on what an art advisor costs.

### Choosing art for a Brooklyn brownstone or townhouse

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-brooklyn-brownstone/

Choose for the house's own architecture: one strong work or a pair for the long parlor wall, a sequence for the stair hall, quieter and more personal work upstairs, and if you are renovating, plan the art before the plaster is closed. Brooklyn is part of my work at THEODORA with private homes across New York City: alongside the architect and the designer, I choose, source and install the art with my own team.

A brownstone or townhouse in Park Slope, Brooklyn Heights, Fort Greene or Carroll Gardens asks different things of art than an apartment does. The rooms are often narrow and tall, the walls are broken by windows, fireplaces and doorways, and the house is read vertically, floor by floor, as much as room by room. Here is how I approach it.

### The parlor floor

The parlor floor is where the house shows itself: high ceilings, long walls between tall windows, often a mantel. The long wall usually wants one strong work or a pair that reads as one, not a scatter of frames. Scale matters more than people expect, because the ceiling height makes average sized works look small. From the sightlines, from the entrance, from the seating, I define the main wall, and it is not always the longest one.

### The stair hall

A stair hall gives you something most apartments never have: a vertical run that people walk past every day. It can hold a sequence, works that follow the rise of the stair, or one tall work seen from below and above. Hanging heights follow the stair, not the floor, and the viewing distance is short, so the work has to reward a close look.

### Upstairs

Bedrooms and a study on the upper floors can be quieter and more personal. There are no fixed rules for which wall gets the strongest work; it depends on the space and on you. What I look at is where you wake up, where you work, and what you want to see when the door closes.

### Old walls, and what they need

Many brownstones still have original plaster, sometimes over brick, and a picture rail in some rooms. Plaster needs the right hardware and a careful team, and a heavy work may be better hung from a rail or planned with support in the wall. My own insured team installs, and the wall is checked before anything is fixed. More in who can hang heavy or large art in a NYC home.

### Renovating? Plan the art before the plaster

If the house is being renovated, bring the art in while the drawings are still open. Picture lighting, power for a lit work, support in the wall for heavy pieces, and which walls stay solid are all far easier to decide on paper than after the walls are finished. I can work from the architect's and designer's plans, and I work alongside them, not around them. Plan the lighting before hanging. The same thinking is on art for a new build, written for houses in New Jersey. Your architect can take the checklist from planning art in construction drawings.

### Art you already own, and art made for the house

Many townhouse owners have lived with their art for years. I start with what you own, decide with you where each piece belongs in the house, and then find what is missing. When nothing on the market fits a wall, a commission is often the answer: a work made for that space and for you, which I manage with the artist from concept to installation. See how to commission an artwork for your home.

### How to start

A conversation about you and the house, then a walk through it in person or through the plans. I propose a short selection for the walls that matter first, then source, negotiate, frame and install. You set the budget and the pace.

Questions:

Q: I'm renovating a Brooklyn brownstone. When should I bring in an art advisor?
A: During the renovation, while the drawings are still open, not after. That is when picture lighting, power for a lit work, support in the wall for heavy pieces and the walls that stay solid can still be planned for the art. I can work from the architect's and designer's plans and work alongside them, so the art is part of the house rather than the last delivery.

Q: Who can help me choose art for my home in Brooklyn?
A: An independent art advisor who works in New York City homes: someone who represents you, sources from the whole market rather than one gallery, and handles framing and installation. I work with homeowners across New York City, Brooklyn included, from one piece for the parlor floor to a whole house, and I can work with the art you already have.

Q: Can heavy art be hung on the plaster walls of a brownstone?
A: Usually yes, with the right hardware and an experienced team. Old plaster, sometimes over brick, behaves differently from modern drywall, so the wall is checked first. For very heavy works, a picture rail or support planned into the wall during a renovation are good options. My own insured team installs and decides on the wall itself, not on a guess. More on hanging heavy or large art in a New York home.

Q: What kind of art suits a townhouse stair hall?
A: Work that rewards a close look and follows the rise of the stair: a sequence of related pieces hung along the rake, or one tall work seen from below and from the landing. The viewing distance is short and the light often comes from a skylight or a single window, so medium and glazing matter. Hanging heights follow the stair, not the floor.

### Art for a home in Israel, managed from New York or New Jersey

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-home-in-israel-from-abroad/

Yes. Homes in Caesarea, Herzliya Pituach, Tel Aviv and Ramat Gan are part of my work at THEODORA: I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, I work in Hebrew and English on both sides, and the homes below show what that looks like on the ground in Israel. Here is how it works when you are here and the house is there.

Distance is not the problem people expect it to be. The problem is usually the opposite: a contractor in Israel finishing on his own schedule, a designer sending photos while you are asleep, and nobody holding the art as one whole. What you need is one person who thinks in both places, speaks both languages, and stays responsible until the last work is on the wall. That is what I do.

I managed a gallery in Tel Aviv, and I trained at Tel Aviv University and Ben-Gurion University, so the Israeli artists and galleries I call are people I have worked with, not names from a search.

### How it works from abroad

- Discovery happens where you are. We meet in New York or New Jersey, in person or on video, in the language you think in. I want to know how you live in the house in Israel, who uses which rooms, what you already own, and what you want to feel when you walk in from the airport.

- Research and curatorial development happen on my side. I work from the plans, the designer's material, and photos of the site. You see a concept for the house and a shortlist per room, with scale shown on your own walls, before anything is bought.

- Sourcing is worldwide, not only local. For homes in Israel I have brought works from France, commissioned an artist in Italy, placed a photograph by a Korean artist, and worked directly with Israeli artists and leading galleries. Where the art comes from follows the story, not the shipping route.

- Logistics and installation happen on site. Shipping, import, framing and hanging are coordinated with the site in Israel. You can be there for the installation, or land to a finished house.

The process is the same seven steps as every project: discovery, research, curatorial development, budget planning, art procurement and selection, logistics, installation. I assess market value and negotiate on your behalf, and because I carry none of a gallery's costs, in most cases the art itself costs less than the gallery price.

### Four homes in Israel

### Caesarea, private estate

For a private collector I sourced large scale artworks from France, with layered pigments and 18k gold detailing. The work involved close collaboration with a leading gallery and price negotiations on the collector's behalf, and my guidance was aligned with both taste and long term investment goals. This is the kind of project where the buyer's location matters least and the advisor's relationships matter most.

 

### Herzliya Pituach, sea view apartment

Near the entrance I placed a large scale painting by Yigal Ozeri depicting an aged, textured window, positioned in dialogue with the sea facing windows. Sculptural elements and organic textures run through the rest of the home. A painted window answering a real one is the kind of decision that only works if someone has stood in the apartment and looked both ways.

### Ramat Gan, private home

After a trip to Korea that had changed something for the client, I found a large format photograph by a Korean artist depicting two figures in ceremonial dress, and placed it at the heart of the living space. The line that stays with me from that project is a short one: it gives it memory. That is the whole point of a home you do not live in year round. The art should hold what the house means to you when you are not in it.

### Caesarea, sea view villa

For a homeowner who had come to Israel as a new immigrant, I commissioned a 3.5 meter triptych from an Italian artist. Three storks stand at its center, symbolizing homecoming, strength and belonging, and echoing both the owner's own journey and the seasonal migration of storks through Israel. A commission of that scale, made abroad for a specific wall in Caesarea, is exactly the kind of work that needs one person managing it end to end.

Floor plans or a site survey, photos of the rooms in daylight, whatever your designer has, and an honest budget range. If you are in the New York area, one meeting in person. If you are traveling to Israel soon, tell me the dates, and I will plan the site visit or the installation around them.

In most cases, art bought through me costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery: bidding pushes auction prices up, galleries price with big margins to cover their costs, and I have none of those costs. The price includes private consultation for your home in Israel and my work with you, while you are abroad, until the art is on the wall. I represent you, not a roster of artists.

Where a work is available to view in New York, we see it together. For commissions, you approve the concept and follow the work through the artist's process.

### Buying art for a new apartment on a set budget: how to make it go further

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-new-apartment-on-a-budget/

Put most of the budget into the one or two walls you see every day, buy fewer and better works, and add over time rather than filling everything at once. At THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor, budget planning comes before I source a single work: you set the budget, I work to it, and in most cases buying through a private curator also makes it go further than a gallery or a large auction in New York.

A set budget is not a limitation to apologize for. It is a brief, and a clear one. The question is not how to spread it thinly across every wall, but where it does the most work. Here is how I think about it with clients buying for a new home.

### Where should most of the budget go?

Into the walls you see every day. In most homes that is the wall the living space turns toward and the wall you see from the entrance or from bed. From the sightlines I define the main wall, and a strong work there changes how the whole apartment feels. A secondary wall can hold something quieter, or wait.

### Fewer and better, then add over time

One work you will still look at in ten years is worth more than five you stop seeing in a month. Buying fewer, better works also leaves room for the collection to grow with you. Plan it in stages: the main walls now, the rest as you learn how you live in the space. The budget becomes a plan across a year or two instead of a single spend.

### Do not forget framing, delivery and installation

The price of the work is not the whole cost. Framing, glazing, delivery and installation follow every purchase, and in a New York building installation may need a certificate of insurance and a booked service elevator. Budget for them from the start, so the frame is chosen for the work rather than for what is left over. Budget planning is its own step in my process, before anything is bought.

### Gallery, auction or artist: where does the budget go furthest?

Each route has tradeoffs. At a large auction, many bidders compete for the same work, and every bid pushes the price up. A gallery carries heavy costs, the venue, the inventory and the gallerists, and prices with big margins to cover them. Buying directly from an artist removes the gallery's margin, but you need to know which artist and what the work should cost.

Because I represent you and not a roster of artists, I can look in all three places. I have a network of artists and makers I work with directly, and when the right work is in a gallery I assess its value and negotiate on your behalf. In most cases buying through a private curator costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I have none of those costs. The consultation is included in that price, until the art is on the wall. More on this in what an art advisor costs and how to buy from a gallery without overpaying.

### Prints, editions or originals?

A limited edition print by an artist you admire can hold a secondary wall well, and a good frame makes a real difference to it. The main wall usually deserves an original or a commissioned work, because that is the piece you will live with most closely. A commission can also be sized exactly to a wall, which sometimes makes it the more sensible choice. I help you decide wall by wall, within the budget you set.

### How to start

Tell me the budget, the home and the walls that matter most. I propose a plan in stages and a short selection for the first walls, then source, negotiate, frame and install. Buying art is also an investment in the home you live in, though no one can promise a work will rise in value.

Questions:

Q: Can I set a budget before working with an art advisor?
A: Yes, and I recommend it. You tell me the budget at the start and I work to it, including framing, delivery and installation, so there are no surprises at the end. A clear budget is a good brief: it tells me where to look and how to divide the spend between the main wall and the rest of the home, now and over time.

Q: Can someone help me buy art at auction for my home?
A: Yes. An advisor can find suitable lots, check condition and history, set a sensible limit and bid for you, which matters because auction prices can climb quickly when several bidders want the same work. I source from auctions as well as galleries and artists, I represent the buyer, and I will tell you when the same money buys more elsewhere.

Q: Is it better to buy one expensive work or several cheaper ones?
A: For the wall you see every day, usually one strong work, chosen for that wall's size and light. Several smaller pieces can work well on secondary walls or as a planned group, but a scatter of small works bought to fill space rarely lasts. I help you decide wall by wall, and plan the rest of the home in stages within the same budget.

### Art for a new build in Bergen County: when it should come in

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-new-build-in-bergen-county/

Bring the art in while the drawings are still open, before the walls are closed and the lighting is fixed, and treat it as part of the architecture rather than the last delivery. I am an art curator and advisor based in Tenafly, and I work with owners, architects and designers in Alpine, Closter, Englewood, Saddle River and the towns around them; here is how the timing works and what it did for a new house in Closter.

The most common thing I see in Bergen County is a beautiful house, finished to the last detail, with art bought in a hurry during the final month because the walls looked bare at the walkthrough. The house deserved better, and so did the owners. The fix is simple: decide early that art is part of the plan, and give it a place in the schedule and the budget from the start.

### The three moments when art comes in

### While the architect is still drawing

This is the moment most people miss, and it is the cheapest one. When walls, ceilings, stairs and the lighting plan are being fixed, a few decisions cost almost nothing: which walls are for art and which are for windows and millwork, where a large work will need support inside the wall, where picture lights or adjustable spots go, whether the stair hall wants one tall piece or a sequence. Made now, these are pencil lines. Made after the drywall, they are an electrician and a patch. The checklist by drawing phase is in planning art in construction drawings.

### When finishes and furniture are chosen

Once the palette is locked and the furniture is selected, I know what the rooms will feel like. This is when I do the research and the curatorial development: a concept for the house as a whole, a shortlist per room, a budget plan you can approve. It is also when commissions start, because an artist making a work for a specific wall needs time, and a new build gives us that time if we use it.

### After the dust has settled

Installation comes last, with the furniture in place, so heights are set to how the rooms are lived in and not to an empty shell. I manage production, framing and installation with printmakers, framers and installers I work with regularly. The work is not complete until every piece is on the wall and you are fully satisfied.

If your house is already finished, it is not too late. There are simply fewer options for lighting and hanging structure, and I work with what is there.

### A new house in Closter

The Closter residence was newly built when I was brought in. The commission was to curate a collection that would strengthen the architectural character of the house and bring depth to the interior design. I worked closely with leading New York City galleries, and the collection brings together works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices. For many families in this part of New Jersey, that mix is not a theme. It is who they are, and the art is where it shows without a word being said.

The result transforms a well designed house into a space with soul, where art and architecture speak the same language.

### Working alongside your architect and designer

I work alongside architects and interior designers, not around them. In a new build that means I read the drawings and put my requests into the same schedule everyone else is working from. The designer keeps the house. I bring the art, and I make sure it lands where the design already made room for it.

I have spent years building art collections for hotels and cruise ships, where the opening date does not move and every piece for every room is produced and installed to it. A house with a move-in date is familiar ground.

The process is the same seven steps on every project: discovery, research, curatorial development, budget planning, art procurement and selection, logistics, installation. You see a shortlist, not a flood. I assess market value and negotiate on your behalf, and because I carry none of a gallery's costs, in most cases the art itself costs less than the price on a gallery wall.

### What it costs

In most cases, art bought through me costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry none of the costs that push their prices up. The price includes private consultation for your new house and my work with you until the last work is hung, and on a new build I would rather see the plans first. I represent you, not a roster of artists.

### Where I work

I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere, Tel Aviv included. Bergen County projects are a short drive, which matters when a site meeting is called on a Tuesday morning. Write to stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page, and send the floor plans if you have them. If your project is an apartment in the city, read what an art advisor does for a Manhattan apartment. If you also own a home in Israel, I handle those from here as well.

Questions:

At that stage I can tell the architect which walls are for art, where large works need support inside the wall, and where the lighting should go, all at almost no cost. Waiting until the house is finished still works, but it removes the cheapest options and shortens the time available for commissions.

Q: Do you work with the architect and interior designer, or separately?
A: With them, always. I read their drawings, palette and furniture plan before I propose anything, and I put my requests for wall support and lighting into the schedule everyone else is already working from. Many of my projects come to me through designers and architects on behalf of their clients. The designer keeps the house; I bring the art that belongs in it.

In the Closter house the collection brought together works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices, so the result reads as a considered collection rather than a themed one. The mix is set by who you are, not by a label.

Q: How much should I budget for art in a new house?
A: There is no fixed ratio, and I would be careful of anyone who gives you one. The budget follows the rooms that matter, the scale of the walls, and whether you want available works, commissions, or a mix. Budget planning is a step in my process: I propose a plan by room, you approve it, and I source within it. In most cases the works themselves cost less through me than at auction or in a gallery, because I carry none of their costs.

Q: Do you serve Alpine, Saddle River and Englewood, or only Tenafly?
A: All of Bergen County, with New York City and Tel Aviv beyond it, and online with clients anywhere. I am based in Tenafly, so Alpine, Closter, Englewood, Saddle River and the neighboring towns are a short drive, and I can be on site when a meeting is called. Send a photo of the wall or the floor plans to stav@stavtheodor.com and I will tell you what I see.

### Art for a new condo in Manhattan or Brooklyn: bare walls, glass and light

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-new-condo-nyc/

In a new condo with floor to ceiling glass, you have fewer walls, so each one matters more: decide which few walls carry the art, choose work and glazing that can live with strong light, and consider sculpture where walls run out. For new development apartments from Manhattan to Brooklyn and Queens, I choose, source and install the art through THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor, in step with the designer's furniture schedule. I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere.

New development apartments look finished on the day you get the keys: clean surfaces, big windows, a view. They are also some of the hardest homes to hang art in. The glass that makes them feel open takes away wall space, open plans leave few solid walls, and the sun is strong for much of the day. In Hudson Yards, the Financial District, Downtown Brooklyn or Long Island City, the questions are the same.

### Which walls carry the art?

With fewer walls, each one matters more. I read the sightlines, from the front door, from the kitchen island, from the sofa and from bed, and define the main wall from them. In many condos the strongest candidates are the entry wall, the wall behind the bed and the one solid wall the living space turns toward. A long corridor can hold a sequence. The rest may be better left calm.

### Standing next to the view

A skyline or river view is the strongest image in the room, and art should not try to compete with it by being louder. It needs presence of a different kind: scale, surface, a color the view does not have. Often the best place for the main work is a wall you see with your back to the windows, so art and view each get their moment.

### Strong light, and what it does to art

Direct sun can fade works on paper, photographs and some pigments over time, and glare can make a glossy surface or glazed frame unreadable at certain hours. Watch how the light moves, keep sensitive works out of direct sun, and choose glazing that filters UV for works under glass. Plan the lighting before hanging, so evening light is as considered as daylight.

### When walls run out: sculpture and objects

When solid walls are scarce, sculpture and three dimensional works can carry a space: on a console in the entry, on a plinth in an open living area, or in a corner where the windows meet. They also read well against glass, from both sides.

### In step with the designer's schedule

New condo owners often work with a designer who is ordering furniture months ahead. If the art is chosen in step with that schedule, the home is finished when the furniture lands, not months later, and the work belongs to the scheme rather than being added after it. I work alongside designers, not around them, and I can work from their plans before the apartment is furnished. More in why bring in an art advisor alongside your designer.

### Walls, rules and installation

New buildings often mean drywall over metal studs or concrete, which need the right hardware for heavy works, and condo boards have rules for contractors: a certificate of insurance, service elevator bookings and set hours. I carry insurance and can provide a certificate naming the managing agent, and my own team installs, after hours when needed. See who can hang heavy or large art in a NYC apartment.

### How to start

A conversation about you and the apartment, the plans or photos, and the designer's schedule if there is one. I propose the few walls that matter and a short selection for them, then source, negotiate, frame and install. You set the budget before I begin.

Questions:

Q: I bought a new condo in Manhattan and the walls are bare. Who helps with art for new development apartments?
A: An independent art advisor, ideally one who works alongside your designer. New development apartments have glass walls, open plans and strong sun, which make art choices harder. I help clients decide which few walls matter, source works that can live with the light, and install them with my own insured team, in step with the designer's furniture schedule.

Q: Will sun damage art in a glass walled apartment?
A: It can. Direct sun fades works on paper, photographs and some pigments over time, and it creates glare on glossy surfaces and glazed frames. Careful placement is the first protection: keep sensitive works out of direct light. Glazing that filters UV helps for works under glass, and some mediums are more robust than others, which is part of choosing the right work for the wall.

Q: Where does art go when an apartment has few solid walls?
A: Start with the walls the sightlines give you: usually the entry wall, the wall behind the bed and the one solid wall the living space faces. A long corridor can hold a sequence. When walls run out, sculpture and three dimensional work on a console, a plinth or in a corner can carry the space, and they read well against glass.

Q: Do you work with condos in Long Island City, Astoria or Brooklyn?
A: Yes. I work with homes across New York City and across the river in Hoboken and Jersey City, and newer apartments in Queens and Brooklyn raise the same questions as those in Manhattan: fewer walls, big windows and a need for scale. I can work from plans and photos before a visit, and my own insured team installs, including in buildings that ask for a certificate of insurance and set working hours.

### Art for a new office in Manhattan: how companies choose, buy and install it

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-new-office-manhattan/

Plan the art together with the fit-out, decide what clients should understand about the company when they walk in, and schedule the installation around the move so work never stops. Through THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor I plan and source art for offices in Manhattan, across New York City and in New Jersey, from a single work for reception to a complete collection, and my own insured team installs it after hours so the office keeps working.

Clients and staff read your walls before anyone speaks. In a new office, the art is one of the few things that says something about judgment and culture rather than about budget. It is also one of the last things companies think about, which is why it so often ends up as whatever fills the space the week before the move. Here is how to do it properly.

### Moving offices: when should the art be planned?

With the fit-out, not after it. When the architect and designer are still drawing, the art can be planned into the space: which walls stay solid, where the picture lights and the power go, what the reception wall must carry, and where heavy works need blocking in the wall. I can work from the architect's and designer's plans, before the space is built. If the office is already finished, I work with what is there. What to mark on the drawings, phase by phase, is in planning art in construction drawings.

### What should the art say?

Start with one question: what should a client understand about you in the first moments after the elevator doors open? Calm and established, precise, creative, international. The art at reception answers it first; the meeting rooms, corridors and private offices follow. The leadership decides how the company should feel and what positioning it projects to clients, and my job is to make the space look strong and confident in that direction. More on this in art for an office, a clinic or a business.

### Where does the art go first?

- Reception. The work visitors remember. One strong piece usually does more than several small ones.

- Meeting rooms. Where clients spend the most time. Work that holds attention without distracting from the conversation.

- Corridors and open areas. A rhythm rather than a series of unrelated frames.

- Private offices. Often chosen with the person who works there.

### Buy, commission or lease?

Companies get office art in three ways. Buying makes the art part of the company and, bought well, it is also an investment, though no one can promise a work will rise in value. Commissioning gives a reception wall or boardroom a work made for that exact space and identity. Leasing programs typically rent works for a set term, which some companies choose for short leases. I help companies choose, buy and commission art for their offices. The routes are compared in buy, lease or commission.

### Install day, without closing the office

Manhattan office buildings have rules for contractors: certificates of insurance, freight elevator bookings, set hours. I carry insurance and can provide a certificate naming the landlord or managing agent, and my team installs after hours so the office keeps working. I manage framing, delivery and installation within the agreed timeline and budget, so the art is on the walls when the team arrives, not months later.

### A small company, not a corporate program

Most companies do not need a corporate art program. A small office often needs a few strong works for reception and the main meeting room, chosen with care, and a plan for the rest over time. The work is sized to the company, and the process is the same: a conversation, research, a short selection, the budget, the purchase, and installation. If you are a law firm, an investment firm or a wealth management office, the law firms page, the investment firms page and the wealth managers page speak to your space directly.

Through THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor, I work with offices and businesses in Manhattan, across New York City and in New Jersey. I can work from the architect's plans, and my own insured team installs after hours.

Q: How do we choose office art that does not look corporate?
