The leadership sets how the office should feel; I find work that says it with confidence, sourcing from galleries and artists or commissioning a piece for a key wall. Personality comes from specific choices, not from quantity.

### Choosing art for an Upper East Side or Upper West Side prewar apartment

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-prewar-apartment-upper-east-side/

Choose work with enough presence for classic proportions, frame it to respect the architecture without copying it, and plan installation around plaster walls and co-op rules. Through THEODORA, my art advisory practice, I help clients in prewar apartments on the Upper East Side and the Upper West Side choose, buy and install art, including new works that sit well with the art they already own.

Prewar apartments on both sides of Central Park were built with pictures in mind. Plaster moldings, real walls between windows, long gallery halls, a proper dining room: they are generous to art in a way most new buildings are not. They are also demanding. Old plaster, co-op boards, service elevators and working hours all shape what can go where, and how it gets there.

### What reads well in a prewar apartment

Classic proportions need works with enough presence to hold a wall between two tall windows or above a mantel. A timid work gets lost among the moldings. That does not mean the art must be traditional. Some of the strongest prewar rooms put contemporary work into the classic frame of the architecture, and the contrast gives both of them life. What matters is scale, and a conversation between the work and the room.

### The gallery hall

Many prewar apartments have a long entrance gallery that runs past the main rooms. It is one of the best walls in New York for art: seen every day, lit from the rooms beside it, and long enough for a sequence. Hang it as one composition rather than a row of separate decisions, and plan its lighting, since these halls are often the darkest part of the apartment.

### Framing that respects the architecture

A frame in a prewar room sits next to moldings, paneling and old doors. It should respect them without copying them: a slim contemporary frame can look deliberate against rich plaster, while an ornate frame that imitates the moldings can look like costume. I choose frames for the work first and the room second, with expert framers.

### Old and new together

Many prewar owners already live with art, sometimes inherited, sometimes collected over years. I start with what you own: which works still belong, which need a different wall or a new frame, and what is missing. New pieces are then chosen to sit well with the old ones, so the apartment reads as one collection rather than two.

### Plaster walls and co-op rules

Prewar plaster needs the right hardware and a careful team, and heavy works may be better hung from a picture rail or with support in the wall. Co-ops usually require a certificate of insurance and set working hours and service elevator bookings. I carry insurance and can provide a certificate naming the managing agent, and my own team installs, after hours when a building requires it. Details are on who can hang heavy or large art in a NYC apartment.

### Light

Prewar apartments often have deep rooms, with strong light at the windows and dim corners behind. From the sightlines I define the main wall of each room, then consider how daylight reaches it and where a picture light is needed. Plan the lighting before hanging.

### How to start

A conversation about you, your apartment and the art you own, then a look at the rooms in person or through plans and photos. I propose a short selection for the walls that matter first, then source, negotiate, frame and install. For more on Manhattan apartments in general, see what to expect from an art advisor for a Manhattan apartment.

Questions:

Q: I need help choosing art for my Upper East Side apartment. Who should I call?
A: An independent art advisor who knows prewar Manhattan buildings: plaster walls, co-op rules and classic rooms change what works. I help clients on the Upper East Side choose, buy and install art, including works that sit well with art they already own. I represent you, not a roster of artists, and my own insured team installs.

Q: Who can help me choose art for a prewar apartment on the Upper West Side?
A: Look for an advisor who understands prewar rooms, the moldings, the plaster and the long gallery halls, and who can install within co-op rules. I work with Manhattan apartments on both sides of the park, choosing works in dialogue with the architecture and managing installation with my own insured team, including the certificate of insurance the building asks for.

Q: Does contemporary art work in a traditional prewar apartment?
A: Often very well. Contemporary work set into the classic frame of prewar architecture can give both a new life, as long as the scale is right and the framing respects the room without imitating it. What matters is the conversation between the work and the space. I can mix older works a client owns with new ones, so the whole apartment reads as one collection.

### Choosing large scale art for a Tribeca, SoHo or West Village loft

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-a-tribeca-or-soho-loft/

Go bigger than feels comfortable, choose work that can hold long walls, high ceilings, brick and hard light, and plan the logistics of a very large piece before you buy it. Downtown lofts in Tribeca, SoHo and the West Village are a brief I take on through THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor: I source and commission the large scale work, and my own insured team manages the whole installation.

A loft gives you what most New York apartments cannot: long walls, high ceilings and room to step back. It also brings cast iron columns, exposed brick, big windows and strong light that can overpower timid work. Here is how I think about art for a loft in Tribeca, SoHo or the West Village.

### Scale is the first decision

The most common mistake in a loft is art that is simply too small. A work that would dominate a bedroom disappears on a 30 foot wall under a high ceiling. Before anything is bought, the size is tested against the wall and the distance you will see it from. Often the answer is one very large work, a pair, or a triptych that reads as one image across the wall.

Very large work is something I have managed before. For a sea view villa in Caesarea, the answer to one long wall was a 3.5 meter triptych commissioned from an Italian artist, three storks at its center, made for that wall and that family's story. See the triptych project.

### Brick, columns and windows

Exposed brick is a strong background with its own texture and color; work that fights it looks nervous, work that contrasts with it cleanly, in scale, color or surface, looks deliberate. Columns break a long space into bays, and each bay can be treated as its own wall. Big windows mean hard light at certain hours, so glazing, finish and placement are chosen with the light in mind. Plan the lighting before hanging.

### From the sightlines

An open loft has few doors and many views. From the entrance, the kitchen and the seating I read the sightlines and define the main wall, which is rarely the biggest one. The rest of the space is planned from there, so the works relate to each other across the room rather than competing.

### When nothing fits the wall, commission

When nothing on the market is right for a very long or very tall wall, a commission is often the answer: a work created for that space and identity. I work directly with a wide network of artists, and I manage a commission from the first concept to the final installation. More in how to commission an artwork for your home.

### Logistics: getting it upstairs

Downtown buildings have freight elevators of fixed size, stairs that turn, and rules for contractors. A very large work has to be planned around them from the start: whether it travels crated, in panels, or is planned differently. I carry insurance, can provide the certificate of insurance many buildings require, and my team installs, after hours when needed. The chain is described on framing, shipping and installing large scale art.

### Downtown galleries, on foot

Tribeca and SoHo are among the densest gallery neighborhoods in New York, and some clients like to see work in person. My Art Radar covers shows there, for example a September gallery walk in Tribeca. When we find the right work in a gallery, I negotiate on your side; I represent you, not a roster of artists.

Questions:

Q: I need art for my Tribeca loft. Who can help me pick large pieces?
A: A loft needs someone who can judge scale and handle big logistics: very large works, freight elevators and crating. I source and commission large scale work for homes in downtown Manhattan and manage the whole installation with my own insured team. One of my projects is a 3.5 meter triptych commissioned from an Italian artist for a single long wall.

Q: How big should art be on a loft wall?
A: Usually bigger than you think. High ceilings and long walls make average sized works look small, so the size is tested against the wall and the viewing distance before anything is bought. Often the right answer is one very large work, a pair, or a triptych that reads as one image. Columns can divide a long wall into bays, each treated as its own wall.

Q: Will a very large work fit through my freight elevator?
A: It has to be planned, not hoped for. The elevator, the doors and the turns on the way are measured early, before the work is bought or commissioned. A large work can travel crated, be made in panels, or be planned differently from the start. I coordinate the building's rules, the certificate of insurance and the freight elevator booking, and my own team installs.

Q: Do you work with West Village and Greenwich Village townhouses too?
A: Yes. A West Village townhouse is a different brief from a loft: narrower rooms, stairs, period details and shorter viewing distances. I work with private homes across Manhattan and New York City, choosing, sourcing, framing and installing, and the same principles apply: define the main wall from the sightlines, choose for the light, and plan the logistics before the purchase.

### Corporate art consultant for offices and businesses: six steps from choosing the art to installing it

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-an-office-or-business/

Art in an office works when you decide first what a client should understand about you in the ten seconds before you speak, then choose fewer, larger works that say it, and plan where they hang and how they are lit before they arrive. A corporate art consultant runs that path for a company; here it is in six steps: choose, plan, buy, hang, light and install, each linked to the guide that covers it in full.

Most offices get their art the way they get their carpet: something has to be there, it should not offend anyone, and the designer will handle it. The result is the office art you see in every waiting room, chosen so nobody objects, so nobody looks. The work on your wall speaks before you do.

For a specific kind of office, see art for law firms, art for investment firms and family offices, art for wealth management offices and art for medical and aesthetic practices. For every office, the path is the same.

### 1. Choose: what should the art in your office say?

Start with who you really are, not the brand book: what you love, where you come from, how the day should feel. Then choose for who walks in: calm for patients, steadiness for a firm's clients. Give each area one job: welcome at reception, focus in the meeting space, rhythm along the corridor, something personal in your own office. Office wall art, area by area takes each space in turn; law office decor, financial advisor offices, medical offices and dental practices go deeper by profession.

 

### 2. Plan: decide the art walls while the drawings are open

If you are building out or moving, the art belongs in the drawings. Decide which walls stay solid for art, where blocking goes behind heavy works, and where picture lights and outlets go. A wall decided early leaves time for a commission; a wall decided the week before the move gets whatever is in stock. I can work from your architect's and designer's plans. Planning art in construction drawings shows what to draw on every art wall, and how I work with your interior designer explains who does what. Designers can compare the four routes to sourcing art.

 

### 3. Buy: fewer, larger, better

One strong work in the room where decisions are made says more than ten small ones in the corridor. Prints suit the back office, signed editions suit a corridor series, and reception and the meeting space deserve originals or a work commissioned for the wall. Buying, commissioning or leasing office art compares the routes in relative terms, and ten questions before you buy covers the first serious purchase. In most cases the art costs less through me than at a gallery or a large auction, my consultation is part of that price, and I represent you, not a roster of artists (see what an art advisor costs).

 

### 4. Hang: the height, the size and the spacing

On a wall people pass standing, the center of the work sits 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor; how to hang pictures gives the nail formula and the hardware by weight. A reception anchor takes about two thirds of its wall. In the meeting space everyone sits, so the work goes on the wall the chairs face, never the screen wall, and hangs lower; test the height from a chair with a paper template before anyone drills. A corridor series shares one centerline with equal gaps, as in gallery wall layouts, and a big wall gets one decision, sized with large wall art ideas.

 

### 5. Light: plan it before the work arrives

Aim a ceiling spot or track at the center of the work at about 30 degrees from vertical, with a warm white bulb of 2700 to 3000 K and a color rendering index of 90 or more. On an office ceiling grid, take the line nearest that setback, usually the first from the wall, and give the art its own circuit. How to light art covers glare on glass and which works a bright open office can take.

 

### 6. Install: after hours, so the office keeps working

I manage production, framing and installation with my own installation team; I carry insurance and can provide a certificate of insurance naming your landlord or managing agent, and I install after hours. Framing and installing large scale art walks through each stage. If your company is moving to a new office in Manhattan, art for a new office in Manhattan times the steps to the move.

### A home office in Caesarea: horses and music

A client with a home office in a luxury residence in Caesarea had two loves, horses and music, and those two words were the brief. I looked for artists living and working in the client's country of origin, acquired one existing painting and commissioned a second work from the same artist (see the Caesarea home office). That is the test in any workplace: the art should be true, and it should be yours.

 

### Who runs the path: a corporate art consultant

A corporate art consultant takes a company through all six steps. I am Stav Theodor, art curator and advisor, founder of THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor in Tenafly, New Jersey, with more than 15 years in the art world, including art concepts for Waldorf Astoria Chengdu, St. Regis Amman and Holland America Line. You approve the direction and the works; I manage everything in between, and the job is done when the work is on the wall and you are fully satisfied. I work with businesses across New Jersey and New York City, and online anywhere. Write to me with photos of the space and a sentence about what you do.

Questions:

Q: How many artworks does a small office need?
A: Fewer than you think. One strong work in the room where clients sit, a piece in reception that sets the tone, and something personal in your own office is usually enough for a small firm or clinic. Corridors can carry a coherent series later. Fewer, larger and better made works read as confidence. Many small pieces read as filler.

Q: In what order should a company plan art for its office?
A: Choose, plan, buy, hang, light, install. Decide first what clients should read on your walls, and give each area one job. Mark the art walls in the drawings while they are open, with blocking and lighting. Buy fewer, larger works, with an original or a commission for reception. Hang standing walls with the center at 57 to 60 inches and seated walls lower. Aim the light at about 30 degrees. Install after hours, so work never stops.

Q: What art should I put in a home office?
A: The most personal work in the house. A home office is seen on video calls and by the occasional visitor, so it still speaks for you, but you are choosing mainly for yourself. In a Caesarea home office I placed two works reflecting the client's two loves, horses and music, one acquired and one commissioned from the same artist. Start from what you love, not from what looks professional.

Q: How do I choose art for a reception area?
A: Choose one anchor work sized to hold the wall from the door, rather than several small pieces. It should say something true about the people behind the desk: restraint for a firm, warmth for a clinic, energy for a studio. Plan the lighting for it before it arrives. A commissioned work is often the best answer for a reception, because it is made for that wall and cannot be seen anywhere else.

Q: Is there an art advisor for offices in New York or New Jersey?
A: Yes. I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work with businesses in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere, with projects in Tel Aviv and across Israel and hospitality work abroad. For a business space I start with photos, plans and a conversation about what you do, and much of the research and selection happens before a site visit.

Q: What does a corporate art consultant do?
A: A corporate art consultant plans, sources and installs art for a company's spaces. The work runs from a short concept drawn from the space and the brand, through works proposed within an approved budget, to framing, delivery, installation and a record of what was bought. I represent the company, not a roster of artists, so I can look for the right work anywhere. In most cases the company also pays less than it would at a gallery or an auction, and my consultation is part of that price.

### Art for hotels and hospitality: how it works, and what it means for a private home

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/art-for-hotels-and-hospitality/

Hospitality art is built from a concept, an artwork schedule and an approved budget, area by area, with every piece for every space produced, framed and installed to an opening date that does not move. I did this work for Waldorf Astoria Chengdu, St. Regis Amman, Holland America Line and Costa, and it is the same discipline I bring to a single wall in a private home.

A hotel does not buy art the way a person does. It buys a story, told across a lobby, a bar, a restaurant, hundreds of guest rooms and sometimes a wing of private residences, and it needs that story delivered by a date printed on the marketing. For years I built artistic concepts and contemporary art collections for luxury hospitality groups, on land and at sea. Here is how the work is actually made, and why it matters if you are a private client with one apartment. If you are opening or renovating a property, the service itself is on art for boutique hotels, and for a dining room, art for restaurants.

### How hotel art is actually made

### Concept

Everything starts with a narrative rooted in the place and the brand: what this building is, where it stands, who walks through it. The concept is written, presented and approved by the owner, the operator and the design team before a single work is sourced. At the St. Regis Amman, that thread runs from the horse mosaic in the bar through the guest rooms and the residences. In the Waldorf Astoria Chengdu lobby it took the form of sculptural works.

### The artwork schedule

Every area of the property gets a line: public areas, restaurants, corridors, guest room types, suites, residences. For each line, what kind of work (original, commission, edition), what size, what budget. This document is where art stops being a wish and becomes a plan that a project manager can track.

### Sourcing and commissions

Signature spaces get commissions and original works, often from artists connected to the place. Repeated spaces get editions and series that hold quality at volume. This is where the network matters: artists and makers in several countries, access to exclusive works, and in most cases a better price than a gallery or an auction, because there is no gallery margin or bidding war on top.

### Production

Printmakers, framers and materials chosen for spaces that will be used hard for years, all managed within defined timelines and approved budgets. On a ship, the work must be made for the sea. For Holland America Line I worked on restaurant and stateroom art. I have also worked with Costa Cruises. A vessel leaves the shipyard whether the art is ready or not, so it is ready.

### Logistics and installation

Shipping to a site in China or Jordan, or to a shipyard, then installation crews working alongside the fit out. The job is not finished when the crates arrive. It is finished when every piece is on the wall, lit, and signed off.

### Who I have done this for

- Waldorf Astoria Chengdu, China. Lobby, sculptural works.

- St. Regis Amman, Jordan. The bar with its horse mosaic, the guest rooms, and the residences.

- Holland America Line. Restaurant and stateroom art on the ships.

- Costa Cruises.

Other names on my client and partner list include Four Seasons, Rosewood Hotels and Resorts, The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, Accor, Carnival, Guesty, Eagle Hills and Mandarin.

 

### What this means for a private client

When you hire me for a home, you get the hotel discipline without the hotel. In practice:

- Scale does not worry me. A 3.5 meter triptych commissioned from an Italian artist for a villa in Caesarea is work I know how to run, not a special event.

- Budgets and timelines are managed, not hoped for. You approve a budget plan and a schedule, and I deliver inside them. That is a habit formed by opening dates.

- The network is already built. Artists and makers across several countries, and the printmakers, framers and installers I work with regularly, and in most cases no gallery margin on top of the price.

- Your home gets a concept too. A bar in a Manhattan apartment got a work that references Manet's "Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère". That is hotel thinking, applied to one wall and one person's love of entertaining.

- Nothing is finished until it is installed. The same rule on a ship and in a living room.

### How do I commission an artwork made for my new home?

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/commissioning-art-for-a-new-home/

You commission a work for a new home by briefing an artist who is right for the space, agreeing the concept, size, budget and timeline up front, and then approving the work at each stage until it is installed. How long it takes depends on the artist, the scale and the technique, so I fix the timeline with the artist at the start rather than guess it here.

A commission is the only purchase where, on the day you say yes, the work does not exist. That is its risk, and its whole point: nothing on the market was made for your wall, your light and your story. So the process matters more than the shopping, and here it is.

### When a commission is the right answer
When the wall is unusual: very wide, very tall, a stairwell, a foyer that needs a pair. When the story is personal and nothing on the market says it. When you want a specific artist and their existing works are the wrong size or already gone. Artworks created with a specific space and identity in mind carry deeper meaning, greater value, and a presence that cannot be replicated. And when a commission is not the answer: if a work you love already exists and fits the wall, buy it. I will say so.

### From "I want to commission art for my home" to the work on the wall
It moves in stages, from the brief to the installation, with full transparency at each one.

- The brief. Discovery first: the room, the plans if the house is not finished, the light, how you live, and the thing you want the work to hold. In a sea view villa in Caesarea, the homeowner had come to Israel as a new immigrant. That fact became the brief.
- The artist. I propose artists from my network whose language fits the brief, with examples of their existing work and my reason for each name. You choose the hand.
- Concept and agreement. The artist responds to the brief with a concept, usually with sketches or studies. We fix the dimensions, materials, price, delivery, and the points at which you see the work in progress. Everything is agreed before the first brushstroke, and managed within the approved budget and the defined timeline.
- Making. The artist works. I stay close, you see progress at the agreed points, and small course corrections happen here, where they are still easy.
- Production, framing and shipping. For a triptych or a large canvas, this stage needs planning: crating, transport, the route into the house, the structure of the wall. On a new build, I coordinate this with the architect and the contractor while the walls are still open.
- Installation. Professional installers, managed by me to the end. The work is not complete until it hangs and you are fully satisfied.

### Two commissions, two very different briefs
In the Caesarea sea view villa, the result is a 3.5 meter triptych by an Italian artist. Three storks at its center stand for homecoming, strength and belonging, echoing the homeowner's journey as a new immigrant and the seasonal migration of storks through Israel. Nobody could have bought this. It had to be made.
 In a private residence in Tel Aviv, the brief came from a television series. The client loved the intimate imagery of Shtisel, so I commissioned the artist whose paintings appeared in the series. The work: a mother caressing her baby, rendered with quiet warmth. A modest subject, a precise match.
And in a home office in Caesarea, the two routes met. The client's two loves are horses and music, the artists live and work in the client's country of origin, and of the two works one existing painting was acquired and the second was specially commissioned from the same artist. Buying and commissioning are not opposites. They are two tools, and the brief decides which one to pick up.

### How long does it take?
It depends, and I will not give you a number I cannot stand behind. What sets the timeline: the artist's technique and calendar, the scale of the work, whether it needs special production, and how far it has to travel. What I can promise is that the timeline is set with the artist before we start, that you will know the stages and when you will see progress, and that on a new home I plan the commission alongside the construction schedule so the work is ready when the house is. The earlier you bring me in, the more of the house can be designed around the work rather than the other way round.
A commission is one route among several. For the full seven step engagement, read how the art advisory process works. For what it costs to work with me, read what an art advisor costs.
If you are building or renovating now, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com with the plans and the wall you keep thinking about. That is where a commission starts.

By the time the work is finished, you have already seen and approved the idea, the direction and the progress. What remains is the pleasure of seeing it on the wall.

### Framing, shipping and installing large scale art: how it works and who manages it

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/framing-and-installing-large-scale-art/

Large works are produced, framed, crated, shipped and hung by a chain of specialists, printmakers, framers, art handlers and installers, and one person has to manage that chain against a timeline and a budget. For the works I place at THEODORA, managing that chain is part of my service: I run every stage from the artist's studio to the moment the work is level on your wall, and the job is not complete until it is installed and you are fully satisfied.

The work you fell in love with in a studio in Italy has to survive the journey to your living room. Most of what can go wrong with art happens on that journey, not in the choosing: a canvas rolled the wrong way, a frame that fights the work, a crate that does not fit the stairwell, a wall that cannot take the weight. At THEODORA, production, framing and installation are part of how I work for the works I place, and I treat them as seriously as the selection.

### Production

Not every large work arrives finished. Editioned photographs and digital works are produced to order, and how they are produced changes the result: paper or acrylic, matte or gloss, mounted or floating. For a Bauhaus residence in Tel Aviv, a hyper collage digital artwork was printed on glossy anti reflective acrylic to become the central focal point of the home. Gloss gives a print depth, and an anti reflective surface keeps the reflections of nearby windows off it. I work with expert printmakers. Whoever produces your print, ask to see a proof first and check it against the artist's intention.

Commissioned works are followed from initial concept to final execution, with full transparency at each stage, so that there are no surprises when the crate opens.

### Framing

A frame should serve the work, not compete with it. For a garden villa in Caesarea, two large scale portraits of women with rich layered texture face the front door in slim contemporary framing, so that the surface stays the subject. A large painting does not have to be framed: large canvases are often float framed, or left unframed on a deep stretcher. Works on paper, and photographs printed on paper, need glazing, and the choice of glass changes how a work reads under your lighting. For them, ask for conservation materials: acid free mats, UV filtering glazing and reversible mounting, which can be undone without harming the work.

I work with expert framers. Whoever frames your work, give them the measurements of the wall, not only of the work, and agree the frame before it is made.

### Shipping and crating

Works I have placed came from France, in close collaboration with a leading gallery, from a commission with an Italian artist, and from New York City galleries. Logistics is one of the steps of every project. Plan each shipment the same way: a custom crate for the work, professional art handlers at both ends, and a clear answer, in writing, to who is responsible for the work at each stage of the journey. Very large canvases can sometimes travel rolled and be restretched on site, which is common practice in the industry and avoids a crate that will not fit through the door. That decision is made with the artist, never without.

### Installation

Before install day, the site is surveyed: wall construction, weight, height, sightlines from the doorway and from the seating, the lighting already in place. Then the installers arrive with the right hanging hardware for the wall and the work. Hanging height, spacing and level are set to my brief, and the work is checked before the installers leave. If it does not sit correctly, it is not finished. Building rules in New York (the certificate of insurance, the service elevator, the working hours) are covered in who can hang heavy art in a New York apartment.

### A 3.5 meter triptych in Caesarea

For a sea view villa in Caesarea, I commissioned a 3.5 meter triptych from an Italian artist. Three storks at the center symbolize homecoming, strength and belonging, echoing the homeowner's own journey as a new immigrant and the seasonal migration of storks through Israel. Three panels of that size have to be produced, shipped and installed as one image: the gaps between them are part of the composition, and a few millimeters of drift would show from across the room. It hangs on a double height wall, lit from above, and every stage was managed within a defined timeline and an approved budget.

 

### Who manages framing, delivery and installation?

I do, for the works I place. You have one point of contact from the moment a work is chosen until it is on the wall, and every stage (production, framing, transport and installation) runs within a defined timeline and an approved budget. The printmakers, framers and installers work to my brief and my timeline, and the work is not complete until it is installed and you are fully satisfied. If your interior designer is running the project, I coordinate directly with them so the works arrive when the walls are ready; see how I work with interior designers.

If you have a wall waiting for a large work, or a work you are about to buy, write to me with the dimensions and a photo of the space. For the full picture of a project from concept to installation, read how the process works.

Questions:

Q: How do you hang a very large or heavy painting safely?
A: With a site survey first: what the wall is made of, what it can carry, where the studs or the concrete are, and where the work sits in the sightlines. Then professional installers use hardware rated for the weight, often a cleat system that spreads the load across the wall, and the work is leveled and checked against the brief before they leave.

Q: Can a 3 meter artwork get into an apartment with a small elevator?
A: Usually, with planning. Some large canvases can travel rolled and be restretched on site, which is common practice in the industry, and some works are made as panels, like a triptych, and joined on the wall. The decision is made with the artist before shipping, never on the sidewalk. Measure the route first.

Q: Do you frame digital art and photographs?
A: Yes, when they are works I place. Digital works and photographs are produced to order, and how they are printed and finished is part of the artwork: paper or acrylic, matte or gloss, mounted or floating, framed or edgeless. For one Tel Aviv residence a digital collage was printed on glossy anti reflective acrylic. I decide this with the artist and the client.

Q: Who is responsible if a work is damaged in transit?
A: Responsibility for a work in transit has to be set in writing before the work moves, and part of my job is making sure it is: who packs, who carries, who is responsible at each stage of the journey. Professional art handlers, a custom crate and clear terms prevent most problems. Ask any advisor or gallery this question before you pay.

Q: Do I need special lighting for a large artwork?
A: Often, and it is best planned before the work arrives. Direct sun and harsh downlights can damage some materials and flatten others, and a large work usually wants even light across its full surface. I look at the existing lighting when I survey the space and advise on what to change. Plan any new fixtures with your designer or electrician; where the light goes and which bulb to use are in how to light art.

Q: Where can I get art framed properly in Manhattan?
A: At a framer who works to conservation standards: ask for conservation framing, with acid free mats, UV filtering glazing and reversible mounting, and a frame chosen for the work first and the space second. Then ask who delivers and hangs the framed work, because framing is only one link in the chain. For the works I place, framing is part of my service: I work with expert framers, and my own team installs the work.

### Who can hang heavy or large art in a NYC apartment? Building rules, COI and after hours installs

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/hanging-heavy-art-nyc-apartment-coi/

Hire a professional art installer, or an art advisor who installs, rather than a general handyman, especially for heavy works, plaster walls or anything that must go up a service elevator. At THEODORA, the art I choose for New York City apartments is installed by my own insured team: I can provide the certificate of insurance your building asks for, naming the landlord or managing agent, and my team installs after hours when needed.

A large mirror or a small framed print is a job for anyone with a level. A heavy canvas, a framed work under glass the width of a sofa, or a triptych is not. The wall has to hold it, the building has to let it in, and the people carrying it need to know how art behaves. Here is what matters in a New York apartment, and how I handle it.

### Why not a general handyman?

Art installers do one thing: move and hang works of art safely. They know how to handle a canvas without touching the surface, how to carry glazed frames, and which hardware suits the wall and the weight. A handyman may be skilled, but a heavy work on the wrong fixing, or a corner knocked in a narrow hallway, is an expensive lesson. New York walls vary a great deal, from old plaster in a prewar building to drywall over metal studs and concrete in newer towers, and each needs a different approach.

### What does my building require?

Most Manhattan and Brooklyn buildings with a managing agent have rules for contractors, and art installers count. Typical requirements:

- A certificate of insurance. Proof that the installer carries insurance, often naming the building, the landlord or the managing agent.

- A service elevator booking. Large works cannot use the passenger elevator in many buildings, and the service elevator has fixed hours and dimensions.

- Working hours. Many buildings allow work only on weekdays, within set hours.

Ask your building for its requirements before a large work is delivered. I carry insurance and can provide a certificate of insurance naming the landlord or managing agent on request, and I plan the install around the building's rules, so nothing arrives that cannot get upstairs.

### Before install day

- Know the wall. What it is made of and what is behind it, so the right hardware is chosen.

- Measure the route. The service elevator, the doors, the turns in the hallway. A very large work may need to travel crated or be planned differently from the start.

- Agree the exact positions. Heights and centers decided in advance, with the lighting in mind. Plan the lighting before hanging, not after.

- Protect the floors and furniture. A good team brings what it needs.

### After hours installs

When a building, a household or an office needs it, my team installs after hours, so life and work carry on. For offices this is often the only sensible way to install; in apartments it can mean fitting around a building's schedule or a family's routine.

### One person from choice to wall

I choose and source the art and install it with my own team, so the person who chose the work is there when it goes on the wall. I work with expert framers and printmakers, and I manage the whole chain, production, framing, crating, shipping and installation, within agreed timelines and budgets. The details of that chain are on framing, shipping and installing large scale art. If you already own the art and only need it hung, a professional art installer is the right call; installation is part of my work for the works I choose and place.

Questions:

Q: I need someone to choose the art for my apartment and also hang it. Who does both?
A: An art advisor who also installs covers both, so the person who chose the work is there when it goes on the wall. I choose and source the art and install it with my own insured team, including a certificate of insurance for your building and after hours work when needed. One person is responsible from the first idea to the last hook.

Q: My building requires a certificate of insurance to hang art. Who can provide one?
A: Many New York buildings require a certificate of insurance before any installation, from art installers as from any contractor. I carry insurance and can provide a certificate of insurance, naming the landlord or managing agent on request. Send me your building's requirements early, together with the service elevator hours, and I plan the install around them.

Q: Can heavy art go on a plaster wall in a prewar apartment?
A: Usually yes, with the right hardware and an experienced team. Old plaster behaves differently from drywall, and what sits behind it matters, so the wall is checked before anything is fixed. For very heavy works there are other options, such as a hanging system from the picture rail or ceiling where the building allows it. My team decides on the wall, not on a guess.

Q: Do you install after hours?
A: Yes, when a building, an office or a household needs it. Many New York buildings restrict working hours, and offices, practices and restaurants usually cannot stop for an install. My team works after hours so the space keeps running, and I coordinate the service elevator, the certificate of insurance and the exact positions in advance so the install itself is quick.

### I need someone to help me choose art for my home in New York. Who do I call?

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/help-choosing-art-for-my-home-nyc/

Call an independent art advisor, a curator who represents you rather than a gallery's artists and stays with the project until the work is on your wall. I am Stav Theodor, the founder of THEODORA, and I do exactly this for homes across New York City: I read the rooms and the light, bring you a short, edited selection from any gallery, auction or artist, negotiate on your side, and manage framing and installation.

Most people who ask this are not looking for a shop. They want a person with a trained eye who will listen, look at the home and take the decisions off their plate. That person is an independent art advisor, sometimes called a private art curator. Below is what that person does, how to tell the options apart, and how the first steps work with me.

### What does an art advisor do for a New York home?

An art advisor decides with you what to buy, finds it across the whole market, negotiates on your side and manages everything until it hangs. I have spent more than 15 years in the art world: curatorial work in museums, managing a gallery in Tel Aviv earlier in my career, and working closely with emerging and established artists. That is the background I bring to a New York apartment or townhouse.

- I listen first. Who comes over, where you sit in the evening, what you already own and what you never want to see again.

- I read the space. The light and how it moves, the sightlines from the door and the sofa, and the building's rules. From the sightlines I define the main wall, which is rarely the biggest one. I can work in person or from your designer's plans.

- I bring a short selection, not a catalog. A few works chosen for your walls, with the reasoning behind each.

- I handle the rest. Negotiation, framing with expert framers, delivery and installation with my own insured team.

### Who else could I call, and what is the difference?

Several people can put art on your walls, and each is an honest choice. A gallery's advisory service shows you its own artists, which is its job. An online platform suggests works from its inventory. A decorator or designer shapes the whole room and may place art as part of it. An installer hangs what you already own. The question that separates them is whom they represent.

I represent the client. I have no closed roster and I am not obligated to any set of artists, so I can reach out to any gallery, auction house or artist in the world. When there is a designer on the project, I work alongside them, not around them: the designer keeps the room, I bring the art.

### What does it cost to work with an advisor?

In most cases, buying through a private curator costs less than buying at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction, many bidders push the price up. A gallery carries the venue, the inventory and its staff, and prices with big margins to cover them. I have none of those costs. The price includes private, tailored consultation for your own home, and I stay with you until the art is on the wall. The full answer is on what an art advisor costs.

### How long does it take?

It depends on the scope. One anchor work for a living room moves faster than a whole apartment, and a commission follows the artist's timeline, which I fix with the artist at the start. You decide the pace and the budget before we begin, and I work to both. The steps are the same each time, from discovery to installation; they are set out on how the art advisory process works.

### How do I start?

Write to me with a line about the home and, if you can, a photo of the wall you look at most. From there we talk, I look at the space, and I come back with a first direction. I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere. If you are in Manhattan, what to expect from an art advisor for a Manhattan apartment goes deeper into buildings, light and working with your designer, and my New York page covers apartments, offices and collections.

Q: How do I find the right art for my home without spending months looking?
A: Narrow the search before you start it. Decide which one or two walls matter most, measure them, and note the light and what you already own; then look only for works that fit those walls. The fastest route is to hand the search to an advisor: I bring you a short, edited selection for those walls from galleries, auctions and artists, so you choose from a few works instead of hundreds.

### How does the art advisory process work, step by step?

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/how-the-art-advisory-process-works/

My art advisory process runs in seven steps: discovery, research, curatorial development, budget planning, art procurement and selection, logistics, and installation. It starts with a conversation about you and the space, and it ends when the work is on the wall and you are fully satisfied.

Most people who write to me have never hired an art advisor. They want to know two things: what happens, and where they get to say no. Here is the whole process in the order it actually happens. Three of the seven steps end with a decision that is yours alone: the direction, the range, and the works themselves.

### The seven steps

- Discovery. We meet, ideally in the space, or on a call with photos and plans if the house is still being built. I ask how you live, what you already own, what you love and what you cannot stand. In one Caesarea home office, discovery came down to two loves, horses and music, and both are on the wall now. If an architect or interior designer is involved, they are in the room. I work alongside them, not around them.
- Research. I go back to my desk with the plans and the conversation, and I look: the artists I work with directly, leading New York City galleries, galleries in Tel Aviv and further afield, works available now, and artists who could make something for the space. In a Manhattan apartment, the client's love of entertaining guided everything, and the research led to a large format digital collage that draws on the visual language of glamorous social gatherings, with a reference to Manet's “Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère”. It now anchors the apartment's custom bar.
- Curatorial development. This is where the collection gets its logic. Which wall carries the anchor, how the works talk to each other and to the architecture, where a commission makes more sense than a purchase. Sometimes the logic is one work, not many: in an open, light saturated villa in Hod Hasharon, where concrete and nature meet, a single large scale figurative digital artwork defines the emotional center of the space. You receive a proposal you can see, with options, not a list of names. The direction is the first decision that is yours.
- Budget planning. Before anything is sourced, we agree the range: for the art, and for framing, production, shipping and installation. The range is yours to set, and I build inside it. Everything that follows is managed within approved budgets and defined timelines.
- Art procurement and selection. I bring you the works, in person where possible, on screen where not. I assess market value, negotiate on your behalf, and manage every step with care, discretion and precision. You choose. My job is to make sure you are choosing between right answers.
- Logistics. Shipping, including across borders, crating, framing with expert framers, printing with expert printmakers where the work calls for it, and the coordination between the framer, the installer and your contractor. The photo at the top of this page is this step: a work sourced from France arriving at the front door of a private estate in Caesarea. Building collections for hotels and cruise ships, from a hotel lobby in Chengdu to staterooms on Holland America Line ships, taught me this step. A private home gets the same discipline, and you do not have to chase anyone.
- Installation. Professional art installers hang the work, and I manage the hanging to the end. Height, lighting, the relationship to the furniture and the windows: this is the last chance to get it right, and it matters as much as the choice. In a sea view apartment in Herzliya Pituach, a large scale painting by Yigal Ozeri of an aged, textured window was positioned near the entrance so that it speaks to the sea facing windows. Where a work hangs is part of the work. It is not complete until it is installed and you are fully satisfied.

### What it looks like in a real house
In Closter, New Jersey, I was commissioned to curate a collection for a newly built private residence, to strengthen the architectural character of the house and bring depth to the interior design. Working closely with leading New York City galleries, I brought together works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices. The result turns a well designed house into a space with soul, where art and architecture speak the same language.
In Ramat Gan, discovery was the whole story. The client had returned from a transformative trip to Korea. The research led to a large format photograph by a Korean artist, two figures in ceremonial dress, and it now sits at the heart of the living space. It gives it memory.

### How long it takes, and what you need to bring
It depends on the scope. An existing work for one wall moves faster than a commission or a collection for a house under construction, and I set the timeline with you at the budget planning step rather than promise one here. What you need to bring is small: photos or plans of the space, an honest sense of your range, and the names of anyone else involved in the home.
If you want to know what it costs, I have written about why art usually costs less through a private curator. If your home is not built yet, read about commissioning art for a new home.
If you are ready to start, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com. Discovery begins with your first message.

Questions:

Q: Do I need a budget before I contact an art advisor?
A: No. You need a sense of your range, not a fixed number. Budget planning is the fourth of my seven steps, after discovery, research and curatorial development, so by the time we set it you already know what the space wants and what the options look like. If you do have a firm figure, tell me on the first call and I will build the whole project inside it.

Q: Do you work with my interior designer, or instead of them?
A: With them, always. I work with interior designers and architects on behalf of their clients, and I see my role as a bridge between art history, what is happening in the art world now, and the creative vision of the designer. The designer stays in the room from discovery to installation. What I add is the art: the artists, the sourcing, the negotiation, the logistics, and the hanging.

Q: Can I see the works before I commit to buying?
A: Yes. At the procurement and selection step I bring the works to you, in person where possible and on screen where not, and you choose. Nothing is bought without your approval. For commissions, the work is developed from initial concept to final execution with your specific space in mind, and you approve the concept before the artist begins.

Q: Do you handle framing, shipping and installation too?
A: Yes, end to end. Production, framing and installation are one of my four services, with expert printmakers, framers and art installers, and every stage is managed within defined timelines and approved budgets. Logistics and installation are the last two of the seven steps, and I manage the hanging to the end. The work is not complete until it is installed and you are fully satisfied.

Q: Does the process work if my home is still under construction?
A: It works better. With plans in hand I can propose walls for the anchor works early, coordinate with the architect and contractor, and start a commission while the house is still being built. Closter, New Jersey is the closest example: a newly built residence where the collection was curated to strengthen the architectural character of the house, working closely with leading New York City galleries.

### How do I buy art from a gallery without overpaying?

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/how-to-buy-from-a-gallery-without-overpaying/

You avoid overpaying at a gallery by knowing what the work should cost before you ask, by asking for the right things, and by having someone negotiate who does it for a living. That is what I do: I assess the market value, negotiate on your behalf, and manage the purchase to the end.

Galleries are not the enemy. The best of them represent artists you cannot reach any other way, and I work closely with leading New York City galleries, after managing a gallery in Tel Aviv myself. I have sat on the gallery's side of the desk, and I have built collections for hotels and cruise ships, where you learn quickly what a list price is made of. I know how the number is built, and how much of it is conversation.

### Why private buyers overpay

- They fall in love in the room, on a gallery walk in Chelsea, and buy the same day.
- They do not know the artist's market: what comparable works, by size, date and medium, have sold for elsewhere.
- They assume the price on the list is the only possible price. In the industry it rarely is, and galleries decide for themselves who receives a better one.
- They forget what is not in the price: framing, crating, shipping, installation, and sometimes tax. The number on the wall is not the number on the invoice.
- They negotiate alone, once, with nothing to offer the gallery but this one sale.

### What I do in the negotiation
Before I speak to the gallery, I know what the work should cost. I read the artist's market, compare the work against others by the same hand, and agree with you the number that makes sense and the number at which we walk away. Then I talk to the gallery as a professional they know they will see again. That changes the conversation. A gallery treats an advisor's client as a collector, not a passer-by, because I bring them the next project too.
I also ask for what a private buyer does not think to ask: the full details and documentation of the work, including where it has been, exactly what is included in the price, the condition, and the terms of delivery. And I will tell you when a list price is already fair. The goal is the right price, not the thrill of a discount. And I keep your name and your budget out of the room until they need to be in it. Discretion is part of the negotiation.

### Caesarea: works from France, a leading gallery, a negotiated price
For a private estate in Caesarea, the collector wanted large scale works with layered pigments and 18k gold detailing. The right works were in France. I worked closely with a leading gallery, led the price negotiations, and kept every choice aligned with the client's taste and with long term investment goals, because a work bought well is also a work that holds its value. The collector got the works, at a price reached by someone who knew what they should cost. That is the whole job in one sentence.
 

### Sometimes the answer is not the gallery
The biggest saving is often not a better gallery price but a different route to the work. A work can often be acquired or commissioned at the source, without the gallery margin, and because I carry no venue or inventory of my own, in most cases that brings the total cost of the work down. In Closter, New Jersey, the collection was built with leading New York City galleries, because that is where the right works were. For a home office in Caesarea, one painting was acquired and a second was commissioned from the same artist. I do not have a preferred route. I have a preferred outcome: the right work, at the right price, on your wall. If you are still deciding where to look, galleries, fairs, auctions and studios are compared in where to buy original art in New York.
If you want to see why buying through me usually costs less than an auction or a gallery, read what an art advisor costs. If the work you want does not exist yet, read about commissioning a work for your home.

### If you are about to buy something
Do not sign today. Send me the gallery's details for the work, a photo of the wall it is meant for, and the price you were quoted, and I will tell you what I see. Write to me or email stav@stavtheodor.com. A day of patience is the cheapest advice in this business.

Questions:

Q: Can you negotiate gallery prices, and do galleries give discounts?
A: Yes, and in the industry they often do, though never as a rule you can count on. The price on the list is a starting point, and galleries decide for themselves who gets a better one: collectors they expect to see again, advisors who bring the next project, buyers taking more than one work. I negotiate on your behalf with a number in mind that comes from the artist's market, not from the gallery's mood that day.

Q: Is it cheaper to buy directly from the artist than from a gallery?
A: Often, because there is no gallery margin in between, and I carry no venue or inventory of my own to add back. But not every artist sells directly, and an artist represented by a gallery will usually send you back to it. The honest answer is that the route depends on the artist and the work. I use whichever gets you the right work at the right price, and I tell you which one it is.

Q: What should I ask a gallery before buying a work?
A: Ask what exactly is included in the price: framing, crating, shipping, installation, and whether tax is added. Ask for the full details and documentation of the work and its condition. Ask about the artist's market, and whether comparable works have sold elsewhere and at what level. Ask how the price was set and whether there is room in it. If you do not want to ask these questions yourself, that is precisely what I am for.

Q: Does bringing an advisor make the gallery price higher?
A: No. I work for you, not for the gallery or its artists, and I negotiate on your side of the table. In the industry an advisor tends to bring the price down, not up, because the gallery is speaking to someone who knows the artist's market and who represents future projects, not a one time buyer. Why art usually costs less through me is on the page about what an art advisor costs.

Q: Can I bring you in after I have already found the work I want?
A: Yes. Send me the gallery's details for the work, a photo of the wall it is meant for and the price you were quoted, before you sign anything. I will tell you what I see: whether the work suits the space, whether the price sits right against the artist's market, and whether I can negotiate it or find a better route to the same artist.

Q: How do I know if a piece of art is priced fairly?
A: Compare it with the artist's market: what comparable works by the same artist, of similar size, date and medium, have sold for in galleries and at auction. Then ask exactly what the price includes, framing, crating, shipping, installation and tax, because two prices that look alike can cover different things. If you want a professional view before you commit, I assess the market value of the work and negotiate on your behalf.

### We just moved to New York and the walls are empty. Where do we start with art?

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/moved-to-nyc-empty-walls-art/

Start with the one or two walls you see every day, hang those well, and let the rest of the apartment show you what it needs over the following months. For people who have just moved to New York City, my work at THEODORA starts with a walk through the new home to decide which walls come first; then I choose, source and install art they will actually live with.

A move to New York often means arriving with a few boxes of framed things, a lease or a closing date, and a lot of white walls. The instinct is to fill everything in a weekend so the place feels like home. Resist it. Empty walls for a few weeks cost you nothing; the wrong art on the main wall costs you every day.

### Which walls come first?

Walk the apartment the way you will live in it. Stand at the front door, sit where you will sit in the evening, lie where you will wake up. The walls you see from those places are the ones that matter. From those sightlines I define the main wall of each space, and it is rarely the biggest one.

In most homes that means two starting points: the wall the living space turns toward, and the wall you see from bed or from the entrance. Put your energy there first. Hallways, the second bedroom and the office can wait until you know how you use them.

### What about the art we brought with us?

Plan around it before you buy anything. Lay out what you own, including the pieces you are not sure about anymore, and decide what still belongs. A work that looked right in a house with low ceilings may need a different wall, a different frame, or a partner beside it in a tall New York room. Reframing is often the fastest way to make an old piece feel new in a new place.

Then fill the gaps. Knowing what you already have tells you what is missing: scale, color, a medium you do not own yet, or one work strong enough to hold the main wall.

### Live with the light for a while

New York light is not one thing. A west facing living room in a tower gets hard sun in the late afternoon; a garden floor in a townhouse may barely see direct light at all. Watch how the light moves for a few weeks. It decides where a glossy surface will glare, where a work on paper needs protection, and where a picture light will be needed. Plan the lighting before hanging, not after.

### Building rules come before install day

Many New York buildings ask for a certificate of insurance before any installer comes in, and set working hours and service elevator bookings. It is easier to know this before a large work is delivered. I carry insurance and can provide a certificate naming your landlord or managing agent, and my own team installs, after hours when a building requires it. More in framing, shipping and installing large scale art.

### How I help after a move

I start with a conversation about you: where you came from, what you loved about your last home and what you want this one to feel like. I look at the new apartment in person or from plans and photos, go through the art you brought with you, and propose a short selection for the first walls. Then I source, negotiate, frame and install, and I add the rest when you are ready. You set the budget before we begin, and I work to it. The steps are described in how the art advisory process works.

Questions:

Q: I just bought an apartment in NYC and have no idea what art to put on the walls. Who should I hire?
A: Start with an independent art advisor before you buy anything, so the first pieces fit the rooms, the light and the way you live. I walk the space with you or work from the plans, decide with you which walls matter first, then source, frame and install, alongside your designer if you have one. You set the budget at the start and I work to it.

Q: Should we fill every wall right away?
A: No. Hang the one or two walls you see every day first and give the rest time. After a few weeks you will know how the light moves, which rooms you actually use and where you want quiet. Walls filled in a hurry tend to be filled twice. A few strong works in the right places make a new apartment feel lived in faster than many small ones.

Q: Can you help us rehang the art we moved with?
A: Yes. Often the first step after a move is deciding what still belongs. I go through what you brought, suggest where each piece works in the new space, what should be reframed, and what is missing. Then I install it all with my own team, so the art you already love becomes the starting point of the new home rather than a leftover from the old one.

### Residential art consultant for private homes, from one wall to the whole house

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/residential-art-consultant/

A residential art consultant chooses, sources and installs art for a private home, from a single wall to a whole house, and works for the homeowner, not for a gallery's artists. That is my work at THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor: I am Stav Theodor, an art curator, advisor and consultant based in Tenafly, New Jersey, working in person across New Jersey and New York City and online with clients anywhere.

Art is not an accessory. It is a meeting point between a person and a space, and in a home the job is to find that meeting point for the people who live there. Below: what that takes, when to start, and three real homes.

### What does a residential art consultant do for a home?
A residential art consultant takes the art of a home from the first idea to the work on the wall. I have spent more than 15 years in the art world: curatorial work in museums, managing a gallery in Tel Aviv earlier in my career, and working closely with emerging and established artists. For a home, the work has four parts:

- Consulting: from a single artwork to a complete collection, pieces that fit the space, its style and the story of the people who live in it.
- Sourcing and acquisition: I assess market value, negotiate on your behalf and manage every step with discretion.
- Commissions: one of a kind works developed with artists for a specific space, from the first concept to the finished piece.
- Production, framing and installation: with expert printmakers, framers and my own installation team, within the timeline and budget you approved.
Some call it residential art consulting, others residential art advisory. The general difference between the two job titles is in my guide to art advisor or art consultant. In a home I am both, and the seven steps of my process are the same either way.
 

### When is the right time to bring one in?
The earlier you call, the more choices you keep, but there is no wrong moment, and you do not need to wait for finished walls:

- From the plans. I do not have to be on site to start: I can work from your designer's or architect's plans, so walls and lighting can be thought through for the art before they are built.
- After the house is built and designed. In a new house in Closter, New Jersey, I came in after it was built and designed, and curated a collection to bring depth to the interior.
- After a move. Empty walls in a new home are a good moment to start, before the gaps get filled in a hurry.
- For one wall. A single work for the wall everyone sees is a complete project on its own.
Whatever the stage, think about the lighting before anything is hung. A spot that lands beside the work is easier to prevent than to fix.
 

### What it looks like in real homes
In every home I first survey the space and its sightlines, and define the main wall from them. A foyer is read in seconds, so whatever hangs there has to hold from the doorway. In the foyer of a garden villa in Caesarea, I placed two large scale portraits of women, painted with rich layered texture, in slim contemporary frames. Slim framing keeps the eye on the paint, not on the edges.
In a sea view apartment in Herzliya Pituach, a large scale painting by Yigal Ozeri of an aged, textured window sits near the entrance, in dialogue with the windows that face the sea. In the Closter house, works by Jewish and Israeli artists sit alongside other contemporary voices, found working closely with leading New York City galleries.

### Whom does a residential art consultant work for?
A residential art consultant should work for you, and I do. A gallery's job is to represent its artists and get them the highest price possible; that is its essence. I represent the client. I have no closed roster and I am not obligated to any set of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. I still source from galleries, and negotiate there on your behalf.
It also shows in the price. With a private art curator you can, in most cases, buy the art for less than at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction, many bidders fight for the same work, which pushes the price up. A gallery carries a venue, its inventory and its gallerists, and prices with margins to cover them. I have none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable than almost anywhere else. Private, tailored consultation for your home, until the art is on the wall, is included. More in what an art advisor costs.

### Working alongside your designer or architect
I work alongside architects and interior designers, not around them. My part is to bring art history, a sharp eye for what is being made now and your designer's vision into one conversation, so the art and the architecture speak the same language. How that works from your side is in working with your interior designer on art.
