### How to start an art collection, seriously

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/starting-an-art-collection/

Begin with one work you would keep even if it were worth nothing tomorrow, by an artist whose practice you have looked into, at a price you understand. Almost every mistake new collectors make comes from skipping one of those three, and at THEODORA my job as your advisor is to make the second, fifth and twentieth decision as good as the first.

People often tell me they want to "start collecting" as if it were a door you walk through. It is closer to a habit. You look, you learn what you keep returning to, you buy something, and you live with it long enough to find out whether you were right. A collection is what those decisions look like after a few years, if they were made with some consistency.

### Where to begin

Look before you buy. Museums, galleries, art fairs, artists' studios, and not only the ones in your city. Keep a note of what stopped you. After a month the note has a pattern in it: a medium, a scale, a mood, a period. That pattern is the beginning of your taste, and taste is the only thing that makes a collection more than an inventory.

Then buy one work. Not the safest, not the most expensive, the one you will be glad to see every day. Hang it well. Live with it. The second purchase will be better because of the first.

The best first purchases I have seen are the ones that carry something of the buyer's life. For a home in Ramat Gan, a client came back from a transformative trip to Korea, and a large format photograph by a Korean artist of two figures in ceremonial dress now sits at the heart of the living space. It gives the room memory. That is the kind of work a collection grows from.

### What mistakes do new collectors make?

- Buying for the wall instead of the work. A painting chosen to match the sofa is furniture. It will leave with the sofa.

- Buying names without looking. A known artist has weak works too. Provenance, condition and where the piece sits in the artist's career matter as much as the signature.

- Paying the first price. Prices in the art market are negotiated far more often than newcomers assume. Walking in alone, without market knowledge, means paying more than you need to.

- Keeping no records. Invoices, certificates, condition reports, correspondence with the gallery. A collection without a paper trail is hard to insure, hard to lend and hard to sell.

- Rushing. The fair closes on Sunday, the dealer says someone else is interested. Good collections are rarely built under that kind of pressure.

### Who can help you build a collection over time?

An independent art advisor who represents you, not a gallery, and holds the thread across years; that is the role I take at THEODORA, from a single work to a complete collection.

Access, first. An extensive network of artists, galleries and makers opens exceptional and often exclusive works to you. Then judgment, from more than 15 years in the art world: curatorial work in museums, managing a gallery in Tel Aviv earlier in my career, and building collections for hotels teach you to tell a strong work from a fashionable one. Then the market: what a work should cost, when to negotiate, and why, in most cases, a work bought through a private curator costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery.

Finally, coherence. A collection built one impulse at a time looks like it. An advisor keeps the whole collection in view, so that the twentieth work belongs with the first, and manages the parts nobody enjoys: shipping, framing, installation.

On cost: in most cases, a collection built through me costs less than one bought at large auctions or through galleries, because I carry none of their costs; the price includes my help until each work is on the wall, and I represent you, not a roster of artists. More on that in what an art advisor costs.

### From one work to a collection: two projects

For a private collector in Caesarea, I sourced large scale works from France, layered pigments with 18k gold detailing, in close collaboration with a leading gallery. I handled the price negotiations and gave guidance aligned with the collector's taste and long term investment goals. Taste comes first, always. A work you do not love is a bad investment even when the price goes up.

In Closter, New Jersey, a newly built private residence needed a collection rather than a single work. Working closely with leading New York City galleries, I brought together works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices, so that the house would have one voice on its walls rather than many. Each piece was chosen for its wall, and the walls were chosen for what they could hold.

### A first step

If you are ready to buy your first serious work, or you have five works and want to find out whether they are becoming a collection, write to me. Send a few photos of what you own and what you have been drawn to. The first conversation is where I find out what you love, and that is where every collection starts. If you want to understand how a project runs from there, read how the process works.

Questions:

Q: How much money do I need to start an art collection?
A: Less than the market makes you think, and I will not name a number because it depends entirely on what you want to live with. Works on paper, photography and editions from serious artists sit far below paintings by the same artists. What matters at the start is buying one work well, with a real record behind it, not reaching a total.

Q: Should I buy art as an investment?
A: Buy it because you want to live with it, and then buy it intelligently: fair price, good provenance, a strong example of the artist's work, properly documented. A work bought well is also an investment, though no one can promise it will rise in value. Some works do and many do not, and I am not a financial advisor. Bought with that discipline, a collection stays worth living with long after a trend has passed.

Q: Where do serious collectors buy art?
A: Galleries, directly from artists' studios, art fairs, auction houses, and increasingly through private sales that never reach the public market at all. Each has its own pricing logic and its own risks. Part of my work is knowing which door to use for which work, and having the relationships that open it. For New York, see where to buy original art in New York.

Q: What is the difference between an art advisor and a gallery?
A: A gallery represents artists and sells their work; its interest is in placing that inventory. An advisor works for you, across every gallery, studio and auction house, and has no inventory to place. I look for the right work for your walls wherever it is, negotiate on your behalf, and manage the acquisition through installation.

Q: How do I keep records for an art collection?
A: Keep the invoice, the certificate of authenticity where one exists, a condition report or good photographs at the time of purchase, and any correspondence about provenance. Note where and when each work was made, framed and installed. I recommend setting this up from the first purchase, because it is much harder to reconstruct later, and it is what an insurer, a museum or a buyer will ask for.

Q: How do I start an art collection on a budget in New York?
A: To start an art collection on a budget in New York, look before you buy: Chelsea, Tribeca and Lower East Side galleries are free to walk into, and museum programs such as Museums on Us are worth knowing. Then set the budget per wall, not per piece. Put the best original you can on the wall you see most, and let editions and prints carry the rest. See where to buy original art in New York and art for a new apartment on a budget.

### What does an art advisor cost? What you pay, and why it is usually less

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/what-does-an-art-advisor-cost/

With a private art curator, in most cases you pay less for the art than you would at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry none of the costs that push their prices up. That price includes private consultation tailored to your own home, venue or office, and I work with you until the art is on your wall. I represent you, not a roster of artists.

The number that decides what you spend is the price of the art itself, so that is where I start. Below are five answers: what drives the price of a work, why buying through me usually costs less than an auction or a gallery, what the price includes, whether an advisor is worth it for one or two pieces, and whom I represent.

### What drives the price of a work of art?
Two things: the work, and the route it takes to your wall. The work sets the starting point: whether it is a print, an original or a commission, its size, and the artist's standing. Framing and installation follow every purchase.
The route sets the rest. The same work can cost very different amounts depending on who sells it to you and what that seller has to cover. That is the part of the price most people never see, and it is where a private curator changes the most.

### Why does art usually cost less through a private curator than at auction or in a gallery?
At a large auction, many people bid for the same work, and every bid pushes the price up. The competition in the saleroom sets the price, not what the work is worth on your wall.
A gallery carries heavy costs: the venue, the inventory it holds and the gallerists who run it. It prices with big margins to cover them, and those margins sit inside the price you pay. I know this from the inside: I managed a gallery in Tel Aviv.
I have none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable than almost anywhere else. In more than 15 years in the art world, in museums and building collections for hotels, resorts and cruise ships, I built a network of artists and makers I work with directly. When a work is acquired or commissioned straight from the artist, there is usually no gallery margin in between. When the right work is in a gallery, I assess its market value and negotiate on your behalf, because I know what the work should cost and where the room is.
Both routes are in my projects. For a private collector in Caesarea, I sourced large scale works with layered pigments and 18k gold detailing from France, in close collaboration with a leading gallery, handled the price negotiations, and aligned every choice with the client's taste and long term investment goals. For a sea view villa in the same town, the answer was a commission: a 3.5 meter triptych by an Italian artist, made for that wall. And for a home office in Caesarea, one existing painting was acquired and a second was commissioned from the same artist, one of the artists living and working in the client's country of origin. Purchase, commission, or both: the route is chosen for the wall.

### What does the price include?
Private consultation, tailored to your own home, venue or office, and a professional who works with you until the art is on your wall. I work through the seven steps of my process, discovery, research, curatorial development, budget planning, art procurement and selection, logistics, and installation, and budget planning comes before I source a single work, so you know the range before anything is bought. My own installation team hangs the works, and my work is not complete until the artwork is installed and you are fully satisfied. The seven steps are written out in full in how the art advisory process works, the gallery side of the price question in how to buy from a gallery without overpaying, and how to set a budget and make it go further in buying art for a new apartment on a set budget.

### Is an art advisor worth it for one or two pieces?
Often, yes. The one or two works people ask about are usually the anchor of the home, the piece a guest sees first, and everything else is read against them. In a villa in Hod Hasharon, a single large scale figurative digital artwork was chosen to define the emotional center of the space. An advisor is worth it when you are unsure what the wall needs, when the purchase matters to you, or when nothing on the market fits and a commission is the answer. If you already know the work, where it is sold and what it should cost, you may not need one, and I will tell you so.

### Whom do I represent?
You. A gallery's job is to represent its artists and get them the highest price possible; that is what a gallery is for. I represent the client. I have no closed roster and I am not obligated to any set of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world, and the only question is which work is right for your space.
If you want to know what your project would take, the fastest route is a short conversation. Write to me or email stav@stavtheodor.com with a photo of the space and a line about what you have in mind, and I will tell you what I see and what it would take.

Questions:

Q: Is buying art through an art curator cheaper than an auction or a gallery?
A: In most cases, yes. At a large auction, many bidders compete for the same work and push its price up. A gallery carries the costs of its venue, its inventory and its gallerists, and prices with big margins to cover them. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable than almost anywhere else. I will not promise a saving on every work; on yours, I will show you how the price is built.

Q: What is included when I buy art through you?
A: The consultation is part of the price. You get private advice tailored to your own home, venue or office, and a professional who works with you from the first conversation until the art is on your wall: the concept, the shortlist, the negotiation, framing, delivery and installation by my own team. My work is not complete until the artwork is installed and you are fully satisfied.

Q: Does an art curator represent the artist or the buyer?
A: It depends on whom she works for, and it is worth asking. A gallery's job is to represent its artists and get them the highest price possible; that is its purpose. I represent the client. I have no closed roster and I am not obligated to any set of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world, and when the right work sits in a gallery, I negotiate its price on your side of the table.

### Where to buy original art in New York (and how to avoid buying the wrong thing)

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/where-to-buy-original-art-nyc/

Original art in New York is bought in four places: galleries in Chelsea, Tribeca and the Lower East Side, the spring and fall art fairs, auction houses, and directly from artists' studios. My work at THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor is to search all four for you, check what matters before you pay and negotiate on your side, because I represent you, not a roster of artists. I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and online with clients anywhere.

New York has more places to buy original art than almost any city in the world, which is a gift and a problem. There is always another gallery, another fair, another sale. The hard part is not finding art; it is finding the right work for your wall, at the right price, and knowing what you are buying. Here is where to look and what to check.

### Galleries

Chelsea has the largest concentration of galleries, from established names to younger programs. Tribeca has grown into a gallery neighborhood of its own, and the Lower East Side is where many emerging artists show. A gallery's job is to represent its artists and get them the best price; it does that well, and it is often the best place to see a body of work in person. My Art Radar covers current shows, for example a September gallery walk in Tribeca.

### Art fairs

The spring and fall fairs bring many galleries under one roof for a few days. They are a fast way to see a lot and compare, and a hard place to decide calmly. If you fall for a work at a fair, ask for the details in writing and take a day.

### Auctions

Auction houses sell works from private collections, with published estimates and condition reports. The price is set in the room: when several bidders want the same work, every bid pushes it up. Know your limit before the sale, and remember the price at the hammer is not the whole price.

### Artists' studios

Buying directly from an artist removes the gallery's margin and lets you meet the person behind the work. Open studio days and graduate shows are good places to discover artists early. Many established artists, though, sell only through their gallery.

### What to check before you pay

- What it is. A unique work, a limited edition (and its number), or an open print. The invoice should say so.

- Condition. Especially for older works and works on paper.

- Provenance. Where the work has been, for anything bought on the secondary market.

- The full cost. Framing, delivery and installation follow every purchase.

- The wall. Measure it, and think about the light, before you fall in love with a size.

More questions are in ten questions to answer before you buy your first serious artwork.

### Where an advisor fits

An independent advisor can look in all four places at once, for your wall and your budget. I have no closed roster, so I can reach out to any gallery, auction house or artist in the world, and I have a network of artists and makers I work with directly. When the right work is in a gallery, I assess its value and negotiate on your behalf; see how to buy from a gallery without overpaying. In most cases buying through a private curator costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry none of their costs, and the consultation is included until the work is on your wall.

Questions:

Q: Where should I buy original art in NYC?
A: The main places are the galleries of Chelsea, Tribeca and the Lower East Side, the spring and fall art fairs, auction houses and artists' open studios. Each suits a different buyer and budget. If you want someone to search all of them for your wall and negotiate on your side, an independent advisor can; I source from galleries, auctions and artists anywhere.

Q: Where do people with good taste buy art for their homes in New York?
A: Mostly from galleries, art fairs and auctions, and often through an advisor who has access across all three and represents the buyer. Taste shows less in where a work was bought than in how well it fits the space and the person. I have no closed roster, so I can reach out to any artist or gallery and bring you a short selection chosen for your walls.

Q: I want original art for my home, not prints. Where do I start in New York?
A: Start with the wall, not the shop. Measure it, watch the light and decide the scale the space needs, then look at originals with those numbers in hand: in the galleries of Chelsea, Tribeca and the Lower East Side, at the spring and fall fairs, and in artists' studios. Ask whether a work is unique or part of a limited edition, a fixed number of identical impressions, and which number yours is. An advisor can search all four places for you, auction houses included.

Q: How do I avoid buying the wrong artwork?
A: Decide the wall before the work: measure it, watch the light and know what the space needs. Then check what you are buying, a unique work, an edition or a print, its condition and, on the secondary market, its provenance, and budget for framing and installation. Take a day before deciding at a fair. An advisor who represents you can do these checks and tell you honestly when a work is not right.

### Your interior designer is finishing the house. Why bring in an art advisor?

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/advisory/working-with-your-interior-designer-on-art/

Because your designer's job is the space and mine is what hangs in it: the artists, the galleries, the market, the negotiation, the framing and the crew on install day. We work as one team, the designer keeps the lead on the interior, I bring the art to the table, and you get one coherent house instead of two visions competing on the walls.

Interior designers and architects bring me in on behalf of their clients, and much of my work starts that way. They do it because they know the difference between their profession and mine. A good designer can pick a painting. A good designer cannot also spend more than 15 years inside museums, galleries and artists' studios, and no one should expect them to.

### Two different jobs

Your designer owns the architecture of the interior: layout, materials, joinery, furniture, lighting, the schedule and the contractors. Every decision there is about how the house works and feels.

I own the art: which artists, which works, at what price, from which gallery or studio, in what frame, hung where and how. An art curator's role is to bridge between a deep knowledge of art history, a sharp eye for current trends, and the creative vision of architects and interior designers, and to bring all of it into one dialogue. I work alongside designers, not around them.

### How we work together without friction

- Early is better. The best moment to bring me in is when the drawings exist and the finishes are being chosen. Then walls can be sized for the works, lighting can be planned for them, and the art budget sits inside the project budget instead of being what is left at the end.

- I read the design first. Before I propose anything I study the concept, the palette, the materials and the mood the designer is building. In a sea view apartment in Herzliya Pituach, a large scale painting by Yigal Ozeri of an aged, textured window hangs near the entrance in dialogue with the sea facing windows. The work answers the architecture. That only happens if you have read the architecture first.

- Options come through the designer. I present works to the designer, or to designer and client together, never around the designer. The designer keeps the client relationship and the lead on the interior.

- One timeline. Sourcing, commissions, framing and installation are scheduled against the design timeline, so the works arrive when the walls are ready and not before.

- I take the logistics off the designer's desk. Production, framing, shipping and installation are managed by me, with the printmakers, framers and installers I work with. The designer's crew does not have to hang a 3.5 meter triptych, which is what arrived at a sea view villa in Caesarea.

### What goes wrong when art is an afterthought

The house is finished, the budget is spent, and the walls are empty. Then art gets bought fast, to fill space, to match the sofa, at whatever the first gallery quoted. The lighting was never planned for it. The one long wall that could have carried a serious work now has three small ones. The house is well designed and has no soul, and everyone involved can feel it.

### Hod Hasharon: one work to hold the room

A private villa in Hod Hasharon, open and saturated with light, where concrete and nature meet. The design was already strong. What the living space needed was an emotional center, and I chose a single large scale figurative digital artwork to define it. One work, the right scale, the right wall, and the room stopped being a well appointed space and became someone's home.

In Closter, New Jersey, I was commissioned to curate a collection for a newly built residence and bring depth to the interior design. Working closely with leading New York City galleries, I brought together works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices. The result transforms a well designed house into a space with soul, where art and architecture speak the same language. That is the whole point of the collaboration.

### If you are the designer

I have a page written for you: working with THEODORA as an interior designer or architect. The short version: you keep the lead, I bring the art and the logistics, and your client gets a house that is finished on the walls too.

If you are the homeowner and your designer is already on the project, write to me and copy them in. The first conversation is with both of you. For what happens next, read how the art advisory process works, and for the part that comes after the choosing, framing, shipping and installation.

Questions:

Q: Does an art advisor replace the interior designer's role in choosing art?
A: No. The designer keeps the lead on the interior and stays in the room for every art decision. I add what a designer's practice does not include: artist and gallery relationships, market knowledge, negotiation, commissions and installation logistics. In practice I present options through or with the designer, and the client chooses. Two professions, one house.

Q: When in a renovation should the art advisor come in?
A: When the drawings exist and the finishes are being chosen, ideally before the walls are painted. That is when walls can be sized for the works, lighting can be planned for them, and the art budget sits inside the overall budget. Coming in after the furniture is placed still works, but there are fewer options. The decisions to make while the drawings are open are listed in planning art in construction drawings.

Q: Will my designer be offended if I bring in an art advisor?
A: Most designers are relieved. Sourcing art properly takes time they do not have, and many of my projects come from designers who bring me in themselves. I approach every project as the designer's collaborator, respect their concept, and never present around them. If you are unsure, introduce us early and let us speak.

Q: Who decides on the art: the designer, the advisor or me?
A: You do. The designer defines the space and the direction, I bring works that belong to that direction and explain why, and you choose from what you see. I never buy on a client's behalf without approval of the specific work, the price and the placement, and I say so at the first meeting.

Q: What if the designer and the advisor disagree?
A: We talk, before it reaches you. Disagreements are usually about scale or placement, and they resolve quickly once we are both standing in the room with the drawings. If a real difference remains, you hear both views plainly and decide. In practice this is rare, because I read the design before proposing anything.

### A collection with intent
The people you look after buy carefully in most areas of their lives and then buy art by accident: a piece from a trip, a gift, something a decorator found to fill a wall. A collection with intent starts with the person, not the wall: what they return to, what they want the home to say, which artists they have already looked at. From that I build a plan, a small number of works of real quality, acquired at fair prices, that will still make sense together in twenty years.
Art is not an accessory. It is a meeting point between a person and a space, a conversation, a reflection of identity.

### What THEODORA does for your client

- Consulting. From a single artwork to a complete collection, with deep research, market insight and a sharp aesthetic eye.
- Sourcing and acquisition. I assess market value, negotiate on the client's behalf and manage every step with care, discretion and precision. In most cases the client pays less for the art through me than at a large auction or through a gallery, and I represent the client, not a roster of artists.

- Production, framing and installation. Printmakers, framers and installers, within defined timelines and approved budgets. The work is not complete until it is installed and the client is fully satisfied.
I do not give investment advice and I do not promise returns. I do buy with long term value in mind: the artist's standing, where the work sits in their career, condition and provenance, and a price that holds up to scrutiny.

Questions:

Q: Is art a good investment for a high net worth client?

What I can say from more than 15 years in the art world is that works bought well, by artists whose practice has been looked at closely, in good condition, with clear provenance and at a negotiated price, tend to hold their meaning and their value far better than works bought on impulse. ### For real estate brokers and developers: art for the new home

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/for-brokers/

If you sell or build homes in Bergen County, Manhattan or Israel, I can give your buyers the one thing the closing folder never contains: art chosen for that home by an art curator and advisor, and installed on its walls. You make one introduction, I do the work, and the buyer remembers who thought of it.

A new home closes with everything but the walls. The buyer has spent months on the kitchen, the floors and the lighting, then moves in to blank plaster. Choosing art is the decision nobody has energy left for. You can close that gap for your buyers with a single introduction.

### The offer: art for the new home
For brokers and developers in Bergen County, Manhattan and Israel, I offer every buyer you introduce the process I follow with every client, from discovery to installation, tailored to the buyer's budget and timeline, and the buyer decides.
Discovery, the first step, covers two things:

- How they live. Who they are, what they keep returning to, how they will use the rooms. The art follows from that, not from the sofa.
- The key walls. The entrance, the living room, the one wall guests see first. Scale, placement, and what is possible at more than one level inside a budget the buyer sets.
If the buyer goes ahead, I do the rest: research and sourcing from galleries in New York and Tel Aviv and from artists I work with directly; market value assessed and the price negotiated on the buyer's behalf; printmakers, framers and installers I know. In most cases the buyer pays less for the art through me than at a large auction or a gallery, because I carry none of their costs. The job ends when the work is on the wall and the buyer is happy, whether that is one decisive work for the entrance or a collection for the whole house.

### How you look
You introduced something the buyer will look at every day, long after the closing gift is forgotten. For a broker, it is a reason to be in touch after closing, which is when the next referral happens. For a developer, the home is handed over finished to the walls, not only to the paint.
The credit is yours. I say so to the buyer.

Closter, New Jersey: a newly built private residence, where I curated a collection to give the architecture depth, working with leading New York City galleries and placing works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices. Manhattan: a large format digital collage chosen to anchor an apartment's custom bar, because the client loves to entertain; the work draws on the visual language of glamorous gatherings and references Manet's "Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère". Herzliya Pituach: a sea view apartment where a large scale painting by Yigal Ozeri, an aged and textured window, hangs near the entrance in dialogue with the sea facing windows.
For buyers moving to Israel, one project says most of it. A sea view villa in Caesarea needed a work at architectural scale, so I commissioned a 3.5 meter triptych from an Italian artist: three storks at its center, for homecoming, strength and belonging, echoing the owner's journey as a new immigrant and the storks that migrate through Israel each season.
Alongside private homes, I have built art concepts and collections with luxury hospitality groups, including the residences and guest rooms of the St. Regis Amman. Names on my client and partner list include Eagle Hills, Four Seasons and Rosewood Hotels and Resorts.

### The arrangement between us
The mechanics, including whether the service is offered as your closing gift or as my introduction, and whether it carries your name or mine, are agreed together at the start of the first project, in writing. I would rather have a few brokers and developers who send me every closing than many who send one.

### How to start
Send me the listing or the floor plan and a line about the buyer. Write to stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. You may also want to read about art for a new build in Bergen County, art for a home in Israel managed from abroad, and how I work with interior designers and architects.

Questions:

Q: Can a real estate broker offer art advisory as a closing gift?
A: Yes. It is the one closing gift that stays on the wall. The broker introduces me to the buyer, and I take the buyer through the process I follow with every client, from discovery to installation; the buyer decides what to acquire within a budget they set. Whether the broker funds part of this as a gift under their own name, or the buyer engages me directly, is agreed between the broker and me at the start of the first project.

Q: When should a new home buyer think about art, before or after moving in?
A: Before, when the timing allows. Between contract and move in, the floor plan exists, the walls are empty and the buyer already knows which rooms matter, so a commissioned work has time to be made; the 3.5 meter triptych I commissioned from an Italian artist for a sea view villa in Caesarea needed that time. After moving in is also fine. I work from the finished rooms, and one decisive work for the entrance can be chosen, framed and installed without the house becoming a project again.

Q: How much should a buyer budget for art in a new home?
A: There is no fixed rule, and I do not start from a number. I start from the buyer's approved budget and plan against it, with options at more than one level, so the buyer sees what one decisive work and what a fuller collection would each look like. In most cases the art costs the buyer less through me than at auction or in a gallery, since I carry none of their costs, and I negotiate with galleries on the buyer's behalf.

Q: Do you work with buyers moving to Israel from New York or New Jersey?
A: Yes. I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and my projects run across Tel Aviv, Caesarea, Herzliya Pituach, Ramat Gan and Hod Hasharon. The buyer and I can meet here before the move, and I manage sourcing, framing and installation in Israel, in Hebrew, with the buyer approving each step remotely or in person. Brokers and developers on both sides of the move can introduce me.

Q: Should the art in a model home stay with the buyer?
A: Sometimes, and offering the model home's art to the buyer can help the close. Buyers who fall for a model may ask for the art along with the furniture. A developer can plan for that by choosing works that suit a home rather than a showroom, agreeing on their price in advance, and offering them at closing. Because I can in most cases buy for less than a gallery would ask, that price can stay fair to the buyer. When the buyer would rather build their own collection, the model is a good starting point for a conversation about their walls.

### Art consultant for interior designers and architects

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/for-designers/

As an art curator and advisor, I work alongside interior designers and architects, not around them. The client stays yours, the credit stays yours, and I take the art off your plate: sourcing, budget, artists, commissions, framing, installation.

You know the moment. The house is nearly done, the walls are ready, and the client turns to you and asks what should go on them. I take that question. You keep the client, the credit and the design language; I bring the art, on your schedule and inside the budget you and the client have already agreed.

### What I take off your plate
Art is usually the last line item and the first thing a guest sees. I run it as its own project, in parallel with yours:

- Research and sourcing. Galleries in New York and Tel Aviv, artists I work with directly, and access to works that are often exclusive.
- Budget and negotiation. I assess market value and negotiate on the client's behalf. In most cases the client pays less for the art through me than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry no venue, inventory or gallery staff, and I represent the client, not a roster of artists.
- Commissions. When the wall needs a piece that does not exist yet, I brief the artist and manage the work from concept to delivery. For a sea view villa in Caesarea that meant a 3.5 meter triptych by an Italian artist, three storks at its center, because the owner had come to Israel as a new immigrant and storks pass through the country every season.
- Production and framing. Printmakers, framers and installers, matched to your finishes, within the timeline and the approved budget.
- Installation. I manage the installation. The work is not done until the piece is on the wall and the client is happy.
That keeps the art budget visible from the start, gives commissions time to be made, and means the walls are sized and lit for the works they will carry.

### Art from the client's story
Where the client has a story, the art starts there. For a Manhattan client whose love of entertaining guided the selection, I chose a large format digital collage to anchor the custom bar, drawing on the visual language of glamorous social gatherings and referencing Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère. The project is the Manhattan skyline residence.

### The client stays yours
Your drawings, your palette and your intent lead; the art answers them. The way I see the job is to bridge between a deep knowledge of art history, a sharp eye for what is current, and your creative vision, and bring the three into one dialogue on the wall. I present to the client with you or through you, whichever you prefer, and the project is credited to your studio. I have more than 15 years in the art world, including managing a gallery in Tel Aviv and curatorial work in established museums, and an M.A. in art history.

In Closter, New Jersey, the house was new construction and I was brought in to curate a collection that would give the architecture depth. Working with leading New York City galleries, I placed works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices. A well designed house became a space with soul, where art and architecture speak the same language.

Alongside private homes, I have spent years building art concepts and collections while collaborating with luxury hospitality leaders, among them the Waldorf Astoria Chengdu, the St. Regis Amman and Holland America Line. Those projects run on drawings, schedules and approved budgets. So do mine.

I would rather build a long working relationship with a handful of studios than take one off projects. If you want a referral arrangement, we agree its mechanics together, in writing, at the start of the first project and before any client is involved, so both of us know exactly where we stand.

A drawing set or a few photos, the dimensions of the walls that matter, the palette and a line about the client. No names are needed at the start. I reply with how I would approach it inside your scheme.
