## Guides

### Art above a bed: what to hang, how big and how high

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/art-above-bed/

Art above a bed should be about two thirds as wide as the bed or headboard, roughly 40 inches (102 cm) over a queen, and hang 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above the headboard, fixed on two points, with no heavy glass over the pillows. And remember the wall facing the bed: it is the one you see when you wake up.

The bedroom is the one room in a house where art is chosen only for you. Guests rarely see it; you see it every night and every morning, often lying down. That changes both the rules of placement and the choice of work. Here is how I approach it.

### What size art above a bed?
The work, or the group, should span about two thirds of the width of the bed, or of the headboard if it is wider than the mattress. Standard American mattress widths make this easy:
 Measure the bed frame or headboard you actually have: an upholstered headboard can add several inches on each side. For a single wide work you can go to three quarters, but never wider than the bed.
2/3of the bed or headboard width8 to 10inabove the headboard (20 to 25 cm)2points of fixing, never one nail

### How high above the headboard?
 Leave 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) between the top of the headboard and the bottom of the frame, the same gap I use above a sofa. Closer, and you knock it when you sit up to read; much higher, and the art floats away from the bed.
With no headboard, the art itself becomes the headboard. Make up the pillows as you use them, and hang the bottom of the frame 8 to 10 inches above their top. Your head will touch the wall there when you sit up, so choose acrylic or an unglazed work, fixed at the top and the bottom. Then check that the center is not far above 60 inches (152 cm); if it is, choose a wider, lower format.

### Five ways to fill the wall above a bed

- One wide horizontal work. The calmest option, and the easiest to get right.
- A pair, either side by side above the bed with 3 to 4 inches (8 to 10 cm) between them, or one above each nightstand, centered on the nightstand rather than on the bed.
- A triptych or a row of three, with equal 2 to 3 inch gaps, above a king bed.
- A small gallery wall, tight and low, kept within the width of the headboard. See gallery wall ideas for the spacing rules.
- A textile or a work on panel, light and unglazed, when you want something soft above the pillows.
 Two special cases. Twin beds side by side take one work above each bed, sized to that bed, or one work centered on the nightstand between them. A bed under a window does not need art squeezed into the strip above the frame: give the work to the wall facing the bed instead.
 

### The wall that matters most may be the other one
 The wall above the bed is the one you see when you walk into the room. The wall facing the bed is the one you see from the pillow, last thing at night and first thing in the morning. Which of the two gets the strongest work depends on the room and on the client. When it is that second wall, often above a dresser, the work can hang at a normal height: the bottom of the frame 6 to 10 inches above the dresser, about two thirds of its width. The wall above the bed then takes something quieter.

### Choosing bedroom art: for you, not for guests
Most advice says bedroom art should be calm: soft abstracts, pale landscapes. Calm is a good default, but it is not a rule. Choose the work you want to see first in the morning. For some people that is a quiet horizon; for others a portrait, a strong color or a photograph of a place they love. Because the bedroom is private, it is also the right place for work that is personal, intimate or too particular for the living room.
For color, use the method that works everywhere else in the house: repeat one color the room already has, and let the work bring one it lacks. If you are starting to buy seriously, read how to start an art collection.

### Hang it safely
 
- Two points of support, two D-rings on two hooks or a French cleat, never a single nail and a wire.
- Into studs or anchors rated for at least twice the weight of the work. Set the two hooks for a wide frame on two separate studs.
- Acrylic instead of glass for glazed works above the pillows: lighter, and it does not shatter.
- No picture ledges with leaning frames above a bed. Whatever leans can fall. Above a sofa I allow a lipped ledge with light, acrylic-glazed frames; above a bed, never.
- Bumpers on the lower corners, so the frame stays straight when a headboard knocks the wall.

### Light and sun
Bedside lamps throw light up the wall and can glare on glass, so matte or anti-reflective glazing helps. The Northeast Document Conservation Center advises keeping framed color photographs and watercolors out of direct sun, so keep them off a wall that takes the morning light. See how to hang pictures for the lighting angle and hardware in detail.
 

### The mistakes I see most often

- A small frame lost above a wide bed.
- Art hung so high it no longer belongs to the bed.
- A heavy glazed frame on one nail above the pillows.
- A pair above the nightstands that is not centered on them.
- Leaving the wall facing the bed empty, when it is the one you see first each morning.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
A bedroom is the most personal space to plan, and the work in it is often the one you live with longest. I help clients find it, and handle framing and installation so it is hung safely. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. For the rules above a sofa, see art above a couch. To ask about your bedroom, write to me through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What size art should go above a bed?
A: Art above a bed should be about two thirds of the width of the bed or headboard, up to three quarters for a single wide work, and never wider than the bed. That is roughly 36 inches over a full bed, 40 inches over a queen and 50 inches over a king. Measure the headboard you actually have, since it is often wider than the mattress.

Q: How high should art be above a bed?
A: Art above a bed should hang 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above the top of the headboard. With no headboard, make up the pillows as you use them and hang the bottom of the frame 8 to 10 inches above their top, in acrylic or unglazed, fixed at the top and the bottom. If the center ends up far above 60 inches, choose a wider, lower work.

Q: What should I put above my bed?
A: Above a bed, one wide horizontal work is the simplest choice. A pair, a row of three above a king bed, a small tight gallery wall within the headboard's width, or a light textile also work well. Whatever you choose, keep it about two thirds of the bed's width and fix it securely on two points.

Q: Is it okay to hang a picture above a bed?
A: Yes, a picture above a bed is fine as long as it is hung safely. Use two points of support into studs or rated anchors, choose acrylic rather than glass for glazed works, avoid heavy frames directly over the pillows, and do not put picture ledges with leaning frames above a bed. Hung this way, it is as safe as art anywhere else.

Q: What artwork is best for a bedroom?
A: The best artwork for a bedroom is the work you want to see first thing in the morning. Calm landscapes and soft abstracts are a good default, but a portrait, a strong color or a personal photograph can be right too. The bedroom is private, so it is the one room where art can be chosen only for you, not for guests.

### Art above a couch: what size, how high, and which layout

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/art-above-couch/

The 2/3 couch rule says art above a couch should be about two thirds as wide as the couch, with its bottom edge 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above the top of the sofa back. Above an 84 inch sofa, that means a work or group about 56 inches wide. Hang it on two points, securely, because people's heads rest just below it.

A small print over a long sofa reads like a sticky note on a door: you notice it, but it does not hold the wall. The wall above the sofa is the one most people fill first, and the one where small mistakes show most: a work too small floats, a work too high loses the sofa. These are the rules I use, and why.

### How high should art hang above a couch?
Leave 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) between the top of the sofa back and the bottom of the frame. You will see 4 to 6 inches recommended too, by Studio McGee among others. I prefer the extra space on a sofa because people lean back, stretch an arm along the top and rest their heads; closer than that, the frame gets knocked and the glass gets smudged. Much more than 10 inches, and the art stops belonging to the sofa and starts floating on the wall.
 2/3of the sofa's width, arms included8 to 10infrom the sofa back to the bottom of the frame (20 to 25 cm)57 to 60inwhere the center should land (145 to 152 cm)Then check the center against the 57 to 60 inch eye-level line from how to hang pictures. With a typical sofa back of about 32 inches and a 9 inch gap, a work 32 to 38 inches tall centers at 57 to 60 inches: 32 + 9 + half of 38 is exactly 60, as in Fig. 1. A lower back needs a taller work, a higher back a shorter one. If the center lands far above 60, the work is too tall for that wall: choose a wider, lower format.
 

### What size art above a couch?
The work, or the whole group, should be about two thirds of the sofa's width. For a single wide work you can go up to three quarters. Never go wider than the sofa itself. The ratio gives you the width; it cannot tell you whether the work will hold the wall. A strong work at two thirds beats a thin image stretched to three quarters.
 Measure the sofa's full width, arms included. Before you buy, tape the outline of the work on the wall above it, and look from the doorway you usually walk in through. Nearly everyone discovers the work they had in mind is too small.

### Six layouts that work above a sofa
 
- One large horizontal work. The calmest and usually the strongest.
- A pair. Two vertical works of the same size, 3 to 4 inches (8 to 10 cm) apart, read as one wide piece.
- A triptych or a row of three. Equal gaps of 2 to 3 inches. Good for a long sofa.
- A grid of four or six identical frames, for a series of prints or photographs.
- A gallery cluster built around one anchor, for a collection that will grow. The layout rules are in gallery wall ideas.
- A picture ledge with a front lip, 8 to 10 inches above the sofa back, for anyone who likes to change the wall. Only light frames, glazed with acrylic, never glass: heads rest just below. Above a bed I do not use a ledge at all.

### Sectionals, low backs and sofas under windows
 
- Sectionals. Size the art to the part of the sectional against the wall you are hanging on, and center it on that section's seats, not on the corner or on the whole L.
- A sofa off center on its wall. Center the art on the sofa, not on the wall: the two are read as one composition.
- Low-back sofas. Keep the 8 to 10 inch gap. If that puts the center well below 57 inches, choose a taller work so the center rises.
- A sofa under a window. Do not force art into a strip of wall. Hang it on the side walls, or on the wall facing the sofa, where it will be seen.
- A sofa floating in the room. The art goes on the wall people face, not behind the sofa.
 

### Choosing the work itself
The sofa wall is usually the first thing you see in a living room, so I treat the work on it as the main work of the space, not filler. Start from what you love and let the size rules decide the format. The sofa will change before the art does, so match the room's temperature rather than the upholstery: a warm room of wood and linen can take a cool blue painting, and the contrast is what makes both look considered. If you are building toward a collection, this is a good first serious purchase; how to start an art collection covers how I would approach it.
 Light it as well. A ceiling spot aimed at about 30 degrees from vertical keeps reflections off the glass and out of the eyes of whoever sits facing it. Table lamps at each end of the sofa warm the room but do not light the art. The setback for your ceiling and the bulb are in how to light art.

### Hang it safely, because heads are below it

- Two points of support, two D-rings on two hooks, or a French cleat for heavy works. A single nail lets a frame swing and drop.
- Into studs or rated anchors, chosen for at least twice the weight of the work.
- Acrylic instead of glass for large glazed frames above a sofa: it is lighter and does not shatter. Ask your framer for an anti-reflective version.
- A bumper on each lower corner, so the frame stays straight when someone leans back into the wall.

### The mistakes I see most often

- A work a third of the sofa's width, floating in the middle of the wall. Go to two thirds, or group it.
- Art hung 18 inches or more above the sofa back. Bring it down to 8 to 10 inches.
- A pair hung too far apart, which reads as two separate works. Keep them 3 to 4 inches apart.
- A wide, heavy frame on a single nail above people's heads.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
If the sofa wall is the heart of the space, the work on it deserves a proper search, not a rushed purchase to fill a gap. I look for works with clients and with interior designers, and see how I handle framing and installation. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. Send me a photo of the wall through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What are the rules for hanging art above a couch?
A: The rules for art above a couch come down to three numbers. Make the work, or the group, about two thirds of the couch's width. Leave 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) between the top of the sofa back and the bottom of the frame. Check that the center lands near 57 to 60 inches from the floor, and hang it on two points into studs or rated anchors.

Q: What size art should go above a couch?
A: Art above a couch should be about two thirds of the couch's width, up to three quarters for a single wide work, and never wider than the couch. A 72 inch sofa takes art about 48 inches wide, an 84 inch sofa about 56 inches, and a 96 inch sofa about 64 inches. Tape the outline on the wall before you buy.

Q: How high above a couch should you hang a picture?
A: The bottom of a picture above a couch should sit 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above the top of the sofa back. Less than that and heads and arms knock it; much more and it looks disconnected from the sofa. If the center ends up far above 60 inches, choose a wider, lower work instead of hanging higher.

Q: What is the 2/3 couch rule?
A: The 2/3 couch rule says art above a couch should be about two thirds as wide as the couch, measured arms included. The proportion makes the sofa and the art read as one composition. The rule applies to the whole group when you hang a pair, a triptych or a gallery wall, not to each frame.

Q: What should I put on an empty wall above a sofa?
A: One large horizontal work is usually the strongest choice for an empty wall above a sofa. A pair of vertical works, a row of three, a grid of prints, a gallery cluster, or a lipped ledge with light, acrylic-glazed frames all work too, as long as the group spans about two thirds of the sofa and sits 8 to 10 inches above its back.

Q: Can you hang a vertical painting above a couch?
A: A single vertical painting usually looks too narrow above a sofa and forces the center too high. Two vertical works side by side, 3 to 4 inches apart, solve both problems and read as one wide piece. A single vertical work suits a narrow loveseat or an armchair better.

### Art advisor or art consultant: what each does and which one you need

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/art-advisor-vs-art-consultant/

An art advisor works for a buyer, usually a private collector, to find, assess and negotiate artworks for a collection. An art consultant works for a space, such as an office, a hotel, a clinic or a home, choosing and installing art that fits the design, the brand and the budget. In the art advisor vs art consultant question, the titles overlap, and many professionals do both. I am Stav Theodor, and at THEODORA in Tenafly, New Jersey, I work as both.

The title on a business card tells you less than two questions: whom does this person work for, and does the job start with the art or with the space?

### The short answer
An art advisor starts from the buyer and the work; an art consultant starts from the space and its walls. The two titles overlap, so judge the person by what they do and whom they represent, not by the title.
 

### What does an art advisor do?
An art advisor helps a buyer decide what to buy and at what price. The work is research and judgment: which artists fit the buyer's taste and plans, what condition a work is in and where it has been, and how to negotiate. A good advisor thinks in years, because a collection grows with its owner.
In my art advisory services this is sourcing and acquisition: I assess market value, negotiate on my client's behalf and manage every step with care, discretion and precision. For a private collector in Caesarea, that meant large scale works sourced from France, close collaboration with a leading gallery, price negotiations, and guidance aligned with the collector's taste and long term goals.
For an independent art advisor, one professional body sets a high bar. The Association of Professional Art Advisors, founded in 1980, admits members by invitation after at least five years as the principal of an advisory firm and advanced study of fine art, and its members may not hold inventory or take consignments.

### What does an art consultant do?
An art consultant, sometimes called a fine art consultant, starts from the space and works back to the art. The questions are practical first: who uses the space, what it needs to say, where the light falls, how big each wall is.
For an office, a practice or a restaurant, that becomes one plan for every wall, built to a timeline, with framing, delivery and installation included. I have my own installation team, I carry insurance and can provide a certificate that names the landlord or managing agent, and I install after hours so the business keeps working. More on that in art for an office or a business.
When the right piece does not exist yet, I work with an artist to create it for that one space. The same approach runs through collections built while collaborating with luxury hospitality leaders.

### Who does each one represent, and what does it mean for your price?
Whoever represents you works on your side of the price. In most cases, buying art through a private curator who represents you costs less than buying it at a large auction or through a gallery. At a large auction, many bidders compete for the same work, and that pushes the price up. A gallery carries its space, its inventory and its gallerists, and prices its works with big margins to cover them. A private curator carries none of those costs, so in many cases buying through one is more affordable than almost anywhere else.
The service sits inside that price: a private consultation for your own home, office or venue, and someone who works with you until the art is on the wall.
A gallery's job is to represent its artists and get them the highest price, and good galleries do that job well. I represent the client, not the artist. I have no closed roster, I am not obligated to any set of artists, and I can reach out to any artist in the world. For what shapes the total, read what working with an art advisor costs.
 

### Which one fits a home, a collection or an office?
Hire for the job in front of you, not for the title. Most private projects need both halves, and most offices need the consultant's half first.

- One important work. Advisor skills: the right artist, a fair price, the condition checked.
- A collection built over years. Advisor skills, from someone who remembers what you own and why.
- A new or renovated house. Both. In a newly built house in Closter, New Jersey, I worked with leading New York City galleries on works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices.
- An office, a practice or a hotel. Consultant skills first: a plan for every wall and a schedule.
- A house with an interior designer. Someone who works alongside the designer, not around them. More in working with your interior designer on art.
What doing both looks like in my practice:
4services: consulting, sourcing and acquisition, commissions, and production, framing and installation7steps, from the first conversation to the work on the wall2010the year I started in the art world: more than 15 years 

### What should you ask before hiring an art advisor or consultant?
Ask five questions, and expect plain answers.

- Whom do you represent? The buyer, a gallery, a supplier or a set of artists. That tells you whose price they work for.
- Do you hold stock or represent artists? If the works are their own inventory, you are talking to a seller. Fine, if it is said out loud.
- What is your training, and can I see work like mine? Mine is an M.A. in art history from Ben-Gurion University and a curatorial and museum studies diploma from Tel Aviv University. Ask to see installed work, not only mood boards: a mood board shows taste, an installed wall shows judgment about scale and light.
- Who handles framing, delivery and installation, and is it insured? A project is finished when the art is on the wall, not when it is bought.
- Where do I get to say no? In my seven step process, three decisions are yours alone: the direction, the range and the works themselves.
 

### What are the red flags?
Walk away from anyone who will not tell you whom they represent. Five more warning signs:

- A proposal before anyone has seen the space or its plans.
- Every option comes from one gallery or one catalog, and nobody says so.
- A promise that a work will rise in value. Nobody can promise that honestly; buy what you will want to live with.
- No written scope, so you cannot tell what is included.
- Pressure to decide today.
Based in Tenafly, I work across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online anywhere. Here is how I work as an art consultant in Tenafly. Before you hire, start with how my process runs and what shapes the cost.

Questions:

Q: What does an art consultant do?
A: An art consultant chooses art for a space and sees it installed. The work starts with the space: who uses it, what it needs to say, the light and the size of each wall. From there an art consultant plans the art for every wall, sources or commissions the works, and manages framing, delivery and installation. Many art consultants, me included, also advise private buyers on individual purchases.

Q: What is the difference between an art advisor and an art consultant?
A: The difference between an art advisor and an art consultant is where the job starts. An art advisor works for a buyer, usually a private collector, and focuses on which works to buy and at what price. An art consultant works for a space, such as an office, a hotel or a home, and focuses on art that fits it. The two roles overlap, and many professionals do both, as I do.

Q: What is a personal art curator, and do I need one for my home?
A: A personal art curator chooses art for one client's home and sees it through: what to buy, where it goes, and how it is framed and installed. The titles overlap; I work as curator, advisor and consultant. You likely need one when the art is a meaningful purchase, when there are walls you cannot resolve, or when you want one person responsible from the first idea to the installed work. For a single print you love, you may not.

Q: What should I look for in an art consultant?
A: Look for an art consultant who tells you plainly whom they represent, can show installed work in spaces like yours, and has real training in art. Ask whether they hold stock or represent artists, who handles framing and installation, and whether that work is insured. A good art consultant sees the space, in person or from its plans, and asks how you use it before proposing anything, and puts the scope in writing.

Q: Is it more expensive to buy art through an art consultant?
A: In most cases, buying art through a private art consultant who represents you is not more expensive than buying at a large auction or through a gallery, and in many cases it is more affordable. Bidders push auction prices up, and a gallery prices in its space, its inventory and its staff; a private consultant carries none of those costs, and the consultation is part of the price. I explain why in what working with an art advisor costs.

### Art for a small apartment: how to make a small space feel larger, and what to keep when you downsize

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/art-for-a-small-apartment/

Art for a small apartment works best as fewer, larger pieces: one anchor work per space, on the wall you see first from the door or the sofa, makes a small space feel calmer and larger than a scatter of small frames. At THEODORA I start a small apartment the way I start any home: I survey the space and its sightlines and define the main wall from them, then put the best original your budget allows on that wall and let editions and prints carry the rest.

Small apartments tempt people to think small: a few modest frames on every wall. That instinct is what makes a small space feel busy. Here is how to plan a studio or a one bedroom wall by wall, and what to bring when you downsize.

### Should art in a small apartment be small?
No: one larger work usually makes a small apartment feel calmer than several small ones, because the eye settles on one thing instead of hopping between many. Every small frame adds an edge and a gap, and in a compact space those add up to clutter. When the choice is between one large piece and several small ones, one large piece is almost always the stronger answer.
Larger does not mean as large as the wall allows. Size the work to its wall and to where you first see it from, often only a few steps away, and leave clear wall on every side so the wall still reads as a wall.
 

### Which wall comes first: the view from the door
The first wall is the one your eye meets as you open the front door, or the one you face from the sofa; in a small apartment they are often the same wall. I survey the space and its sightlines and define the main wall from them. To test it, stand in the open doorway and note where your eye lands, then look again from the sofa: the wall that wins both sightlines is your anchor wall.
 Many New York apartments open straight into the living space, so that first view does most of the work (the art curator in New York page shows how I start there).

### One anchor per space, the rest quiet
Give each space one anchor and let the other walls stay quiet, or bare: editions, prints, a few small works on a shelf, or nothing. Bare wall is what lets the anchor be seen.
 In a Manhattan skyline residence, I selected a large format digital collage to anchor the apartment's custom bar; the client's love of entertaining guided the selection (see the project page). Decide what each space is for, and let one work say it.
 

### Where does art go in a studio apartment?
In a studio, art goes where it marks a zone: one anchor for the living zone, a quieter work for the sleeping zone, and open wall between them. With no internal walls, the art shows where one part of the day ends and the next begins, so keep the bed zone softer, with less contrast.
Tie each zone to its furniture: a work above the sofa, the bed or the table belongs to it, and that pairing draws the zone on an open floor. An open bookcase used as a divider can hold small works on both faces. Where glass takes most of the wall, art for a new condo covers sculpture and objects.
 

### Size and height in tight quarters
Size does not shrink with the apartment: above furniture, a work spans about two thirds of the furniture below it, and large wall art ideas covers how big to go on a bare wall. Height does not change either: the center sits 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, with 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) between a sofa back and the frame, as how to hang pictures and art above a couch explain.
 

### Leaning, ledges and shelves
Leaning art on a console, a deep shelf or a picture ledge suits a small apartment: few holes, easy changes, and a large work without committing the wall. A large canvas on a console looks deliberate when it rests securely and is the only work on that wall. A ledge with a front lip works above a sofa, 8 to 10 inches above the back, with light frames glazed in acrylic; above a bed I do not use a ledge at all.
 If you rent, check your lease before any hole goes in; the options that leave no marks are in how to hang art without nails, and I never use adhesive strips for original works. A gallery wall works in a small apartment when it is hung as one piece around one anchor: see gallery wall ideas.

### Downsizing: what to keep, give, sell or store
When you downsize, keep the works you love that have a wall waiting for them, and decide the rest one work at a time: give, sell or store. Start from the new floor plan, not the old walls: count the walls that can hold a work, mark the one you will see from the door, and choose its work first.
 Before you give or sell anything of value, have it appraised and gather its paperwork: invoices, certificates, letters from the artist or the gallery. Starting an art collection explains how to keep those records. Store only what you mean to hang again: storage that never ends is a way of deciding not to decide.
 

### Reframe and rehang what you keep
The works you keep deserve to be seen fresh: a new frame, a new wall or a new neighbor. A heavy frame chosen for a large house can crowd a small space, while a slimmer frame or a wider mat makes a familiar work look new. Rehang around the new anchor rather than copying the old layout, and plan the light before you hang: one lamp or picture light often decides whether the anchor still reads at night.
The first weeks in a new home are in empty walls after a move; working with art you already own is in art advisor for a Manhattan apartment.

### When a curator helps in a small space
A curator is worth calling when the walls are few and every choice shows: which wall comes first, which of your works earns it, what to add at the right scale. My first question is never about style; it is what you want to feel at home. Then I find the work, negotiate on your behalf and install it with my own team: installation is part of how I work, not a separate service, for the works I place.
In most cases you can also buy the art for less than at a large auction or through a gallery, because I carry none of the costs that push their prices up (what an art advisor costs explains why). I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and work in person across New York City and New Jersey, and online with clients anywhere; see art curator in New York. To hand over the search entirely, start with who to call for help choosing art.

Questions:

Q: What art works in a small NYC apartment without making it feel cramped?
A: Art that keeps a small NYC apartment from feeling cramped is fewer, larger works: one anchor per space, on the wall you see first from the door or the sofa, with quiet or bare walls around it. Leave clear wall around each work, stand a work on a picture ledge where holes are limited, and group small frames on one shelf instead of scattering them across every wall.

Q: I'm downsizing to a smaller apartment in Manhattan. What do I do with my art?
A: Downsizing your art starts with the new floor plan: count the walls that can hold a work, choose the work for the wall you will see first from the door, then sort everything else into keep, give, sell or store. Keep what you love and have a wall for. Before you give or sell anything of value, have it appraised and gather its paperwork, and store only what you mean to hang again.

Q: Do mirrors make a small apartment look bigger than art?
A: Mirrors make a small apartment look bigger only where they reflect light or a view; opposite a blank wall they add nothing, and opposite a cluttered corner they double the clutter. Art does a different job: it gives the eye one place to rest. In a small space, put one mirror where it catches a window, often in the entry, and give the main wall to a work of art.

Q: What art works in an apartment with low ceilings?
A: Art for an apartment with low ceilings works best when it gets its size from width rather than height: above a sofa or a bed, a wide format fills the wall without crowding the ceiling. Keep the center near 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, and leave at least 12 inches (30 cm) of wall above the frame. On a narrow wall with no furniture, one slim vertical work can lift the eye.

### Art for home staging and model homes: what sells a home

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/art-for-home-staging/

Model home decor works when the art does two jobs: it photographs well, and it lets buyers picture their own life in the space. The camera sees the art before any buyer does, so for home staging that means fewer, larger works in a calm palette, one clear focal point per space, each sized to the furniture below, and nothing personal or divisive. Below are the scale rules for listing photos, the subjects that sell, the rent or buy decision for model homes, and what to do when the buyer wants the art to stay.

Home staging art is art chosen to make a listing or a model home photograph well and help buyers picture living there: large, calm, broadly appealing and sized to each wall. In a model home it also sets the tone for the whole development. I have spent more than 15 years in the art world, including collections built while collaborating with luxury hospitality leaders, where one concept has to carry through every space.

### What does art do in a staged home?
Art gives a staged home a point of view without giving it an owner. Bare walls read as unfinished in listing photos, and family pictures make buyers feel like guests. The right work says someone thoughtful lives here, and lets the buyer imagine it is them.
In the National Association of Realtors' 2025 Profile of Home Staging, more than four in five buyers' agents said staging made it easier for buyers to picture the property as their future home. That covers furniture and art together; I know of no study that isolates the art.

### How big should staging art be for listing photos?
Bigger than you think, and fewer pieces. Listing photos are usually shot with a wide angle lens, which makes a space look larger and everything on its walls smaller, so a frame that looks right in person shrinks on screen. Staging advice sizes art for the eye in the room; size it for the lens first, then check it from a foot away.
 2/3of the furniture below57 to 60incenter from the floor on an open wall (145 to 152 cm)1focal work per photograph
- Width. Above an 84 inch sofa, one work or a pair about 56 inches wide. See what size art goes above a couch.
- Height. Leave 8 to 10 inches above a sofa back or headboard, 6 to 10 above a console. Full rules: how high to hang pictures.
- The camera check. Photograph the wall with your phone from the photographer's corner. If the art reads as a small dark rectangle, go larger.
 

### Subjects and palettes that sell
Calm, open subjects in a palette taken from the house. Abstracts, landscapes with a horizon and quiet still lifes photograph well and ask nothing of the buyer. Recognizable faces, religious or political imagery, nudes and loud pop pieces ask for an opinion, and a buyer with an opinion about the art is not thinking about the house. Calm is not empty: the work still has to hold the wall.
Should staging art be abstract or figurative? Mostly abstract or loosely representational, so buyers can project themselves into it; one gentle figurative work, a figure seen from behind or at a distance, can anchor a model home. For color, take one tone from the cabinetry or the stone and carry it from space to space, so the listing reads as one home.

### Space by space: entry, living, dining, primary bedroom
Start with the living room and the primary bedroom: in the same NAR report, buyers' agents named them the two most important spaces to stage, in that order.
 Kitchens and bathrooms need one small work at most: there the stone and the fixtures are what buyers came to see. For the entry, see entryway art; for a double height wall, large wall art ideas.

### Model homes: rent or buy?
Stagers usually rent art for a listing that sells in weeks. A model home stays open through the sales season while monthly rent adds up, so developers often compare the rent over the term with the price of owning: owned art can move to the next model or sell with the home.
Where you buy matters. With a private art curator you can, in most cases, buy for less than at a large auction or through a gallery: at auction many bidders push the price up, and a gallery's prices cover its space, its inventory and its gallerists. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable, and I represent the buyer, not a roster of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. More in what an art advisor costs.

### Consistency across a development
Every unit should look as if one person chose the art: three constants, one variable. The constants: one palette drawn from the finishes, one frame family (all black, all oak or all thin gold) and one hanging line. The variable: a different anchor in each unit, so no two feel copied. Write it down as a one page art standard, with sizes and heights.
 

### Where stagers get their artwork
Three sources, three trade offs. A staging company's rental inventory is fast and economical, but the same prints turn up listing after listing. Retail and online prints are fine in a photo and thin up close. Galleries, artists and art advisors supply originals and editions that hold up a foot away; through a private curator they cost, in many cases, less than through a gallery.
Do stagers use original art or prints? For a listing, a well made print is usually enough: it has to read in a photo, not survive a close look. In a model home buyers linger, and an original or a signed edition is what makes them stop.

### The model home look in your own house
Edit first, then scale up: fewer objects, one large work per main wall, one palette, one frame family, one hanging line. Then break the model home's rule: your walls should hold art you love, not art chosen to offend no one.

### After closing: when the buyer wants the art to stay
Plan for it: a buyer who falls for a model home may ask to keep the art. Choose works that suit a home rather than a showroom, agree in advance how they are offered at closing, and the request becomes part of the sale.
Many buyers move into a finished house with bare walls. A newly built house in Closter was complete when I came in, every finish right, and what it lacked was a point of view; I built its collection with leading New York City galleries (the Closter project). A broker or developer can close that gap with one introduction: art for the new home, for brokers and developers. Buyers can read when art should come into a new build.
I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and work across Bergen County, New York City and California (art advisor in Bergen County), and online with clients anywhere. For art in your own home, write to me through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: How to make your house look like a model home?
A: To make your house look like a model home, edit before you add. Clear surfaces, take down what you no longer look at, and replace groups of small frames with one larger work per main wall, about two thirds the width of the furniture below. Carry one palette from space to space, keep frames in one family and hang everything to one line, centered 57 to 60 inches from the floor. Then keep what a model home never has: art that is personal to you.

Q: Where do stagers get their artwork?
A: Stagers get their artwork from three places: their own rental inventory, which moves in and out with the furniture; retail and online print shops, for large decorative prints; and galleries, artists or an art advisor, for originals and editions. Inventory and prints suit a listing that sells in weeks. A model home open for months, where buyers look closely, deserves originals or good editions, and buying them through a private curator is, in many cases, more affordable than through a gallery.

Q: What is the 3-5-7 rule in decorating?
A: The 3-5-7 rule is a styling rule of thumb that groups decor in odd numbers, three, five or seven pieces, because odd groups look more natural than pairs and keep the eye moving. It works well for objects on a console, a shelf or a mantel, and for small gallery walls. For staging art it is best used lightly: in a wide listing photo, one large work on a wall usually does more than a group of small frames.

Q: What kind of art works for home staging?
A: The art that works for home staging photographs well and lets buyers picture their own life in the space: fewer, larger works, a calm palette taken from the finishes, one focal point per space, and nothing personal or divisive, such as family photos, religious or political imagery or nudes. Scale matters most, because a small frame over a long sofa disappears in a wide listing photo. Abstracts, landscapes with a horizon and quiet still lifes are the safest subjects.

### Art sourcing for interior designers: trade programs, commissions or a curator

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/art-sourcing-for-interior-designers/

Art sourcing for interior designers is how a design studio finds, buys and installs art for a client project: through trade programs and wholesale suppliers, galleries and artists, commissions, or an art curator who runs the whole art scope inside the designer's scheme. Trade programs are fastest for many walls, originals and commissions carry the walls a client lives with, and a curator can run all of them for you while the client stays yours. Below, each route with what you get, the lead time, who frames and installs, and how the money works.

The four routes are not exclusive. Spend where people stop and let the catalog carry the walls they pass: trade prints for corridors and secondary walls, one original where the eye lands first, a commission for the wall nothing on the market fits. What goes wrong is rarely the route. It is the order: art is left to the end, when the budget is spent and the lead times no longer fit. Earlier in my career I managed a gallery in Tel Aviv; today I work alongside designers and architects, so I have seen sourcing from both sides.
 

### Where do designers source art today?
Designers source art through four routes: trade programs and wholesale suppliers, galleries and artists, commissions, and a curator who takes on the whole art scope. Each trades speed, uniqueness and your time differently.
 

### Trade programs and wholesale suppliers
Trade programs are usually the fastest route to art for many walls at once. A print publisher, a framed art maker, an online platform or an artist's studio opens a trade account to verified design professionals and sells its own catalog at a trade price. Wholesale art for interior designers works on the same model at volume: one supplier, consistent framing, sizes that repeat across a floor.
The limit is in the word catalog. You choose from what that supplier offers, mostly prints and open editions, and the same print can hang in other projects across town.

### Galleries and artists for originals
Galleries and artists are the route to original work, one of a kind or in small editions. A gallery's job is to represent its artists and get them the highest price, and a good gallery does that job well: it vets the work, knows the market and stands behind what it sells. For a new build in Closter, New Jersey, I built the collection working closely with leading New York City galleries, placing works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices (the Closter project).
Buying from artists directly takes the gallery out of the price and puts its work on your desk: finding the artist, checking condition and edition, agreeing the price in writing, arranging framing and shipping. For a home office in Caesarea, built around the client's two loves, horses and music, I acquired one existing painting and commissioned a second from the same artist, so the two works share a hand.

### Commissions for a specific wall
Commission when the wall is unusual, or the story is personal and nothing on the market says it. A very wide wall, a stairwell, a foyer that needs a pair: these are commission walls. The price, dimensions, materials, delivery and the points at which the client sees progress are agreed with the artist before work starts.
For a sea view villa in Caesarea, I commissioned a 3.5 meter triptych from an Italian artist, three storks at its center, echoing the homeowner's journey as a new immigrant and the seasonal migration of storks through Israel. Nobody could have bought that work; it had to be made. The full process is in how I commission art for a new home.
 

### What does a curator partnership add?
A curator partnership puts one professional on the whole art scope, working for your client and inside your scheme. It makes sense when the art is more than a finishing line item: originals, a commission, many walls, or a timeline that cannot slip. I represent the client, not a set of artists. I have no closed roster and I am not obligated to any set of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world and mix all three routes on one project.
I take research, sourcing, budget, commissions, framing and installation off your plate and stay until the art is on the wall, through the seven steps in how the art advisory process works. I have my own installation team and carry insurance, with a certificate naming the landlord or managing agent on request, and I install after hours when a space must keep working. How I work with studios is on my page for interior designers and architects.
4routes to art for a client project7steps I run, from discovery to installation1studio credited on the project: yoursWeighing an advisor against a consultant? Read what an art advisor and an art consultant each do.

### How does the money work?
In most cases, buying through a private curator costs your client less than buying the same kind of work at a gallery or a large auction. At auction, many bidders compete for the same work and push the price up. A gallery prices in its space, its inventory and its staff. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases working with me is more affordable than almost anywhere else, and the price includes a private consultation for the client's home or office and my work with you until the art is on the wall. And because I represent the client, the search stays open to any artist. More on cost in what an art advisor costs.

### Lead times, framing and installation
Lead time usually grows with uniqueness: trade stock is fastest, available originals come next, and commissions take longest.
 Works on paper and photographs need glazing, and the glass changes how a work reads under the lighting you specified, so choose the glazing with the lighting plan, not after it. Large works need a site survey and the right hardware for the wall and the weight. I run all of this as part of the project, never as a hanging job on its own. The details are in framing and installing large scale art; sizing the big walls is in large wall art ideas.
 

### Keeping the client relationship yours
The client stays yours, and so does the credit. Your drawings, your palette and your intent lead; the art answers them. I present to the client with you or through you, whichever you prefer, and the project is credited to your studio. Homeowners can read their side in working with your interior designer on art. For an office project, my six steps for offices and businesses run from choosing to installing.
 I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work with designers and architects in Bergen County, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. Send me the plans, or a photo of one wall, and a line about the client through my page for designers. I will tell you how I would approach it inside your scheme.

Questions:

Q: Where do interior designers get their art?
A: Interior designers get their art through four routes: trade programs and wholesale suppliers for prints and editions at volume, galleries and artists for original work, commissions for a wall nothing on the market fits, and art curators who run the whole art scope inside the designer's scheme. Many projects mix them. Trade stock suits secondary walls and tight timelines; originals and commissions go where the client looks every day. I work with designers who want the art handled, and the client stays theirs.

Q: Do interior designers get discounts on art?
A: Interior designers often get trade pricing on art through trade programs. A print publisher, framed art maker, online platform or artist's studio opens a trade account to verified design professionals, usually on proof of a design business such as a resale certificate, and offers a trade price on its own catalog. Terms are set by each program. For original work, buying through a private curator is in most cases more affordable than a gallery or an auction, with the consultation included.

Q: What is the difference between trade art and original art?
A: Trade art is made for the design trade: mostly prints, open editions and framed pieces from a supplier's catalog, in repeatable sizes, often available quickly and in quantity. Original art is a unique work, or one from a small limited edition, sold by the artist, a gallery or a curator. Some artists also offer originals through trade programs, so the difference is the work, not the channel. Trade art fills walls consistently; original art gives a space something no other project has.

Q: Where do interior designers in New York source original art for clients?
A: Designers in New York source originals from galleries in Chelsea, Tribeca and the Lower East Side, from auctions and art fairs, directly from artists' studios, and through an art curator who can reach across all of them. As THEODORA Art Advisory by Stav Theodor, I work as that partner for designers in New York City and New Jersey: sourcing, negotiation on the client's side, framing and installation, while the client stays yours.
