A: We talk first and work out together what is right for your client; there is no written scope at the start. I read your plans and palette, propose a short selection that belongs to your scheme, and handle sourcing, framing and installation with my own insured team. I work alongside you, never around you, and any referral arrangement is agreed in writing. The partnership is set out in full on the page for interior designers and architects.

### Buy, lease or commission: how companies get art for the office

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/buy-lease-or-commission-office-art/

Art leasing for offices means renting artworks for a set term, often with installation and rotation included, instead of buying them. Buying builds an asset the company keeps, commissioning creates a work for one wall, and leasing trades ownership for flexibility. For most offices a mix works: buy or commission the works on the walls that define the firm, and consider leasing only for walls you expect to change. Buying is also an investment: the work stays with the company, while rent pays only for time on the wall. Below are the routes side by side, the rule for when each one wins, and where a curator fits.

Most of what you will find about leasing office art is written by the companies that lease it. This is the comparison from the other side of the table: an art curator who chooses art for offices and professional practices. I keep it in relative terms, because the real numbers depend on the works, the scale and the term.

### Three routes to art for an office
An office can buy art, commission it or lease it, and each route settles three things differently: what you pay now, what you pay over time, and what you own at the end. Buying splits into prints or editions and originals, so the tables compare four rows.
 

### Leasing: how it works and what it costs over a lease term
Leasing is renting: a leasing company places works in your office for a set term and charges regular rent. Many programs include delivery, installation and a rotation of the works at agreed intervals, and some let you put rental payments toward buying a work you decide to keep.
Settle the cost over the term first. The rent is low at the start and it keeps running, so on a long lease you can pay much of a work's price and own nothing when the lease ends. Before leasing an anchor work, compare the rent over the whole lease with the price of owning it.
 Leasing also narrows the choice: you usually pick from the works a program holds. That is fine for a corridor, and a compromise on the wall a client faces first.

### Who insures leased art?
It depends on the contract. Some leasing programs include insurance for damage to the works and frames; other agreements make the company leasing the art responsible, usually through the company's own policy. Ask who insures the work on your wall, in transit and during installation.

### How long do art leasing contracts run?
Terms vary from company to company. Ask for the minimum term, the notice needed to end early, the rotation schedule, and whether there is a purchase option. Tax treatment is a question for your accountant.

### Buying: prints, editions and originals
Buying costs more at the start and gives the company works it keeps. Prints and limited editions cost least and arrive fastest; a signed, numbered edition, framed properly, holds a corridor or a private office well. Originals cost more and do more: an original at reception, framed for the piece and hung at the right height, tells a client that details are attended to here. More on the walls clients see first in art for an office or business.
In a workplace, fewer, better, larger works nearly always beat many small ones: one large work reads from across the space, and a scatter of small frames reads as decoration. For ideas wall by wall, see office wall art ideas.
 

### Commissioning for a specific wall
Commissioning means briefing an artist to make a work for one wall. You agree the concept, size, budget and timeline up front, then approve the work at each stage until it is installed. It is the slowest route, and the right one when no existing work fits or the work should belong only to you. More in how commissioning works.
 The routes also combine well. For the home office of a luxury residence in Caesarea, I acquired an existing painting by an artist living in the client's country of origin, then commissioned a second work from the same artist, so the two share a hand across the space.

### When does each route win?
Two questions decide it: how long you will be in the space, and whether you want to own the art at the end.
3routes: buy, commission or lease, chosen wall by wall2questions decide it: how long you stay, and whether you want to own the art1test before leasing an anchor work: the rent over the whole lease against the price of owning it
- Lease when the stay is short or uncertain, when you want the walls to change, or when you want to live with a work before buying it.
- Buy when you will stay for years and clients see the wall first. The work moves with you when your office lease ends.
- Commission when a wall needs something that does not exist yet.
 It is the same position I take for law firms and investment firms.

### Where a corporate art consultant fits
A corporate art consultant plans the art for the whole office, decides which works to buy or commission, sources them and stays until they are installed. Where you buy matters as much as what you buy. In most cases, buying through a private art curator costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction, many bidders compete for the same work, which pushes the price up; a gallery carries its space, its inventory and its staff, and prices with margins to cover them. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable than almost anywhere else.
That price includes a private consultation tailored to your office, and my work with you until the art is on the wall. I represent you, not a set of artists: I have no closed roster, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. You approve the concept, the short list and the budget before anything is bought (how the process works). My own team installs after hours, so the office keeps working, and I can provide a certificate of insurance naming your landlord or managing agent.
I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and work with offices across Bergen County, New York City and California (art consultant in Tenafly), and online with clients anywhere.

### Building a corporate art collection that lasts: records, insurance, moves
A corporate art collection lasts when it is documented from the first purchase. Keep one record per work: artist, title, date, medium, dimensions, framing, location, purchase papers and a photograph. An insurer will usually want that record, so ask your broker how fine art is covered on the company's policy.

### What happens to the art when the company moves?
Owned works move with the company: plan removal, crating and rehanging as part of the move, and measure the new walls before the floor plan is final (framing, shipping and installation). Leased works depend on the contract: ask whether the leasing company moves them, takes them back early, or charges to end the term.
If you are weighing the routes for a new floor or a move, start with art for an office or business, and read what working with an art advisor costs.

Questions:

Q: Is it better to buy or lease art for an office?
A: Buying art is better for the walls that define the firm, and leasing is better for walls you want to change or for a stay that may be short. Buying costs more at the start and gives the company works it keeps. Leasing costs less at the start, but the rent runs for the whole term, so on a long lease you can pay much of a work's price and own nothing. Many offices mix the two: they buy or commission the anchor works and lease the rest.

Q: How does art leasing work?
A: Art leasing works like renting: a leasing company places artworks in your office for a set term in return for regular rent. Many programs include delivery, installation and a rotation of the works at agreed intervals, and some let rental payments count toward buying a work. Terms, insurance and early exit rules vary from company to company, so read the contract for the minimum term, who insures the works and what happens if you move.

Q: How much does corporate art cost?
A: Corporate art costs depend on the route and the scale. Prints and editions cost least, originals and commissions cost more, and leasing starts low but runs for the whole term. In most cases, buying through a private art curator costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery, with no bidding war or gallery overhead on top. That price includes a consultation for your office and my work until the art is on the wall, and I represent you, not a set of artists.

Q: Can you buy leased art at the end of the lease?
A: Buying leased art at the end of the lease is possible under some agreements, but it depends on the contract. Some art leasing programs offer a purchase option, and some credit rental payments toward the price. Ask before you sign whether the option exists, how the price is set and how much of the rent counts toward it. If you already know you want to keep a work, compare the full rent over the term with the price of buying it outright.

### Dental office decor ideas: art for the waiting room, the chair and the corridor

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/dental-office-decor/

Dental office decor is the art and finish a patient sees from the door to the chair, chosen with anxious patients in mind and to show the standard of care. Most practices forget the view a patient looks at longest, the ceiling and upper wall seen from the chair, so I plan that first. Below, space by space: what to hang, what to leave out and how it is cleaned.

Good dental office decor follows the patient through the visit: the front desk, the wall across from the waiting chairs, the corridor, then the ceiling and upper wall once the chair reclines. Most practices plan the walls a patient walks past and forget the one above the chair.
 

### What does dental office decor have to do?
Dental office decor has two jobs: give a nervous patient something calm and readable to look at, and show the standard of care before anyone says a word. A patient cannot judge the dentistry on arrival, but they can see whether a space is kept, lit and considered.
 

### The waiting room: ideas for patients who arrive anxious
The waiting room needs calm images a patient can read at a glance. The dental office waiting room ideas I would start with:

- One large work over many small ones. A single work, or a pair that reads as one, gives the eye one place to rest. For sizing, see large wall art ideas.
- Something to return to. Patients look at the same wall again and again; a landscape with depth holds up to that.
- Warm, quiet color that softens the space without becoming decoration. No stones, orchids or wellness slogans: a practice should not look like a spa.
- Nothing to decode. Ambiguous or unsettling images belong in the staff areas, not in front of someone already uneasy.
2/3of the seating's width8 to 10inbetween seat backs and frame (20 to 25 cm)57 to 60incenter where people stand (145 to 152 cm) There is no reliable published standard for seated eye height, so above seating I work from the furniture, not the floor. For standing heights, see how high to hang art.
Is there evidence behind calm imagery? Some, with limits. In a 2011 study on one psychiatric unit, Nanda and colleagues found less as-needed anxiety medication on days a realistic nature image hung than on days with abstract art or none: one unit, one image, not a dental practice. Cleveland Clinic's art program points the other way: its 2011 article says no convincing study shows one style of art serves patients better than another, and the Clinic buys challenging contemporary work on purpose. I read the two together: calm where people wait anxious, bolder where they pass by choice.

### The operatory: what does the patient see from the chair?
From the chair, a patient sees the ceiling and the top of the wall ahead, sometimes for an hour, so that is where the art goes. Once the chair reclines, a painting on the side wall drops out of view. An operatory is planned standing in the doorway and lived in lying down.
 I would choose one calm work for the wall ahead, placed higher than the standing rule, where a reclined patient looks. Horizon, water and sky can be looked at for a long time; a portrait looking down at a patient cannot. If the only view is ceiling tiles, a lightweight printed or backlit panel in the ceiling grid can carry sky or leaves seen from below. Nothing heavy and no glass hangs over a patient's face.
 

### The front desk, the brand wall and the corridor
The front desk takes one strong work, sized to the wall and to the line of sight from the door, because it is the first thing a patient sees. Dental office artwork here can carry the practice's identity without the logo doing all the work: a palette drawn from the brand, or a subject tied to the neighborhood. Keep the logo smaller and to one side.
 Past the desk, the corridor can take bolder work, because patients walk it briefly and by choice: a sequence on one center line, 57 to 60 inches from the floor, reads as one walk. Diplomas and certificates get a wall of their own.

### Pediatric and family practices
A pediatric practice needs art children can read from their own height. In the waiting area, a mural or large printed wall covering works better than framed art at child height: no glass, no corners, and it can be specified to wipe clean. Framed works go above reach. Choose subjects with things to find and count, such as animals or boats, rather than cartoon characters, which date quickly and, when licensed, need permission. A family practice can keep one pediatric corner and let the rest stay calm for adults.
 

### Cosmetic and premium practices
A cosmetic practice sells a result patients judge with their eyes, so its dental office wall art has to look chosen, not ordered from a catalog. Originals and commissions carry more weight here than decor prints. Keep smile photographs and before and after images in the consultation materials, not on the art walls: a gallery of teeth undoes the calm.

### Cleaning, glazing and durability
Art in a dental practice is specified for cleaning before it is chosen, and your infection control guidance comes first.

- Operatories. Smooth, sealed surfaces your team can wipe with the products it already uses: face mounted acrylic prints, sealed frames, or works behind acrylic. No textiles or open canvas near treatment.
- Glazing. Acrylic rather than glass near patients: lighter and shatter resistant. Some acrylics scratch with the wrong cleaner, so agree products first. Anti reflective glazing where light would glare.
- Works on paper and photographs always go behind glazing, away from direct sun.
- Fixings. Security fixings, so a work cannot be lifted or knocked loose.
More on hardware in framing and installing large scale art. My own installation team hangs the works, I carry insurance, and I install after clinic hours, so no patient sees a ladder in reception.

### Working with your designer on art
Bring the art in while your designer is still drawing, not after the chairs arrive. The designer's plan, palette and lighting come first, and I work alongside designers and architects, not around them. Early matters: a picture light or a backlit ceiling panel needs power. More in working with your interior designer on art; how I plan a practice with your team is on my page for medical practices, and the same process covers art for an office or a business.
On budget: in most cases, buying art through me costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction, bidders push the price up; a gallery's price carries its venue, inventory and staff. I have none of those costs. The price includes a private consultation for your practice and my work with you until the art is on the wall, and I represent you, not a roster of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. More on this in what an art advisor costs.
I am based in Tenafly and work with practices across Bergen County, northern New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere, with more than 15 years in the art world. If you are opening, moving or refreshing a practice, start with art for medical practices.

Questions:

Q: What are some good decorations for a dentist office?
A: Good decorations for a dentist office are calm, readable artworks placed where patients actually look: one strong work at the front desk, landscapes, water or quiet color in the waiting room, one calm work on the wall a reclined patient faces, and a sequence of works along the corridor. Choose fewer, larger pieces over many small prints. Leave out teeth, dental jokes and spa clichés, and specify every frame and surface to be wiped clean.

Q: What should I put in my dental waiting room?
A: A dental waiting room works best with one large calm work, or a pair that reads as one, on the wall patients face from their seats: a landscape, water, light or soft color with enough detail to return to. Hang it 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above the seat backs, about two thirds of the seating's width. Keep ambiguous or crowded images out, and put every work on paper behind glazing.

Q: How do I decorate a pediatric dental office?
A: A pediatric dental office is best decorated at two heights: a washable mural or large printed wall covering at a child's eye level, and framed works above their reach. Pick subjects with things to find and count, such as animals, boats or a busy landscape, instead of licensed cartoon characters, which date quickly and need permission to use. Keep the treatment spaces calmer than the waiting area, and give parents one wall that is simply good art.

Q: What art works on the ceiling above a dental chair?
A: The art that works on the ceiling above a dental chair is light, fixed and calm: a printed or backlit panel set into the ceiling grid, showing sky, leaves or water seen from below. A framed work under glass should never hang over a patient's face. Keep the panel clear of the operatory light and any equipment mounted overhead, and agree its surface and fixing with your designer and your infection control guidance.

### Dining room art: what to hang, how big, and how high

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/dining-room-art/

Dining room art is hung for people who are sitting: one large work, or a pair or row that reads as one, about two thirds the width of the sideboard or table below it. Hang it lower than in a hallway, with the frame clear of the chair backs, and choose a work you can look at for an hour, because in a dining room you do.

The dining room is the one room where people sit facing a single wall for a long time. A work in a hallway gets a few seconds; the work across the table gets the whole dinner. That changes what I choose, how large I go and how low I hang it. Here is how I approach a dining room, with the measurements I use.

### What kind of art belongs on a dining wall?
Choose a work that rewards long looking. Paintings with depth, layered color or a surface that changes as the light moves hold up through a meal and a hundred more. So do large photographs with a lot to discover, and landscapes or abstracts with a strong horizontal line, which echo the table and calm the room. The work does not need to show food; it only needs to hold a long look.
 What rarely works is the loud single-idea image: a slogan, a huge face staring down the table, a joke you stop laughing at the second time. Your guests sit in fixed seats; someone will face that work all evening.
For color, I take one color the room already has, from the chairs, the wood or the rug, and let the work bring one it does not have. A dining room in oak and white can take deep blue or terracotta; matching the art to the upholstery makes it look like part of the furniture order. A mirror doubles the light, but it also doubles the table and the pendants; if you want one, give it a side wall and keep the art on the wall your guests face.

### Four dining wall layouts that work
 
- One main work centered above the sideboard or on the table's axis. The simplest option and usually the strongest, and in a small dining area usually the only one needed.
- A row of two or three smaller works that read as one gesture. In a new house in Closter, New Jersey, three small paintings in blues, pinks and violets hang in a row above the oak table, close in scale and palette, under two black pendants. The key is that they are related, and the gaps are tight: 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm).
- A vertical pair on either side of a doorway or window, when there is no single wide wall.
- A gallery wall on a long wall facing the table, for a collection of smaller works. It suits a dining room that doubles as a library or a family room; see gallery wall ideas for the layout rules.

### How big: the two thirds rule, measured
The art, or the group, should span about two thirds of the furniture under it. Measure the sideboard if there is one on that wall; if the wall is behind the table with nothing against it, measure the table.
 
- 60 inch (152 cm) sideboard: art about 40 inches wide (102 cm).
- 72 inch (183 cm) sideboard: about 48 inches (122 cm).
- 84 inch (213 cm) table: about 56 inches (142 cm).
- 96 inch (244 cm) table: about 64 inches (163 cm), or three works of 19 inches with 3 inch gaps.
Most people buy too small for a dining room, because they judge the size standing close to the wall. Tape the outline of the work on the wall and look at it from the far chair before you buy.

### How high: hang for people who are sitting
Hang dining room art lower than in a hallway, because guests see it from a chair, and keep the frame clear of the chair backs. The standing rule of 57 to 60 inches from how to hang pictures can put a work above seated eyes, and no study gives a seated number. The only published figure is one retailer's: Artfully Walls suggests a center of about 52 to 57 inches (132 to 145 cm) for dining rooms. Test any height from the chairs themselves.
 

### Light, glass and the pendant problem
Pendants and chandeliers hang low over the table, and every glazed frame across from them shows a reflection of the fixture. For that wall, choose canvas or panel without glass, or ask your framer for anti-reflective glazing. Light the work itself with a ceiling spot aimed at about 30 degrees from vertical, on a dimmer, so the art stays visible when the pendants are low. Where that spot goes for your ceiling height, and which bulb to buy, are in how to light art.
 Restaurants follow the same logic at a larger scale, with low evening light and every table as a viewpoint. I work on those rooms too; see art for restaurants.

### Open plan dining areas
In an open plan space, art is what tells you the dining area is a room. Center one work on the axis of the table, not on the wall, even if the wall continues past it. The table and the work together mark the zone, and the living area can carry a different scale.
 

### Protecting the work
A dining room next to an open kitchen gets steam, heat and grease; candles leave soot. Works on paper and photographs need glazing there. The Northeast Document Conservation Center advises keeping framed color photographs and watercolors out of direct sun and spotlights, so give those works the wall the sun does not reach, and keep original canvases away from the kitchen side.
 

### A checklist before you buy

- Measure the sideboard or table and the wall, and write down two thirds of the furniture width.
- Note the chair back height and the pendant position.
- Decide the viewing seat: the host's chair or the seat facing the wall. Judge the work from there.
- Choose one room color to repeat and one to add.
- Tape the outline on the wall and look at it from the far chair.
- Decide glass or no glass according to the pendants and the window.
 

### The mistakes I see most often

- Too small. A 24 inch print above a 96 inch table.
- Too high. Hung for standing guests in a room where everyone sits.
- Glass opposite the chandelier. It shows the fixture, not the work. Choose anti-reflective glazing or no glass.
- Matching the chairs instead of choosing a work. Repeat one color the room has and bring one it lacks.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
A dining room is often where a family's most important work hangs, the one guests face for hours. I plan spaces like this for homes and for interior designers; the Closter house is one of them. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. If you are starting to buy, read how to start an art collection, or send me a photo of your dining wall through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What kind of art should hang in the dining room?
A: Dining room art should reward long looking, because people sit facing it through a whole meal. Paintings with layered color or texture, large photographs with detail to discover, and landscapes or abstracts with a strong horizontal line all work well. Avoid loud single-idea images that someone would have to face all evening.

Q: What size art should go in a dining room?
A: Dining room art should be about two thirds of the width of the furniture below it. Measure the sideboard if one stands on that wall, or the table if the art hangs behind it. A 72 inch sideboard takes art about 48 inches wide; a 96 inch table takes a work or group about 64 inches wide.

Q: How high should art hang in a dining room?
A: Dining room art hangs lower than art in a hallway, because people see it sitting down. No study sets a seated height; one retailer, Artfully Walls, suggests a center of about 52 to 57 inches (132 to 145 cm) for dining rooms. Above a sideboard, leave 6 to 10 inches above its top, and behind chairs keep the frame at least 6 to 8 inches above the tallest chair back.

Q: What is the best wall art for a dining room?
A: The best wall art for a dining room is the work you will still want to look at after a hundred dinners. In practice that is usually a painting with depth, layered color or a surface that changes with the light, in a palette that repeats one color from the room and adds one it lacks. The best choice depends on the room and on you, not on a list.

Q: Should dining room art be horizontal or vertical?
A: Dining room art above a table or a sideboard is usually best horizontal, because it echoes the long line of the furniture. Vertical works suit narrow walls, the spaces beside a doorway or window, and pairs. A row of two or three vertical works hung close together can also read as one horizontal composition.

Q: Should dining room art have glass?
A: Dining room works on paper and photographs need glazing, especially near an open kitchen, where steam and grease reach the walls. If the work faces a chandelier or a window, choose anti-reflective glazing so the fixture does not appear in the picture, or choose a canvas or panel that needs no glass.

### Entryway and hallway art: what to hang where people pass

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/entryway-art/

Entryway art is the first work a guest sees and the last one they remember, so it needs presence, fast: one strong work or a matched pair, sized to the wall, facing or beside the door. Hang it with its center 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 cm) above a console. Hallways and stairs, seen in motion, want a rhythm of works instead.

Entrances and hallways are the most looked-at walls in a house and the least looked-at art. Everyone passes them several times a day, rarely stopping. After more than 15 years in the art world, in museums, in a gallery and in homes, I treat them as their own problem: art seen in passing, often for only a few seconds.

### An entry is read in seconds
A foyer does not give a work time to be studied. It is read on the way in and remembered on the way out. That asks for presence: scale, color, a clear image or a strong surface. It does not ask for detail you need to stand close to see. Whether the work is bold or calm matters less than whether it holds from the doorway.
In a garden villa in Caesarea, the foyer was bright, white and bare, with a black front door and an open staircase. I placed two tall portraits of women, one in greens with a crown of pink, one in deep blues with a flare of orange, facing the front door, so the first exchange in the house is between the person arriving and the two women who meet them. Same scale, same texture, same slim black frames: two works, one statement.
From the door they read as presence and color. Up close they read as paint, built up in layers you want to touch. That double reading is what I look for in entry art: a work that holds from the doorway and rewards the guest who stops. A decorative print that looks the same at every distance cannot do that.
 An office reception is an entryway with a job to do: it tells a client what kind of firm they are visiting. For that version of the wall, see art for law firms and art for an office or a business.

### Where should art go in an entryway?
The strongest work goes on the first wall you see from the open door; the walls beside the door and at the foot of the stair come next.
 
- The wall facing the front door is the first choice: it is what the door frames when it opens.
- The wall beside the door, often above a console or a bench, is the second.
- The foot of the stair, where everyone passes several times a day. In a Closter house, a large framed work in gold and violet sits above a bench and a bonsai at the foot of the stair.
- Near the entrance, not in it, when the house has one overwhelming feature. In a seafront apartment in Herzliya Pituach, a large painting of an aged window hangs near the entrance, so the first window you see is painted and the next ones are real and full of sea.
 

### What size above a console or bench
The work, or the pair, should span about two thirds of the console's or bench's width, with 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 cm) between its top and the bottom of the frame. On a tall entry wall, choose a vertical format or a pair of tall works rather than hanging a small work higher. In a small entry with no console, hang one work on the wall facing the door and keep its frame flat to the wall. A mirror is often wanted in the entry too; hang it on a different wall from the main work, so each has its own place.
 

### Narrow hallways
 In a narrow hallway you stand close to every wall, so large works cannot be seen whole. Choose smaller works that reward a close look: works on paper, photographs, a series of prints. Hang them on one centerline at 57 to 60 inches, with the same gap between every frame, as a rhythm you walk past. Keep frames slim and flat so shoulders and bags do not catch them, and hang on one side only if the hall is very tight.

### Long hallways and the end wall
A long hallway has two jobs for art. Along its length, a rhythm: a series hung on one centerline, with the same gap between every work. At its end, a destination: one stronger work on the end wall, lit, that draws you down the hall. The end wall is the only place in a hallway where a large work can be seen whole, from the far end.
 In a hallway that leads to the bedrooms, family photographs can be the series: framed alike, matted alike and hung on one line, they read as one set rather than as a collection of moments.

### Stairs
On a staircase, the centerline follows the pitch of the stair: measure 57 to 60 inches straight up from the nosing line, the line joining the front edges of the treads, and connect the points. Keep the lowest frames clear of the handrail. A stair wall can take a gallery hang or a single tall work on the landing. The layout rules and a stair diagram are in gallery wall ideas, and the nail formula in how to hang pictures.
 

### Light, glass and wear
Entries and hallways are often the darkest spaces in a house. A ceiling spot aimed at about 30 degrees from vertical, or a picture light, turns a work from a shape into a painting (where it goes and which bulb to use: how to light art). Glass in a dim hallway reflects the light fittings, so choose anti-reflective glazing or unglazed works. These walls also get knocked: fix every work on two points, add bumpers to the lower corners, and consider acrylic rather than glass where people carry bags past.

### The mistakes I see most often

- A small work alone on a tall entry wall. Choose a tall format or a pair instead.
- Large works in a narrow hallway, where they cannot be seen whole.
- Uneven gaps along a hallway, which break the rhythm.
- An end wall left empty, when it is the one place a large work can be seen whole.
- Glass in a dark hallway, reflecting the ceiling light.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
The entry sets the tone for the whole house, and it is one of the few walls every guest sees. I choose and place works for entrances as part of whole-house plans, and handle framing and installation. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, working across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. See the Caesarea garden villa for a foyer from start to finish, or write to me through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What art should go in an entryway?
A: Entryway art needs presence from a few steps away: strong scale, color or surface, rather than fine detail you need to stand close to see. One large work or a matched pair usually works best. Place it on the wall facing the front door or above a console beside it, with its center 57 to 60 inches from the floor.

Q: What size art should hang above an entryway console?
A: Art above an entryway console should be about two thirds of the console's width, with 6 to 10 inches between the top of the console and the bottom of the frame. On a tall entry wall, choose a vertical work or a pair of tall works rather than hanging a small work higher up. Tape the outline on the wall first and look at it from the front door.

Q: What kind of art looks good in a hallway?
A: Hallway art depends on the hallway. In a narrow one, smaller works that reward a close look: works on paper, photographs or a series of prints, hung on one centerline with equal gaps. In a long one, the same rhythm along the walls and one stronger, lit work on the end wall, which is the only place a large work can be seen whole.

Q: What should I put at the end of a long hallway?
A: The end of a long hallway takes one strong work, larger than the works along the hallway, centered on the end wall and lit with a ceiling spot or picture light. The end wall gives the hallway a destination and is the one place in a hall where a large work can be seen from far enough away to read it whole.

Q: How high should art be hung in a hallway or entry?
A: Art in a hallway or entry hangs with its center 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, the same eye-level line used everywhere in the house. In a hallway series, keep every work on the same centerline. Above a console or bench, leave 6 to 10 inches below the frame. On stairs, measure 57 to 60 inches up from the nosing line.

Q: How do I make my front entrance look expensive?
A: A front entrance looks expensive when it has one real work with presence rather than several small decorative pieces, sized properly to the wall, framed simply and lit. A single well-chosen original or signed edition, hung at the right height, does more for an entrance than a wall of decorative pieces.

### Financial advisor office decor: art for the space where clients talk about money

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/financial-advisor-office-art/

Financial advisor office decor is the art and finish of the space where clients talk about money, chosen to feel stable, discreet and personal rather than showy. The meeting space matters most: one strong, calm work does more than a wall of market imagery. Below: the meeting space, reception, what to leave out, the trends that last, clients who collect, and how to buy the art.

A client who has come to talk about money reads the space before anyone speaks. Every wall should say two things: this advisor is steady, and this conversation is private. I have spent more than 15 years in the art world, in established museums and in a gallery I managed in Tel Aviv, and the brief for an advisory office is short: calm, personal, never showy.

### Why decor matters where people talk about money
Decor matters here because clients are paying for judgment, and the walls are the first judgment they see. Good financial office decor should not look expensive; it should look settled. A display of wealth on the walls invites the wrong question, about whose money paid for it.
 Research backs the care but promises nothing. In University of Exeter studies of more than 2,000 office workers, people in spaces with plants and pictures were about 17 percent more productive than people in bare ones, and about 32 percent more when they designed their own space (Knight and Haslam, 2010). The useful finding is the second: people do better in a space they chose.

### The meeting space: calm, one strong work, no clutter
Give the meeting space one strong work that rewards a long look, and keep everything else quiet: no awards wall, no row of small prints. Clients may sit there for an hour, so choose a work that holds attention without competing for it: a landscape, a quiet abstraction, a photograph or a work on paper, well framed. If the wall the client faces is behind you, keep the work calm enough to frame you, not pull their eyes from your face. The first piece of art for a financial advisor office belongs here.
 1strong work on the main wall of the meeting space2/3of the width of the credenza or sideboard below it57 to 60incenter from the floor where people stand, as in reception (145 to 152 cm), not where they sit 
- Size. About two thirds of the credenza's width; on an open wall, see large wall art ideas.
- Height. People sit here, and no reliable seated height rule exists: start from how high to hang art, then check a paper template from the client's chair.
- Light and glass. Glass opposite a window becomes a mirror; use anti-reflective glazing. Keep works on paper and color photographs out of direct sun: light damage is cumulative and cannot be reversed (Northeast Document Conservation Center).
 This is the approach behind my page on art for wealth management offices.

### Reception and the first impression
Reception takes one anchor work that sets the tone in the first minute, because every client sees it. People pass it standing, so center it 57 to 60 inches from the floor, on the wall the eye meets from the door. More on art for reception and the rest of an office.
 

### Your own office
Your own office is where personal belongs. For a home office in Caesarea, I chose two works that reflected the client's two loves, horses and music, by artists living and working in the client's country of origin: one existing painting was acquired, and another was specially commissioned from the same artist (the Caesarea home office).

### What to avoid: bulls, bears, tickers and slogans
Leave out anything that reads as a sales prop: bull and bear sculptures, ticker and chart imagery, stock skylines and motivational slogans. Much of the finance office wall art sold online is exactly this, and it puts the market in the space during a conversation that may be about a client's fear of it.
 More in my guide to office wall art.

### Current office decor trends that suit an advisory firm
The office decor trends worth following are the ones that last: fewer and larger original works, natural texture and landscape, and art by living artists. The test: will you still want to sit across from it in ten years?

- Keep: originals over posters. One original, or a framed limited edition, outlasts a wall of mass produced canvases.
- Keep: living artists, including local ones. A living artist can be met, commissioned and introduced to a client. Collectors are buying closer to artists too: the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2025, which covered 3,100 high net worth collectors in 10 markets, found that participation in buying directly from artists had more than doubled since the previous survey.
- Skip: art matched to the carpet, word art and statement walls. They date with this year's finishes.

### Art as a conversation with clients who collect
The art in your office can start a second conversation, with the clients who collect. Some will ask about a work, and a small wall label with the artist, the title and the year invites them to; a few will ask for help with art at home. Then you want a curator to introduce: forward my page for wealth managers, family offices and private bankers and copy me. Introductions are by email, discretion is the default, and I work within your firm's rules. I bring the same approach to investment firms.
I do not give investment advice. If a client asks whether art is a good investment, the research is sobering: a study of 32,928 paintings sold more than once between 1960 and 2013 found that correcting for selection bias cut average annual returns from 8.7 to 6.3 percent, though some styles and top selling artists may do better (Korteweg, Kräussl and Verwijmeren, 2016). More in starting an art collection.

### Buying, commissioning or leasing
Buy the main work for the meeting space, commission when a wall needs something made for your firm, and lease only when you want the works to change. My guide to buying, leasing or commissioning office art compares them. On a tight budget, start with one original in the meeting space, framed and lit properly.
On price, in most cases you can buy art through a private curator for less than at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction, many bidders compete for the same work and push the price up; a gallery prices with big margins to cover its venue, its inventory and its gallerists. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable than almost anywhere else, and the price includes private consultation for your office and my work with you until the art is on the wall. I represent you, not a roster of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. More on what working with an art advisor costs.
My own installation team hangs the works, after hours if needed, and I can provide a certificate of insurance naming your landlord or managing agent: details on my page on art for wealth management offices.

Questions:

Q: What are the current office decor trends?
A: The current office decor trends worth following are the ones that will last: fewer and larger original works, natural texture and landscape, and art by living artists, including artists from the firm's own region. Among collectors, the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2025 found participation in buying directly from artists had more than doubled since the previous survey. My test: will you still want to sit across from it in ten years? Word art, statement walls and art matched to this year's finishes usually fail it.

Q: How should a financial advisor decorate their office?
A: A financial advisor should decorate the office so it feels calm, settled and personal, never showy. Put one strong, well framed original in the meeting space, one anchor work in reception at eye level, and the most personal piece in your own office. Leave out bulls, bears, tickers, slogans and anything that reads as a display of wealth. Light the work, choose glazing that does not reflect the windows, and keep the rest of the walls quiet.

Q: Should a financial advisor display art they own?
A: Yes, a financial advisor can display art they own, usually in their own office, where a personal work tells clients something true about them. Choose a work you can talk about for its story rather than its value, and do not hang a famous name as a trophy in the meeting space. Check that your insurance covers the work at the office, keep works on paper out of direct sun, and hang anything heavy on two hooks, into studs wherever the wall allows.

### Gallery wall ideas, and how to hang one like a curator

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/gallery-wall-ideas/

A gallery wall is a group of framed works hung close together and read as one composition, not a collection of frames. The gallery wall ideas below all follow one rule: treat the whole group as a single artwork. Center it 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, keep 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) between frames, build it around one anchor piece, and plan it on paper before a single nail goes in.

Most gallery walls that disappoint fail for one reason: they were assembled, not composed. The frames came as a set, the gaps were judged by eye, and the group went up too high. I have seen it in more than 15 years in the art world, in museums, in a gallery I managed in Tel Aviv and in private homes.

### Five gallery wall layouts, and when each one works
Choose the layout by the wall and by how settled the collection is. Whatever the layout, the whole group is treated as one work.
 

### What measurements make a gallery wall look composed?
Four numbers do the work: the center height, the gap, the width and the size of the anchor.
 57 to 60incenter of the whole group from the floor (145 to 152 cm)2 to 3inbetween frames, the same gap everywhere (5 to 8 cm)2/3of the width of the furniture below
- Height. The same 57 to 60 inch line I use for a single work, measured to the center of the group, not of the biggest frame. For single works, see how high to hang art.
- Spacing. 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) between frames on most walls, up to 4 inches (10 cm) when the frames themselves are large. Consistency matters more than the exact number: a wall with gaps of 2, 5 and 3 inches looks accidental.
- Above furniture. The lowest frame sits 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above the back of a sofa or a headboard, or 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 cm) above a console, and the group spans about two thirds of the furniture's width. Above an 84 inch sofa, that is a group about 56 inches wide. More on what size art to hang above a couch.
- Scale. The anchor should be at least two to three times the size of the smallest work. A wall of equal small frames reads as confetti.
- Margins. On an open wall with no furniture, leave at least 12 inches (30 cm) of bare wall at each side of the group.
Odd or even numbers of frames matter less than one outer shape and one anchor. Around a television, treat the screen as one dark frame in the group, with the same gaps around it.
 

### What should go on a gallery wall?
Works that share one thread, around one anchor you love. The thread matters more than the layout: it tells the eye these works belong together. It can be color, subject, medium, the period of the works or the frames, but choose one, two at most. Matching the sofa is not a thread. A wall of black and white photographs with one small oil in deep red has a thread and an accent. A wall with no thread is a pinboard.
Then choose the anchor, the work the rest of the wall answers to. It should be the piece you love most, not the piece that fits the biggest gap. Mix mediums once the thread holds: a work on paper, a small painting, a photograph, even a flat object in a shadow box. Keep the frames in one family, all black, all natural wood or all thin gold, and vary the mats instead: a generous mat gives a small work presence beside a larger one. Mixed frames can work too: whether they do depends on how all the works read together.
 My own rule: leave space for the next work. A collection grows, and a wall that is full on day one has nowhere to go. To start that collection properly, read how to start an art collection.
 

### How do you hang a gallery wall without extra holes?
Plan on paper, test with templates, then nail, anchor first.
 
- Mark the zone. Measure the wall, decide the group's outer size and outline it with painter's tape.
- Compose on the floor. Tape the same rectangle on the floor and arrange the works inside it, anchor first. Photograph each version from above.
- Make templates. Trace every frame on kraft paper and cut it out. Measure from the top of the frame to the hanging point (the taut wire or the D-ring) and mark that point on the template.
- Test on the wall. Tape the templates up, stand back from where you will actually see the wall, and live with it for a day.
- Hang the anchor first. Nail through its template mark, then work outward, checking every gap with a spacer block cut to your chosen distance.
- Tear the paper away and level. A small dot of museum putty or a clear bumper on the lower corners keeps each frame straight.
 For hardware, use two hooks or two D-rings on anything heavier than a small frame, screwed into a stud or into anchors rated well above its weight. Wire on one point lets frames swing; I avoid it on gallery walls.

### Stairs, plaster and other hard walls
 On a staircase, the centerline follows the pitch of the stair: measure 57 to 60 inches straight up from the nosing line, the line joining the front edges of the treads, below each work, and connect those points with a chalk or tape line. Keep the group parallel to the handrail and clear of it. On plaster, drill a small pilot hole first; a hammered nail can crack it. On brick, use masonry anchors. If the wall is tiled or glass, a picture rail or a ledge is the honest answer.

### The mistakes I see most often

- Hanging too high. The group loses the furniture below it. Bring the center down to 57 to 60 inches.
- Gaps that drift. Use a spacer block, not your eye.
- No anchor. Build around one larger work.
- Glass opposite a window. Glare hides the work. Use anti-reflective glazing, or hang works on paper where the light is soft.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
A gallery wall is a small exhibition. When the works are valuable, the wall is tall, or the lighting is still open, plan it with someone who composes walls for a living. I do this for homes and for interior designers who want the art handled, from choosing the works to framing and installation. In an office corridor the same rules hold; the six steps for an office show where a series fits in the whole plan. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. Send me a photo of the wall through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What is the rule for gallery walls?
A: The rule for a gallery wall is to treat the whole group as one artwork. Center it 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, keep 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) between frames, build around one anchor piece that is two to three times the size of the smallest work, and choose a single thread, such as color, medium or frame, so the works read as a family.

Q: How far apart should frames be on a gallery wall?
A: Frames on a gallery wall should sit 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) apart on most walls, and up to 4 inches (10 cm) when the frames are large or the wall is very big. What matters most is that the gaps are equal. Cut a block of wood or card to your chosen width and use it as a spacer as you hang.

Q: How many pictures should be in a gallery wall?
A: A gallery wall has no fixed number of pictures. Three is the smallest group that reads as a gallery wall, five to nine suits most walls above a sofa or bed, and a salon hang on a tall wall can take twenty or more. Decide the outer size of the group first, then fill it with as many works as keep the gaps even.

Q: Are gallery walls out of style in 2026?
A: Gallery walls built from matching print sets feel dated. Walls built from works you chose do not follow trends: salon walls have been hung for centuries. If your wall has a thread, an anchor and room to grow, it will not look like a trend in five years.

Q: What are common gallery wall mistakes?
A: The common gallery wall mistakes are hanging the group too high, letting the gaps drift, using only small frames of the same size with no anchor, hanging glass opposite a bright window, and filling the whole wall on day one. Plan with paper templates and a spacer block, and most of these disappear before the first nail.

### Hotel artwork: how hotels choose art, from the lobby to the guest room

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/hotel-artwork/

Hotel artwork is a property's art program: the arrival piece in the lobby, the restaurant and bar works, the rhythm of the corridors and the guest room art, planned to one concept and bought within a budget per key. Public spaces usually carry originals and commissions, and guest rooms usually carry editions repeated with variation. Below is how I would plan it, zone by zone, for a boutique or independent hotel, and the honest answer for guests: where hotel art comes from and whether you can buy it.

A homeowner can buy one painting and stop. A hotel has to tell one story across a lobby, a bar, corridors and many guest rooms that look alike, and have it on the walls by opening day. I have spent more than 15 years in the art world, since 2010, and my hospitality work includes collections built while collaborating with luxury hospitality leaders. If you are planning one now, the service itself is on art for boutique hotels.

### What hotel artwork has to do for a property
Hotel artwork, like all hospitality art, has three jobs: tell guests where they are, give each zone the right intensity, and survive years of hard use. First, a guest should know which city and which building they are in the moment they arrive, and the strongest collections do this with artists and makers connected to the place, not with postcards of its skyline. The second is volume: a statement at arrival, rhythm in the corridors, calm in the rooms. The third is practical: daylight, cleaning and security.
 

### The lobby: the photograph every guest takes
The lobby carries the arrival piece, the one work guests remember and photograph, so I would choose it, and commission it where the concept calls for it, before anything else. Hotel lobby art is sized for the architecture, not for a living room: it has to read from the doors, the desk and the far seating. The wall behind the desk looks obvious on a plan, but staff and a queue stand in front of it, so the work clears their heads or faces the entrance.
 A single large painting, a relief or a sculptural work usually holds that distance better than a group of small pieces. For proportion, see large wall art ideas, and for works this size, framing and installing large scale art.
 

### Restaurants, bars and corridors
Restaurant and bar art is seen at night, from seats, under low light. It needs strong contrast, surfaces that tolerate heat and steam, and a height judged from the chairs. A bar usually wants one memorable gesture rather than many small works. A hotel restaurant follows the same rules as any other; I cover them on art for restaurants.
Corridors are seen on the move, so they need rhythm more than statements. A series hung at a steady interval, each center on the same eye level line of 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm), carries the story from the elevator to the door. A different series on each floor helps guests tell the floors apart.
 

### Guest rooms: editions, repetition and variety
Hotel room art is where a collection is tested: a work that looks right in one room has to look right in every room of that type, and survive housekeeping. Guest rooms usually carry editions, a family of related works chosen and framed as a set, so the lobby's voice continues without repeating the arrival piece. Variety comes from rotation: several images spread across the floors, so neighbors rarely share a picture. Above the bed, the rules of a home apply.
2/3of the headboard's width, for the work above the bed8 to 10infrom the top of the headboard to the frame (20 to 25 cm)2points of fixing, with security hardware, never one nail Over a pillow, acrylic glazing is lighter and safer than glass. For the same calm at home, see art above a bed.

### Budget per key: how a hotel art program is planned and staged
Budget per key is the art budget expressed per guest room, or key, the unit hotel projects use to budget their fit out. Ask first what the number includes: some owners count only the guest rooms, others fold in the lobby, restaurants and corridors. In most cases a budget goes further with a private curator: there is no gallery margin and no bidding war on top of the work, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable than buying through a gallery or at a large auction. That price includes a private consultation that covers the whole property, and my work with you until the art is on the wall. I represent the client, not a roster of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world the concept needs.
The program runs in a fixed order: a written concept, approved before a single work is sourced; an artwork schedule giving every area a line with the location, type of work, size and budget; then sourcing, commissions first because they take longest. Every stage is planned backward from the opening date; how long it takes depends on the scope, so the art belongs in the plan while walls and lighting are still being designed. More on how art for hotels and hospitality is made, and on what an art advisor costs.

### Originals, editions and commissions
An original is a unique work, and it belongs where guests stop and look: the lobby, the bar, the suites. A commission is an original made for the property, the right answer when the concept needs a subject, a size or a local story that does not exist yet. An edition is one of a limited, numbered run printed from an artist's image, usually by a fine art print studio, and it is how a hotel brings real artists into every guest room. What I avoid is generic hotel wall art: the open edition decor print, produced without limit, which fills a wall and tells guests nothing about where they are.
 

### Where hotel art comes from, and can a guest buy it
Hotel art usually comes from an art program run by a consultant or curator, or from decor prints bought in volume. Loved a piece during a stay? Ask at the front desk: some properties can name their artists. If the work is an edition, the artist or the studio that printed it may still sell one from the run. Some hotels sell work in their shop, and after a renovation, surplus and liquidation sellers resell guest room art. If what you loved was the calm of the room, I can build that for your home.

### Working with a hotel art consultant
A hotel art consultant should give you a written concept rooted in the place and the brand, an artwork schedule you can track, and one approved budget. I work inside the design team's scheme and the brand's standards, not around them, whether the owner brings me in directly or the design firm does. Every piece is signed off before anything is ordered. Printmakers and framers work to my brief, my own installation team hangs the works, after hours where guests are already staying, and I can provide a certificate of insurance naming the owner or managing agent on request. How I take on a property is on art for boutique hotels.
I am based in Tenafly, in Bergen County, New Jersey, and work across New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere; for projects in the city, see art curator in New York.

Questions:

Q: Where do hotels get their artwork?
A: Hotels usually get their artwork through an art program run by a consultant or curator. The consultant sources originals from artists and galleries, commissions the signature works for the lobby and the bar, and has limited editions produced by print studios for the guest rooms. Some properties buy decor prints in volume from suppliers instead. For a boutique hotel, I would plan the whole program to one written concept and one budget, from the arrival piece to the last corridor.

Q: Where can I find hotel art for sale?
A: Hotel art for sale turns up in four places. Ask the hotel first: some properties can name the artist of a work you liked. If the piece is a limited edition, the artist or the print studio may still sell one from the run. Some hotels sell work in their shop. After a renovation, surplus and liquidation sellers resell guest room art. If you want the feeling rather than the exact piece, a curator can find or commission something close for your home.

Q: How to decorate a room like a hotel?
A: To decorate a room like a hotel, choose one calm work in one voice and hang it with hotel discipline. Above the bed, the work should be about two thirds as wide as the headboard and hang 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above it, fixed on two points. Keep the frames in one family, the palette quiet and the lighting soft, and leave the other walls mostly bare. A hotel room feels calm because nothing on its walls competes.

Q: What should a hotel lobby have?
A: A hotel lobby should have one arrival piece: a work sized for the architecture that tells guests where they are the moment they walk in. It should read from the entrance, the desk and the seating, belong to the city and the building rather than repeat a skyline cliche, and be lit as carefully as it is chosen. Everything else in the lobby, from seating to signage, should leave that work the space to be seen.

Q: What does budget per key mean for hotel art?
A: Budget per key is a hotel's art budget expressed per guest room, or key. Some owners count only the guest rooms, others include the lobby, restaurants and corridors, so the first question is what the number covers. In most cases a budget per key goes further through a private curator, because there is no gallery margin or auction bidding on top of the work. The price includes a private consultation for the whole property, and I represent the property, not a roster of artists.

Q: How many artworks does a hotel need?
A: The number of artworks a hotel needs comes from the artwork schedule, not from a formula. I would walk the plans and give every wall that matters a line: the arrival piece and the public spaces, each restaurant and bar, a steady rhythm along each corridor, then each guest room type, with its walls above the bed, the desk and the entry, multiplied by the number of rooms of that type. Suites get their own lines. The total follows from the plans.

### How to choose art for your home

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/how-to-choose-art-for-your-home/

How to choose art for your home comes down to a short sequence of decisions: how you want each space to feel, which wall comes first, how big the work must be, and which budget buys the best version of it. Start with one wall and one feeling, not a shopping list, and buy the work you keep returning to. Below is the order I follow, with the rule for each step and the guide that covers it.

More than 15 years in the art world, from museums to a gallery I managed in Tel Aviv, taught me that the order of decisions matters more than any single choice.
 

### How do you want the space to feel?
Decide the feeling before you look at a single work. Calm, energy, warmth, memory: name one for each space. That one word rules out most of the market. A bedroom that should feel quiet is not helped by the loudest painting you own; a dining room where you host can take a work that starts conversations.
The feeling often comes from your own life. For the Tel Aviv home of singer and actress Roni Daloomi, the answer was three joyful, minimalist works by two contemporary Israeli artists, chosen to reflect her optimistic spirit.
 Will you still like it in ten years? The work you keep returning to, on different days, usually outlasts the one that impressed you once.

### Which wall should you start with?
Start with the wall the space already turns toward: the wall behind the sofa, the one you face from the front door, the long wall of the dining room. Give it the strongest work you can find, and let the other walls support it. One wall done well changes a space more than five done halfway.
 In the Hod Hasharon villa, a single large scale figurative digital artwork was chosen to define the emotional center of the space.

### Size: the rules that prevent most mistakes
Of every rule for how to choose wall art, size prevents the most mistakes. Buy bigger than feels safe: too small is the size mistake design guides name most often.
2/3of the width of the furniture below57 to 60incenter of the work from the floor where people stand (145 to 152 cm)8 to 10inabove a sofa back or headboard (20 to 25 cm) 
- Width. Above furniture, the work spans about two thirds of the furniture's width; design guides range from half to three quarters. On a bare wall, size it to the wall and to where you first see it from.
- Height. Design guides put the center anywhere from 55 to 66 inches; most land at 57 to 60. Where people sit, it comes down; see dining room art and how to hang pictures.
- Test before you buy. Tape the work's outline on the wall and live with it for a day. Paper on the wall shows what a screen hides.
 Is one large work better than several small ones? On a main wall, usually yes: one work reads as a decision, scattered small pieces as clutter. A group works when it is composed as one piece, as in gallery wall ideas.
 

### Color and the space around the work
Art should relate to the space, not match it: art matched to the cushions dates with them. Take one color the space already has, or its temperature, warm or cool, and let the work answer it. Gallerists on a 2026 Artsy panel put it plainly: never match art to your soft furnishings. A work can also bring the color a space lacks. In a renovated Bauhaus home in Tel Aviv, the artwork became the focal point, bringing color and texture into a monochromatic space.
Keep works on paper and color photographs out of direct sun: the Northeast Document Conservation Center notes that light damage is cumulative and irreversible. UV filtering glazing adds protection; it does not replace shade. Glass or gloss facing a window can turn into a mirror. In a Tel Aviv Bauhaus residence, the central work is printed on glossy anti reflective acrylic: the depth of gloss without the mirror.
 Old and new art mix well when the pieces share one thing, a palette or a subject.

### Originals, editions and prints
Put the best original you can on the first wall, the one you see most, and let editions and prints carry the rest. Knowing how to buy art for your home starts with knowing what each one is. An original is one of a kind. A limited edition is a print or photograph made in a stated number, signed and numbered, ideally with a certificate. An open edition print has no limit.
Buy for the wall and for yourself first. A work bought well is also an investment, but no one can honestly tell you which work will rise in value. More on that in starting an art collection. When nothing fits the wall, a work can be commissioned for it. My ten questions before you buy your first serious artwork cover provenance, condition and framing.

### How should you set a budget?
Set the budget per wall, not per piece, and give most of it to the first wall: one strong original does more than many middling pieces. Count the whole cost on the wall: the work, framing, delivery and installation.
Where you buy changes what the budget buys. With a private curator you can, in most cases, buy art for less than at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction, many bidders compete for the same work, which pushes the price up. A gallery prices its works to cover its space, its inventory and its staff. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable than almost anywhere else. More in what an art advisor costs.

### When does a curator save time and money?
A curator, or residential art consultant, saves the most when the stakes are high: a new house with many empty walls, a double height wall, or a collection you want to hold together. The private consultation for your home is included in the price of the work, and I work with you until the art is on the wall; I have my own installation team. A gallery's job is to represent its artists and get them the highest price. I represent you. I have no closed roster and no obligation to any artist, so I can reach out to any artist in the world.
I am an art curator based in Tenafly and choose art for homes across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. See how the art advisory process works, or write to me through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: How do I choose art for my home?
A: Choose art for your home in order. First decide how each space should feel, then pick one wall to start with, usually the wall the space turns toward. Size the work to that wall: about two thirds of the width of the furniture below it, with its center 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor. Then choose an original, an edition or a print within your budget, and buy the work you keep returning to, not the one that fills a gap.

Q: How do you pick wall art for a room?
A: Pick wall art for a room by starting with its main wall and the feeling you want there. Measure the wall and the furniture below it, and look for a work about two thirds of the furniture's width. Relate the art to one color or to the temperature of the room rather than to its fabrics. Test the size with paper taped to the wall, and choose the piece you still want to look at after several visits.

Q: Should art match the room?
A: No, art should not match the room's fabrics or paint. Art chosen to match the cushions reads as part of the upholstery and dates with it. Art should relate to the room instead: share one of its colors, answer its temperature, such as a warm painting in a cool white room, or bring the one color the room lacks. The link is an idea the work and the room share, not a swatch.

Q: Where do I start if I own no art yet?
A: Start with one wall and one work, not the whole house. Spend a few weeks looking before you buy, in museums, galleries and artists' studios, and save images of the works you go back to. Then buy the one work you would be glad to see every day, for the wall you see most, and let the next purchase follow from it. My ten questions before your first serious artwork help you check it before you buy.

### How to hang pictures, and how high to hang art

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/how-to-hang-pictures/

Hang a picture so its center sits 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, a long-standing hanging convention close to a standing adult's eye height. Above a sofa or bed, leave 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) between the furniture and the frame; above a console or mantel, 6 to 10 inches. The rest of how to hang pictures is method: treat a group as one piece, and put the nail where a simple formula tells you, not where your eye guesses.

The most common problem I walk into is not the art. It is the height. Most pictures hang too high, as if the wall had to be filled to the ceiling. I have seen it for more than 15 years in the art world, in museums, a gallery I managed in Tel Aviv and private homes. Here is the rule I use, the nail formula and the exceptions.

### Why 57 to 60 inches?
The 57 inch rule is a long-standing hanging convention: hang a work so its center sits 57 inches (145 cm) from the floor, close to a standing adult's eye height. I work in a band of 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm), and lower where people sit. Eye-level hanging goes back to nineteenth century museums; where the figure 57 came from is undocumented, and published advice spreads from 55 to 66 inches (Emily Henderson uses 57, Studio McGee 60). Treat it as a range, and keep the reason: the center goes where standing eyes rest, so sofas, stairs and chairs move it.
 57 to 60incenter of the work from the floor (145 to 152 cm)8 to 10inabove a sofa back or headboard (20 to 25 cm)6 to 10inabove a console, sideboard or mantel (15 to 25 cm)Measure to the center of the work, not its top edge or the nail, and line up works of different sizes by their centers, not their tops.
 

### How to find exactly where the nail goes
 
- Measure the height of the frame and halve it.
- Measure the drop: pull the wire taut toward the top of the frame and measure from the top edge to the wire. For D-rings or a sawtooth, measure to the hanger itself.
- Nail height = 57 inches + half the frame height, minus the drop.
A 30 inch frame with a 4 inch drop: 57 + 15 minus 4 = a nail at 68 inches. In centimeters, the same frame is 76 cm with a 10 cm drop: 145 + 38 minus 10 = 173 cm.

### When the rule changes
 
- Tall ceilings. Some guides raise the center under ceilings higher than 9 feet. I rarely do: eyes do not move when the ceiling does. A tall wall needs scale instead, a larger work or a group that climbs while its center stays near 60 inches. On any ceiling, I keep the top of a frame at least 12 inches below it.
- Seated spaces. In a dining room or a study, most of the looking happens from a chair, so the center comes down, never so low that a chair back reaches the frame. For dining rooms, one retailer, Artfully Walls, suggests a center of about 52 to 57 inches (132 to 145 cm); see dining room art.
- Pairs and stacks. Two or three works hung together are one composition. For three pictures stacked vertically, keep 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) between frames and put the center of the middle frame at 57 to 60 inches. Larger groups are covered in gallery wall ideas.
 

### How to hang a picture, step by step

- Decide the spot with the frame in hand. Have someone hold it against the wall while you stand where you will usually see it.
- Mark the center line lightly in pencil, then the nail point from the formula.
- Find what is behind the wall. A stud finder locates studs, usually 16 inches (41 cm) apart in American houses, and warns you about pipes and wiring.
- Use painter's tape for two-point hangers. Stick tape across the back of the frame, mark both D-rings on it, move the tape to the wall, level it, and drive the hooks through the marks.
- Hang, level and fix. A clear bumper or a dot of museum putty on the two lower corners keeps the frame from shifting.
 

### Hardware by weight and size
 Choose hooks and anchors rated for at least twice the weight of the work, and screw into a stud whenever you can. With no stud where you need one, spread a heavy work across several rated anchors on a French cleat. On plaster, drill a small pilot hole first; a hammered nail can crack it. On brick, use masonry anchors.

### How to hang art without nails

- Adhesive strips and hooks are fine for light posters and photographs in a rental. Follow the weight rating exactly. I never use them for original works, glazed frames of any size, or in a bathroom, where humidity weakens the bond.
- Picture ledges take a few screws once, then let you lean and swap frames without new holes.
- Leaning a large work on a console, a deep shelf or the floor is a display choice, not a compromise.
- Picture rail systems hang works on cords or rods from a rail near the ceiling, so works slide along it.

### Light it, then check the glare
 A ceiling spot or track light aimed at about 30 degrees from vertical lights the work evenly and throws reflections down toward the floor. The Northeast Document Conservation Center advises keeping framed color photographs and watercolors out of direct sun and spotlights, behind UV-filtering glass or acrylic; ask your framer for an anti-reflective version when a work faces a window.
 

### The mistakes I see most often

- Too high. Bring the center down to 57 to 60 inches.
- Too small for the wall. Group it, or choose a work that can hold the wall.
- One nail for a wide frame. It tilts every time a door closes.
- Guessing the nail point. Use the formula.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
If the work is valuable, heavy, very large or glazed at a large size, or the wall is plaster, stone or over a stair, it should be installed by professionals. Installation is part of how I work, not a separate service: I plan and supervise framing and installation for the works I place, and I help interior designers with the art on their projects. For an office, height is one step of six; working with a corporate art consultant covers choosing, planning, buying, lighting and installing too. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, working across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. To ask about a wall, write to me through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What is the 57 inch rule for hanging pictures?
A: The 57 inch rule is a long-standing hanging convention: hang a work so its center sits 57 inches (145 cm) from the floor, close to the eye height of a standing adult. I use a range of 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm). The rule applies to the center of the work, or the center of a group, not to the top edge or the nail.

Q: What is the 60 inch rule for hanging pictures?
A: The 60 inch rule is the 57 inch rule at the top of the range: the center of the work at 60 inches (152 cm), for spaces where people mostly stand. Very large works often sit lower, not higher; one retailer, Artfully Walls, centers them at about 54 to 57 inches. For the nail, add half the frame height to 60 and subtract the drop to the hanger.

Q: How high do you hang pictures with 9 foot ceilings?
A: Pictures under a 9 foot ceiling hang at the same height as under an 8 foot ceiling: the center at 57 to 60 inches. A higher ceiling does not raise your eyes. What changes is scale. A tall wall can take a larger work, a vertical pair or a salon group that climbs upward while its center stays near 60 inches.

Q: What is the 2/3 rule for hanging pictures?
A: The 2/3 rule for hanging pictures says art hung above furniture should span about two thirds of the furniture's width. Above a 72 inch sideboard, aim for a work or group about 48 inches wide. Leave 8 to 10 inches above a sofa or bed, and 6 to 10 inches above a console, sideboard or mantel.

Q: How high to hang 3 pictures vertically?
A: Three pictures hung vertically are treated as one work. Keep the same gap between them, 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm), and center the middle picture at 57 to 60 inches from the floor, so the stack is centered on eye level. If the bottom frame ends up below the top of nearby furniture, the stack is too tall for the spot.

Q: What is the toothpaste trick for hanging pictures?
A: The toothpaste trick marks the nail point: you dab a little toothpaste on the hanger on the back of the frame, press the frame against the wall where you want it, and the dab leaves a mark where the nail goes. It works, but I prefer painter's tape across the back of the frame: it gives the same marks, handles two D-rings, and puts nothing on the wall.

### How to light art at home and in the office

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/how-to-light-art/

How to light art comes down to one angle and one bulb: aim a ceiling spot or track light at the center of the work at about 30 degrees from vertical, and use a warm 2700 to 3000 K LED with a CRI of 90 or more, on a dimmer.
