Under a 9 foot ceiling that puts the light about 29.5 inches (75 cm) out from the wall, where reflections in the glass fall to the floor instead of into your eyes. Below: the setback for your ceiling, picture lights, how much light each medium can take, glare, and the office ceiling grid.

Light decides whether a work reads as a painting or as a dark shape on the wall. That is why I plan the lighting before the hanging, not after: a spot that lands beside the work is easier to prevent than to fix.

### What is the best way to light art?
The best way to light art is in two layers: soft ambient light for the space, and an accent light on the work itself, at least three times brighter than its surroundings (Lighting Design Lab), and about five times as a common default. Get that contrast by lowering the light around the work, not by pushing more light onto it.
30°from vertical, the aim of the light2700 to 3000Kwarm white90CRIor more, so colors read trueThe main work, usually a canvas, needs its own dimmable light. Give the art walls their own control, separate from the general lighting, so the work still reads when the rest of the space is dimmed for the evening.

### Where should a ceiling spot or track light go?
A ceiling spot or track head goes where its beam meets the center of the work at about 30 degrees from vertical. ERCO, the German lighting maker, judges 30 degrees ideal for pictures: it lights the surface evenly and sends reflections in the glass down to the floor instead of into your eyes.
To find the spot, subtract the height of the work's center from the ceiling height and multiply by 0.58. With the center at 57 inches (145 cm), the usual hanging height explained in how to hang pictures, the setback from the wall is:
 Closer to the wall than that, the frame throws a shadow across the top of the work. Farther out, the reflection climbs toward the eyes of anyone standing close. On a track, set the heads at the setback and aim each one at the center of its work.
Check the beam against the width. Under a 9 foot ceiling the light travels about 59 inches (150 cm) to the work: a 24 degree beam lights a patch about 25 inches (64 cm) wide, a 36 degree beam about 38 inches (97 cm). A work wider than one patch takes two or more heads, overlapping so no seam shows.

### Picture light or ceiling spot?
A picture light suits one framed work of moderate size on a wall with no ceiling light to aim, or a traditional space where the fixture belongs to the look. A ceiling spot or track suits large works, groups, and walls where the art will change, because a head can be re-aimed and a picture light cannot move.
Picture light makers size the light at half to two thirds of the frame's width, so a 30 inch (76 cm) frame takes a light of 15 to 20 inches (38 to 51 cm). Choose an arm long enough to send the light down the face of the work, not only across its top, and keep the lamp clear of the frame. On a tall work a picture light leaves the lower part dim, so light it from the ceiling. A hardwired picture light needs a box in the wall, which is easiest while the walls are open (see planning art in construction drawings).
 

### Which bulb: color temperature and CRI
Use a warm white LED between 2700 and 3000 K, with a color rendering index (CRI) of 90 or more, and make sure it dims. Museums surveyed by the US Department of Energy named 2700 and 3000 K as their targets and a CRI above 85; the same study found that damage potential rises as light gets cooler.
 Keep every light on one wall at the same color temperature, or the white of the wall will look patched. A work reads differently by day and by night, so I check every placement in the space itself, in daylight and under the evening lighting.

### How much light can a work take?
Light damage adds up and never reverses, so the safe level depends on the medium. The Conservation Center for Art and Historic Artifacts sets 50 lux as the most for works on paper, photographs and textiles, and 150 lux for oil paintings. For scale, a living room at night is about 50 lux, an office about 400, and direct sun about 30,000 (Northeast Document Conservation Center).
 The Northeast Document Conservation Center gives a sensitive work about 50,000 lux hours a year. Direct sun spends that in under two hours. So keep watercolors, photographs and works on paper off any wall the sun reaches, frame them behind UV filtering glass or acrylic, and rest them now and then. Ultraviolet should stay under 75 microwatts per lumen and ideally under 10: ask for the lamp's UV figure before you buy. For homes with glass walls, see what strong light does to art in a new condo.
 

### How do you stop glare on glass?
Glare on glass comes from the angle of the light and from what faces the work. At about 30 degrees the reflection of the spot falls to the floor; a light set far out from the wall sends it straight into the eyes of a standing viewer. Moving the head back toward the setback fixes that.
 A window or a lit glass wall opposite the work mirrors in the glazing all day, and no spot fixes that. Frame that work behind anti reflective glass or acrylic, or hang an unglazed work there. In a Bauhaus residence in Tel Aviv, the central work is a hyper collage digital artwork printed on glossy anti reflective acrylic.
 

### How do you light art in an office?
In an office, light the art from the ceiling grid line nearest the 30 degree setback, with adjustable track or spots rather than the fixed fittings in the tiles, and put the art on its own circuit. A suspended ceiling usually runs on a 24 inch (61 cm) grid. Under a 9 foot ceiling the setback is about 29.5 inches, between two lines: the line 24 inches from the wall aims at about 25 degrees, close enough, while the line at 48 inches aims at about 43 degrees, too shallow. Take the line nearer the wall.
 An office runs at about 400 lux, so an accent three times brighter cannot stay inside a 150 lux limit, let alone 50. On a bright open office wall I would hang oil, acrylic, metal, ceramic or glass, keep works on paper and photographs for spaces with their own dimming, such as a private office or a meeting space, and let a work's own contrast against its wall carry part of the job.
Tell the electrician or lighting designer which walls are art walls before the ceiling layout is fixed. I have my own installation team and install after hours, so the office keeps working. For choosing the work itself, see office wall art, and for how I work with companies, art for an office or business.

### Light as part of the plan
Framing, installation and light belong to one plan, and I manage production, framing and installation through to the work on the wall (see framing and installing large scale art). I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work with clients anywhere, in person or online (see art curator in New Jersey).

Questions:

Q: What color temperature is best for lighting art?
A: Warm white between 2700 and 3000 K suits most art. Museums surveyed by the US Department of Energy named 2700 and 3000 K as their targets, and warmer light carries less damage potential than cool light. Pair it with a color rendering index of 90 or more so colors read true, and keep every light on the same wall at one color temperature. I check the choice on the wall in daylight and in the evening, because the same work reads differently under each.

Q: How far from the wall should track lighting be for art?
A: Far enough that the beam meets the center of the work at about 30 degrees from vertical. Subtract the center height from the ceiling height and multiply by 0.58. With the center at 57 inches (145 cm), that is about 22.5 inches (57 cm) from the wall under an 8 foot ceiling, 29.5 inches (75 cm) under 9 feet and 36.5 inches (92 cm) under 10 feet. Closer, the frame casts a shadow; farther, the reflection moves toward the viewer's eyes.

Q: What size picture light do I need?
A: Picture light makers size the light at half to two thirds of the frame's width, so a 30 inch (76 cm) frame takes a light of about 15 to 20 inches (38 to 51 cm), with wider frames toward the larger end. A picture light lights the upper part of a work best, so for a tall canvas or a large work, a ceiling spot or several track heads give more even light.

Q: Are LED lights safe for paintings?
A: Museums have been moving their galleries to LED, but safe depends on the level, the hours and the lamp. Keep oil paintings at or under 150 lux and works on paper, photographs and textiles at or under 50, check the lamp's ultraviolet figure against the conservation limit of 75 microwatts per lumen, and put the light on a dimmer. Keep the lamp clear of the frame, and keep sensitive work out of direct sun, which is far stronger than any lamp.

Q: Should art lights be on a dimmer?
A: Yes. A dimmer is how you hold a sensitive work at its light limit and how you keep the art readable when the rest of the space is low in the evening. The main work, usually a canvas, needs its own dimmable light, and the art walls work best on their own control, separate from the general lighting. Check that the LED lamp and the dimmer are rated to work together, or the light may flicker.

### Large wall art ideas: how to fill a big wall

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/large-wall-art-ideas/

The best large wall art ideas fill the wall with one decision: one work big enough to hold it, a pair or triptych that reads as one image, or a grid of related works; decor scattered across the wall never fills it. The 2/3 rule for wall art says a work above furniture should span about two thirds of that furniture's width. On a bare wall, size it to the wall and to the distance you see it from; about two thirds of the wall's width is a common starting point. Test the size on the wall before you buy.

A big empty wall makes most people want to fill it, and filling it is usually where it goes wrong: many small things spread across a surface that needed one decision. After more than 15 years in the art world, in museums, in a gallery and in homes, I treat a large wall as a stage for one idea. These are the ways that work, and how to size them.

### Seven ways to fill a large wall
Each of these is one decision, not a scatter. If you are choosing between one large piece and several small ones, one large piece is almost always the stronger answer; several small works hold a big wall only when they read as one group.
 
- One large work. The strongest answer, and the calmest. In a villa in Hod Hasharon, one large figurative work on the concrete wall beside the sofa holds the whole open plan, from the dining table at the far end to the sofa beneath it.
- A pair. Two works of the same size and language, hung close, read as one statement.
- A triptych. Three panels hung as one image, with narrow, exact gaps.
- A grid. Six, nine or twelve works of the same size in a strict grid: a series of prints, photographs or small paintings.
- A salon gallery wall. Many works in mixed sizes held by one outer edge; the method is in gallery wall ideas.
- One tall work on a tall, narrow wall, or on the end wall of a long space.
- One long horizontal work above a long sofa or sideboard.
Textiles, reliefs and large works on paper belong on this list too: a tapestry or a relief brings texture a flat print cannot.

### How big should the art be?
The 2/3 rule for wall art says a work above furniture should span about two thirds of that furniture's width; on a bare wall, the art is sized to the wall and to the distance you see it from.
 2/3of the furniture below2/3of a bare wall, a common starting point12inof clear wall at least, on each side (30 cm)
- Above furniture: about two thirds of the width of the sofa, bed or sideboard below, with 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) above a sofa or bed and 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 cm) above a sideboard or console. The details for sofas are in art above a couch.
- On a bare wall: the work, or the group, taking up about two thirds of the wall's width is a common starting point, with at least 12 inches (30 cm) of wall at each side. One retailer, Minted, suggests filling 60 to 75 percent of the wall. Keep the center at 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor.
- From across the room: the farther away the wall is seen from, the larger the work needs to be. Measure where people will usually stand or sit when they look at it, and size from there, not from the tape measure against the wall.
 The most common mistake with large walls is buying one size too small. When in doubt between two sizes, the larger one is almost always right, provided the work is strong enough to carry it.

### Tall and double height walls
On a tall wall, eye level still matters, but the work also has to answer the architecture. In a sea view villa in Caesarea, the wall needed a work at real scale: 3.5 meters. A work that size is almost never waiting in a gallery, so I commissioned a triptych of storks from an Italian artist, with the scale, the palette and the subject decided for that house. From across the room the three panels read as one composition, so they were hung as one: on a triptych, the gaps are part of the image.
 In a private estate in Caesarea, the double height hall has a pale stone wall rising above the fireplace. Large works sourced from France, built from layered pigments with 18k gold detailing, hold it. Gold takes light differently from pigment, so the surface changes as the daylight moves and again under the sconces at night. On a wall like that, material presence matters as much as size.
 The same rules scale up for business. A hotel lobby or an office reception is a large wall with more people passing it, and I plan those too: see art for boutique hotels and art for an office or a business.

### Long walls
A long wall, in a hallway or an open plan, is best divided into zones, each with its own center: one work above the sofa, a pair beside the dining table, with open wall between them. Do not stretch one small group across the whole length. If the wall is one uninterrupted surface, a long horizontal work or a single row of works on one centerline carries it.
 

### Check the scale in the space
Tape the outline of the work on the wall, or pin up paper cut to size, and look at it for a few days from the sofa, the door and the far end of the room. It is the simplest step in the process, and it prevents the mistake that is hardest to undo.
 

### Original, edition or print
Large canvas prints and oversized wall art fill a wall quickly, but a big wall magnifies everything, including a thin image. For a wall everyone sees, consider an original work, a signed limited edition photograph or print, or a commission made to the wall's exact size, which is often the only way to get the right scale; see commissioning art for a new home. For the difference between an original, an edition and a print, and how to set a budget per wall, see how to choose art for your home.

### Getting it through the door
Measure every door, stair turn and elevator on the route before you buy. Very large canvases can sometimes travel rolled and be restretched on site, a decision made with the artist, never without. Check the wall construction and the weight, and plan for two installers. The full process is in framing and installing large scale art.
 

### The mistakes I see most often

- Art one size too small for the wall.
- Many small, unrelated pieces scattered across a large wall. Make one decision instead.
- A work hung too high because the wall is tall.
- A triptych with uneven gaps.
- Buying before checking the route into the house.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
A large wall is usually the one everything else in the space depends on. I choose, commission and install works for walls like these, from the first measurement to the last level. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, and I work across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. See the Hod Hasharon villa, read art for the living room, or write to me through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What are good art ideas for a large wall?
A: Good art ideas for a large wall are one large work, a pair or triptych that reads as one image, a strict grid of same-size works, or a salon gallery wall held by one outer edge. On a tall wall, a single vertical work; on a long wall, one long horizontal work or separate zones. Textiles and reliefs work too. Avoid scattering small unrelated pieces across the wall.

Q: How big should art be on a large wall?
A: Art on a large wall should be about two thirds of the width of the piece below it when it hangs above furniture. On a bare wall, about two thirds of the wall's width is a common starting point, with at least 12 inches clear at each side, and larger the farther away the wall is seen from. Tape the outline on the wall first; most people discover they need the next size up.

Q: What is the 2/3 rule for wall art?
A: The 2/3 rule for wall art says art above a sofa, bed, sideboard or console should span about two thirds of that furniture's width. Hang it 8 to 10 inches above a sofa or bed and 6 to 10 inches above a sideboard or console. The rule keeps the art and the furniture reading as one group. It is a starting point: a strong vertical work or a pair can be narrower and still hold the wall.

Q: How do I decorate a very tall or double height wall?
A: A very tall or double height wall needs one large work, a triptych or a tall vertical format that answers the height of the wall, rather than a small work hung high. On a double height wall, a very large work may center above 60 inches simply because of its size, but never lift a work just because the ceiling is high: keep its lower part within easy view. Check the weight and the wall construction first.

Q: How do I break up a long wall?
A: A long wall is best divided into zones, each with its own center, such as one work above the sofa and a pair near the dining table, with open wall between them. If the wall is one uninterrupted surface, use one long horizontal work or a single row of works on one centerline instead of spreading one small group across the whole length.

Q: Should I buy a large canvas print or an original?
A: A large canvas print fills a wall quickly, but a big wall magnifies a thin image. For a wall everyone sees, an original, a signed limited edition or a commission made to the wall's exact size will hold up for years. A commission is often the only way to get exactly the right scale for a difficult wall.

### Law office decor ideas: art that makes a firm look serious, from reception to partner offices

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/law-office-art/

Law office decor is the art and finish that tell a client, within the first minute, that a firm is established, calm and discreet. The art carries most of that message: one anchor work at reception, works that reward a long look where meetings run long, the most personal pieces in partners' offices, and no gavels or stock prints anywhere. Below, space by space, are the sizes that work, what to avoid, whether to buy, commission or lease, and how to time it all with a move.

A client cannot judge your legal work from reception. They can judge your walls.

### What law office decor has to do: trust, calm, discretion
Law office decor has three jobs: trust, calm and discretion. Trust: a client should see a firm that chose its walls. Calm: clients who arrive worried and stay for long meetings need work that holds a look without agitating anyone. Discretion: nothing should read as a comment on a client's matter or as a display of spending. So for a firm I work with weight and restraint: fewer and better works, original paintings, photography or works on paper, each well framed.
 

### What art should a law firm put in reception?
A law firm's reception should carry one strong work that a client can read from the door, not a scatter of small frames. Every client sees it, often while waiting, so it gets the best light on the floor. Like entryway art in a home, it has seconds to make its point.
On a bare wall facing the door, size the work to the wall, leave at least 12 inches of clear wall on each side, and hang its center 57 to 60 inches from the floor for a standing visitor. Above a row of chairs, the chairs set the height: the work spans about two thirds of the row, 8 to 10 inches above their backs, in acrylic or unglazed, because heads lean back. See my guides to large wall art ideas and how high to hang art.
57 to 60incenter from the floor on a bare wall, standing (145 to 152 cm)2/3of the row of chairs below8 to 10infrom the chair backs to the frame (20 to 25 cm) A commission often suits reception best: it is made for that wall and seen nowhere else. More in art for an office or a business.

### Conference and meeting spaces: art for long meetings
A conference room needs a work that rewards a long look, because meetings last an hour or more. When the end wall holds a screen, the art goes on a long wall: one large work or a pair. Opposite skyline windows, plain glass mirrors the view, so use anti-reflective glazing or an unglazed painting. The 57 to 60 inch line assumes people standing; no published standard exists for seated spaces, so check the height from a seat at the table.
 

### Partner and associate offices
A partner's office takes the most personal work on the floor, one that says something true about the partner. A print shop asks what size fits the wall; I ask who faces it. Behind the desk, the client sees it across the table; facing the desk, the partner sees it all day.
 Sightlines also shaped a home office I worked on in Caesarea, built around the client's two loves, horses and music: above the desk, seen all day, an existing painting of horses I acquired; in the seating corner, a musician at the piano I commissioned from the same artist (the Caesarea home office project).
In associate offices, the partners decide. Before I choose anything, I ask them how they want the firm to feel and what position it should project to clients; then I make sure every associate office reads strong and gives a client confidence.

### Corridors and the library wall
Corridors connect the floor, so a series works best: editioned photographs or works on paper, framed alike, on one centerline with even gaps, so the eye travels instead of stopping at each frame. How many works a floor needs has no fixed answer; it is usually fewer than a firm expects: count the walls clients and staff face, and leave the rest bare.
 A library wall is already full of pattern, so its art should be simple in shape, at the end of a run of shelves. Works on paper and photographs fade in direct sun, and the damage cannot be undone, so the Northeast Document Conservation Center advises keeping them out of direct sun and behind UV filtering glazing.
 

### What should a law office avoid on its walls?
A law office should avoid gavels, scales of justice and stock prints.

- Legal symbols. Gavels, scales, Lady Justice: interchangeable with every other firm.
- Catalog sets. Matching prints bought with the furniture read as filler.
- Subjects that take a side. Political images, or anything a client could read as a comment on their case.
 

### Should a law firm buy, commission or lease art?
A law firm should buy or commission the works that define it, because reception and the rooms where decisions are made carry them for years, and lease only the walls it wants to change often. Before leasing an anchor work, compare the rent over the whole lease with the price of owning it. How I choose the works that define a firm is on my page for art for law firms.
On price: in most cases, a firm buys art for less through a private curator than at a large auction, where bidders push the price up, or through a gallery, whose prices carry the cost of its venue, its inventory and its gallerists. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable, and the price includes a private consultation for your floor and my work with you until the art is on the wall. A gallery represents its artists; I represent the firm, with no closed roster, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. More on what working with an art advisor costs.

### Timing the art with a move date
Bring the art into the plan when the lease is signed and the drawings exist, not after the move.

- The drawings. I work alongside your architect, so the walls for the anchor works are sized and lit for them.
- Commissions. A commission follows the artist's schedule, so it starts first.
- The building. Delivery is coordinated with the management office. My own installation team hangs the works, after hours if the building prefers, and I can provide a certificate of insurance naming the landlord or managing agent on request. More on framing and installing large scale art.
I bring more than 15 years in the art world, since 2010. I am based in Tenafly, in Bergen County, New Jersey, and work with law firms across New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. If your firm has a move date, start with how I work with law firms, and send me the floor plan, photos of the walls clients see first, and the date.

Questions:

Q: What is the best decor for a law office?
A: The best decor for a law office is a small number of strong original works, placed where clients look: one anchor work at reception, a work that rewards a long look in each conference room, and personal pieces in partners' offices. Weight and restraint read as a firm that chose its walls. Gavels, scales and catalog prints read as filler. Frame the works well and light them, because a good work badly lit disappears.

Q: How do I decorate my law office?
A: Decorate a law office in the order clients see it: reception first, then the conference rooms, then partners' offices, and corridors last, where a series ties the floor together. Agree the budget and the off-limits subjects with the partners before looking at any work, then choose between a few works per wall. Size each work to its wall and to the distance it is seen from, and plan everything, commissions first, against the move date.

Q: What art should a lawyer have in their own office?
A: A lawyer's own office should hold the most personal art on the floor: a work connected to something the lawyer loves, a place they come from, or a subject they know deeply. Decide first who the work is for. A work behind the desk faces the client across the table; a work facing the desk is the one the lawyer sees all day. One or two strong works are enough for a private office.

Q: Is legal themed art a good idea for a law office?
A: Legal themed art is rarely a good idea for a law office. Gavels, scales of justice and Lady Justice prints tell a client what they already know, and they make one firm look like every other. If the firm wants a link to its work, make it specific: a historical map or print of the city where the firm practices, or a work tied to the firm's own history, properly framed. Specific reads as chosen; symbolic reads as stock.

Q: What colors work best in a law office?
A: The colors that work best in a law office are grounded ones. Deep greens and blues, warm neutrals and wood tones read as steady. A palette alone will not win a client's trust, so choose it from the building, the finishes and the light. Then let the art carry the strongest color on the floor, at reception, where one confident work gives the space a focus instead of color scattered across every wall.

### Art for the living room: how to choose it, what size, and where it goes

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/living-room-art/

Art for the living room starts with the one wall the space already turns toward. Give that wall the strongest work you can find, about two thirds the width of the furniture below it and centered 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor, then let the other walls support it. Choose what you love first, and let the wall decide the size.

A living room hung well works like a good dinner conversation: one voice leads, others answer, and someone stays quiet. It is the room guests see, the room you spend evenings in, and often the room with the most competition: windows, a view, a television, a fireplace. After more than 15 years in the art world, in museums, in a gallery and in homes, this is the order I work in.

### Which wall should get the main work?
Every living room has one wall that the room already faces, and that wall gets the strongest work. Stand in the doorway, then sit in the seats you use most evenings: the wall those views land on is the main wall. It is often the wall above the sofa, which the doorway and the armchairs look at, but not always; from the sofa itself you see the wall opposite. In a home in Ramat Gan, it was the wall between two runs of oak cabinets at the center of the living space, and a large format photograph now sits there, with the oak shelf and terracotta vessels beneath it. In a villa in Hod Hasharon, it was the concrete wall beside the sofa, under the track lights.
 

### One center, then supporting walls
 The most common mistake in a living room is treating every wall equally. I survey the space and its sightlines, and define the main wall from them; the other walls follow:

- The main wall gets the strongest and usually the largest work.
- One or two supporting walls get smaller works that answer it: a pair, a work on paper, a sculpture on a console.
- At least one quiet wall gets very little, or nothing. The eye needs somewhere to rest.
That is also the answer to how much art a living room needs: one main work, one or two supporting walls, and one wall left quiet.
 

### What size to buy
Above furniture, the work, or the group, should span about two thirds of the furniture's width: about 56 inches (142 cm) over an 84 inch (213 cm) sofa. The full sizing list is in art above a couch. On an open wall with no furniture, leave at least 12 inches (30 cm) of bare wall at each side.
Almost everyone buys too small for a living room, because they judge size standing close to the wall, or on a screen. Tape the outline of the work on the wall and look at it from the doorway before you buy.
 

### How high to hang it
Center the work 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor. Above a sofa, leave 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 cm) between the sofa back and the frame; above a mantel or console, 6 to 10 inches. Above a fireplace the mantel sets the height, so the center usually lands above 60 inches, and that is fine. Tall ceilings do not change the height, only the scale. The nail formula and the exceptions are in how to hang pictures.

### Choosing the work itself
Start with what you love, not with the cushions. The work does not need to match the room: it can repeat a color the room already has, from the wood, the rug or the upholstery, or bring one it lacks. Work with the room's temperature, not its fabrics: a cool room of white plaster and grey stone can take a work full of warm red. Mix mediums across the room: a painting on the main wall, a photograph or a work on paper on a supporting wall, a sculpture on a console. A room hung with one medium in one size reads as a showroom. For the whole home, from the feeling you want to the budget, see how to choose art for your home.
 If the room has a strong view, the art should answer it, not compete with it. In a seafront apartment in Herzliya Pituach, the first work you meet is a large painting of an aged window near the entrance, so the first window you see is painted and the next ones are real and full of sea.
 

### Wall art ideas that last
 
- One large work above the sofa. The calmest option and usually the strongest.
- A pair flanking a fireplace or a window, when the center of the wall is taken.
- A gallery wall for a collection that keeps growing; see gallery wall ideas.
- A large photograph on the main wall, produced at the right size for the wall rather than bought in a stock size.
- A work beside the television, not above it. The screen already owns that spot; balance it with a work beside it or on the adjacent wall.
- Sculpture with a smaller wall work, on a console or a plinth, which gives the room depth that framed works alone cannot.
What lasts is not a trend. It is a space where each work was chosen for its wall.

### Light it for day and for night
A living room changes between noon and evening more than most. I check every placement in the room itself, in daylight and under the evening lighting, before anything is produced. Aim ceiling spots or track lights at about 30 degrees from vertical. The Northeast Document Conservation Center advises keeping framed color photographs and watercolors out of direct sun and spotlights; for any glazed work facing a window, ask your framer about anti-reflective glazing. The setback, the bulb and the light limits by medium are in how to light art.
 

### The mistakes I see most often

- Every wall treated equally, so nothing leads.
- A work too small for the main wall.
- Art hung too high.
- Art chosen to match the upholstery, which leaves with the sofa.
- A work fighting the view. Answer it instead, as the painted window in Herzliya Pituach does.

### When is it worth calling a curator?
If the living room is the heart of the house, the work on its main wall deserves a proper search. I plan living spaces for homes and with interior designers, and handle framing and installation. I am an art curator based in Tenafly, New Jersey, working across Bergen County, New Jersey, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere. See how one work carried a whole open plan in the Hod Hasharon villa, or write to me through the contact page.

Questions:

Q: What artwork should I put in my living room?
A: The artwork for a living room should start with the work you love most, on the wall the space already faces, the one you see from the doorway and from your usual seat. Size it to the wall, then support it with smaller works on one or two other walls. Paintings, large photographs, works on paper and sculpture all belong in a living room.

Q: What size art should go in a living room?
A: Living room art above furniture should be about two thirds of the furniture's width: roughly 56 inches over an 84 inch sofa. On an open wall, leave at least 12 inches of bare wall at each side. Most people buy too small, so tape the outline on the wall and look at it from the doorway before you buy.

Q: Where should art go in a living room?
A: Art in a living room goes first on the main wall, where the sightlines from the doorway and the seating meet, which is often but not always above the sofa. Then on one or two supporting walls, with smaller works that answer the main one. Leave at least one wall quiet so the room has somewhere to rest.

Q: Should you hang art above a TV?
A: Art above a TV usually does not work. The television already occupies that part of the wall, and art above it pushes both too high and competes with the screen. Hang the work beside the television or on the adjacent wall, at normal eye level, so the wall reads as balanced rather than stacked.

Q: Where can I find art for my living room?
A: Art for a living room comes from galleries, artists' studios, open studios and graduate shows for original works; editioned prints and photographs from galleries and publishers for signed, numbered works at lower prices; design shops for open prints. For a main wall, I recommend original or editioned work, because it is the piece you will look at most.

### Medical office wall art: calm, clean and right for patients

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/medical-office-wall-art/

Medical office wall art is art chosen for a practice's waiting area, exam spaces and corridors to give patients something calm to look at, to look professional and to survive clinical cleaning. For a practice I lean toward calm, readable, specific images where patients wait or lie still, bolder work where people pass by choice, and nothing ambiguous, clinical or confrontational where a patient sits. Below, space by space: what to hang, what to avoid, how to frame it for cleaning, and how it fits a buildout.

Most wall decor for a doctor's office is chosen like the carpet: something must be there, and it must not offend. But patients read your walls before they meet you, and they read them anxious, waiting or lying still. A print shop sells an image; I start from where the patient sits and how they feel there. Here is how I would approach a practice.
 

### What art does for patients
Art gives a patient something good to look at and says the practice is cared for. I do not claim it changes clinical results, and the research, read closely, does not either.

- A window, not a painting. In Science in 1984, Roger Ulrich reported that 23 surgical patients whose window faced a natural scene had shorter stays and needed fewer strong painkillers than 23 matched patients facing a brick wall. It measured a view, not art.
- One photograph, one unit. In a 2011 study on one acute psychiatric unit, Upali Nanda and colleagues found less as needed medication for anxiety and agitation on days a realistic nature photograph hung than with abstract art or none.
- The counterpoint. Cleveland Clinic buys challenging contemporary art on purpose; its curator, Jennifer Finkel, wrote in 2011 that visual art has no studies as rigorous as the music studies, and none convincing that one style serves patients better.
My reading: nature imagery is a sensible starting point where patients wait anxious, not a rule.

### What art works in a waiting room?
Waiting room art should be calm, readable and worth a second look. It has to hold a tenth glance without asking to be decoded: landscapes, gardens, light, botanicals, quiet color, or abstraction built on color rather than tension.
Above a row of chairs, a work or a row of works about two thirds of the row's width reads as planned; more in large wall art ideas. There the chair backs set the height: the frame 8 to 12 inches above them, in acrylic, since heads lean back there. On the wall patients face, hang the work lower than the standing rule. No source gives that height, so set it with the chairs in place.
 

### Exam and treatment spaces
One work that rewards a second look is usually enough, on the wall the patient faces from the exam table or the chair. A patient waiting in a gown feels exposed, so this is the last place for anything clinical, ambiguous or loud. Keep the work clear of equipment, sinks and the clinician's path.
 

### Corridors and the front desk
Here the rules relax, because people pass by choice: bolder color, a series by one artist. Where people stand, the center sits 57 to 60 inches from the floor, as in how to hang pictures. The front desk takes one work that sets the tone, sized for the view from the door; more on art for a reception area.
In corridors, watch depth: under the ADA Standards, an object whose leading edge sits between 27 and 80 inches above the floor may project no more than 4 inches into a path of travel, which rules out deep shadow boxes along any corridor. Your architect has the final word on code.
 2/3of the seating's width, for art above waiting chairs57 to 60incenter from the floor where people stand (145 to 152 cm)4inmost a wall object may project into a corridor (ADA Standards)

### Which images calm, and which should a medical office avoid?
The images that work read at a glance and still reward a second look: landscapes, light on water, botanicals, gentle figurative scenes, local views. The images to avoid make a worried person work, or worry more: anatomy, surreal scenes, figures that seem to stare, storms, and prints with inspirational words.
In oncology or mental health I would take extra care: nothing about illness, loss or isolation, no abstraction that reads as chaos, and realistic nature as the starting point. A simple test: would this image feel right to a patient on the worst day of their year?
 

### Frames, glazing and cleaning
Specify medical office art for cleaning from the start; your infection control guidance comes first. CDC guidance for healthcare facilities asks for walls to be cleaned when visibly soiled and high touch surfaces more often; frames in exam spaces still get wiped.

- Glazing. The glazing maker Tru Vue recommends acrylic for children's spaces, high traffic areas and anywhere safety is a concern. Where a window faces the work, anti reflective glazing keeps it readable.
- Cleaning. Tru Vue advises an ammonia free cleaner sprayed onto a soft cloth, never onto the glazing. Ask the framer for the care sheet and check it against your team's products.
- Printed on acrylic. One smooth face to wipe, no mat to trap dust.
- Sealed backs and security hangers, so dust stays out and nothing is knocked off.
 More in framing and installing large scale art. My own installation team hangs the works, after hours, so the practice keeps working.

### Specialties: pediatrics, dermatology, cosmetic practices

- Pediatrics. Clear, bright, figurative work, some of it hung at a child's height.
- Dermatology. Patients often arrive self conscious about their skin, so I would keep close studies of faces and bodies out of exam spaces.
- Cosmetic and aesthetic practices. The same calm with a little more warmth: color that softens the space without becoming decoration.
For dental practices, see dental office decor.

### Timing with a buildout, and how the budget is set
Plan the art while the walls are open: heavy works need blocking inside the wall, and art lighting belongs on the electrical drawings.
 The budget is a plan you approve, with the anchor works first. On price, in most cases, working with a private curator means you buy the art for less than at a large auction or through a gallery. At auction many bidders push the price up, and a gallery prices in its space, its inventory and its staff. I carry none of those costs, so in many cases buying through me is more affordable, and the price includes a private consultation tailored to your practice and my work with you until the art is on the wall. I represent you, not a roster of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. More on what an art advisor costs and how I work with medical practices.
I am based in Tenafly and work with practices across Bergen County, New York City and California, and online with clients anywhere; see art consultant in Tenafly. If you are building out, moving or refreshing, send me your floor plan and a photo of the waiting area through my page for medical practices, and I will tell you where I would start.

Questions:

Q: What art is appropriate for a doctor's office?
A: Art for a doctor's office is chosen for the patient, not for the doctor's taste. Where patients sit or lie still, choose images that read at a glance and hold a second look: a landscape, a garden, water, a botanical. On the wall facing the exam table, one work is enough. Leave out anatomy, puzzles and slogans, and have every frame and glazing specified for your cleaning routine before anything is bought. Stronger work fits corridors and your own office, where people pass or stay by choice.

Q: What is the best paint color for a medical office?
A: From the art side, there is no single best paint color for a medical office: it depends on the space, its light and the practice. What matters is that the wall and the art work as one: a strong wall color can compete with the work, and a high gloss finish can throw back the exam lighting. Choose the paint and the art together, with your designer, so the walls and the works belong to one plan.

Q: What are some creative ideas for a waiting room?
A: Creative waiting room ideas that still keep the space calm: a series of works by one artist along the longest wall, one large landscape that anchors the space, local views patients recognize, a commission made for the wall by the front desk, or a small wall of works on paper that changes from time to time. Creative should never mean confrontational. Keep the work readable at a glance, size it to about two thirds of the seating below, and glaze it for cleaning.

Q: What images should a medical office avoid?
A: A medical office should avoid images that make a worried patient work or worry more: anatomy and clinical imagery, ambiguous or surreal scenes, figures that seem to stare, storms and dark water, and anything that needs a label to explain it. Inspirational slogans and stock prints look ordered, not chosen. In oncology and mental health practices, take extra care with themes of illness, loss and isolation. Keep bolder work for corridors and staff areas.

### Office art ideas: how to find, choose and hang wall art for an office

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/office-wall-art/

Office wall art works when each area of the office gets one job: welcome at reception, focus in meeting spaces, rhythm along corridors and something personal in private offices. Choose fewer, larger, better works, sized to the wall they hold, and on a standing wall hang them with their center 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor. Below, space by space, are where to find office art, the sizes, placements and style directions I use, how to hang and light it, and the relative cost.

Office wall art is the art on a workplace's walls, from reception to the private offices, and it should make the business look as considered as it is. Most offices get it backwards: a print on every wall, chosen so nobody objects, so nobody looks. More than 15 years in the art world taught me to work the other way: fewer, larger, better works, each with one job.

### What does office wall decor have to do?
Office wall decor has two audiences: visitors, who should see that details are attended to here, and the team, who should get something worth seeing every day. So I give each area one job (Fig. 1).

### Reception: the first ten seconds
Reception takes the anchor work, one piece sized to hold the wall from the door, because a visitor reads the office in the ten seconds before anyone greets them. What the work says should be true of the people behind the desk: restraint for a firm, warmth for a clinic, energy for a studio. Plan its light before it arrives: unlit, it reads as an afterthought. More in art for an office or a business.
 57 to 60incenter on a standing wall (145 to 152 cm)6 to 10incredenza top to frame (15 to 25 cm)2/3of the width of the furniture below

### Conference rooms and meeting rooms
A conference room needs one work that rewards a long look, because people sit facing it for an hour. Hang it on the wall the chairs face across the table, never on the screen wall, where it competes with every presentation. Everyone is seated, so hang it lower than on a standing wall, clear of the chair backs; no study gives a seated number, so test it from a chair. Opposite a window, choose anti-reflective glazing. Nothing here should read as a comment on a client's deal or case. For meeting spaces in finance, see art for investment firms and family offices.
 

### Open plan areas and long corridors
Open plan areas and corridors are seen in motion, so they want rhythm, not a statement: a series of editioned photographs or works on paper. At the end of a long corridor, one stronger work, lit, gives people somewhere to walk toward. In an open plan, a large work can mark where the meeting area begins. Group layouts are in gallery wall ideas.
 

### Private offices and the home office
A private office takes the most personal work in the building. For a home office in a residence in Caesarea, the brief was two words: horses and music, the client's two loves. I looked for artists living and working in the client's country of origin, acquired one existing painting and commissioned a second work from the same artist. The Caesarea home office now holds two works that could belong to no one else. That is the test in any office: the work should be true, and it should be yours.
 

### Should a large office wall get one work or a group?
A large office wall is held by one decision: one work big enough for it, or a group that reads as one image. One large work is usually the stronger answer. Tape the outline on the wall and look at it from the door before you buy. The sizing method is in large wall art ideas, and the nail formula in how to hang pictures.
 

### Hanging office art: standing walls, seated walls and the light
On a wall people pass standing, center the work 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor. Where people sit, in a meeting space or facing a desk, hang it lower and test the height from the chair with a paper template before anyone drills. The nail formula is in how to hang pictures.
 Light every key work from the ceiling at about 30 degrees from vertical. On an office ceiling grid, that is usually the first grid line from the wall; the setback for each ceiling height is in how to light art.
 

### Style directions that stay professional
Professional office art does not mean neutral; it means deliberate. Three directions work in most offices:

- Abstraction with a real surface. Abstract art suits an office when it has texture or strong color; bland abstraction reads as filler.
- Photography. Architecture, landscape and your own city, in signed editions, give a series a sense of place.
- Texture. A relief or a textile brings a depth a flat print cannot.
In an office with no windows, a horizon or open color gives the eye somewhere to go. Avoid motivational slogans and stock canvas prints: they say nobody chose. See also art for law firms, art for medical practices, law office decor and dental office decor.

### Where to find office art, and what it costs
Where you find office art depends on the wall. For the back office, a framed print from a retailer or an online shop is fine, kept in one frame family and sized to the wall. For a corridor series, look for signed, numbered editions from galleries and photographers. For reception and the conference wall, look for an original or a commission, in galleries, artists' studios and art fairs. Take the wall's width and the height of its center with you. Prints cost least, originals and commissions vary with the artist and the size, and leasing spreads the cost over a term without ownership.
 In most cases, buying through a private curator costs less than at a large auction or through a gallery: I carry none of a gallery's costs, the price includes my work with you until the art is on the wall, and I represent you, not a roster of artists. The trade offs are compared in buy, lease or commission art for an office.

### A small office or a full floor
A small office needs fewer works than most people expect: one strong work where clients sit, one in reception and something personal in your own office. A full floor needs a plan: anchor works first, then meeting spaces, then corridor series. Either way, I manage framing and installation: my own team installs after hours so the office keeps working, and on request I provide a certificate of insurance naming your landlord or managing agent.
I am based in Tenafly, in Bergen County, New Jersey, and work on offices in Manhattan, across New Jersey and in California, and online with clients anywhere, as an art curator in New York. When you would rather have someone find, buy, hang and light it for you, that is the work of a corporate art consultant, step by step from choosing to installing; send me photos of the walls your clients see and your move date.

Questions:

Q: What kind of art should I put in my office?
A: Put art in your office that gives each area one job: one anchor work in reception that holds the wall from the door, a work in meeting spaces that rewards a long look, a series along the corridors, and the most personal piece in your own office. Choose fewer, larger and better made works rather than a print on every wall. Originals, signed editions and commissions read as deliberate; stock canvas prints read as filler.

Q: What is the best art to put on my office wall?
A: The best art for an office wall is a work that says something true about the people who work there, sized to the wall and hung at the right height. On a standing wall, center it 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) from the floor. Above a credenza, leave 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 cm) and span about two thirds of its width. One original or signed edition usually does more than several decorative prints.

Q: What to put on an empty wall in an office?
A: An empty office wall needs one decision: one large work, a pair, or a group that reads as one image. On a bare wall, about two thirds of the wall's width is a common starting point, with at least 12 inches (30 cm) clear on each side and the center 57 to 60 inches from the floor. Tape the outline on the wall first and look at it from the door before you buy anything.

Q: How to decorate a conference room?
A: Decorate a conference room with one strong work on the wall the chairs face, a work that rewards a long look, because people sit with it for an hour. Keep art off the screen wall, use anti-reflective glazing opposite windows, and hang the work lower than on a standing wall so it reads from a chair, clear of the chair backs. Avoid anything a client could read as a comment on the meeting.

Q: What are some professional office decor ideas?
A: Professional office decor ideas that work: one anchor work in reception, a series of photographs or works on paper along the corridor, one large work that marks where the meeting area begins, a relief or textile for depth, and a personal piece in each private office. Keep the frames in one family, light every key work, and hang standing walls on one centerline. Deliberate choices read as professional; filler does not.

### Planning art in construction drawings: what to decide before the walls close

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/planning-art-in-construction-drawings/

Planning art in construction drawings means deciding, while the set is still open, which walls stay solid for art, where blocking goes behind heavy works, where picture lights and outlets sit, and how large works reach their walls, because each of those costs least to change on paper. I can start from the plans alone: at THEODORA I work alongside architects and designers, not around them, from their drawings through to installation.

### Why art belongs in the drawing set
Art belongs in the drawing set because a large work depends on things that are built, not bought: a solid wall, structure behind it, and light and power around it. On paper each is a line; once the wall is closed, each means opening it again. The works can be chosen later, as long as the drawings carry an envelope for each one: where it hangs, how big and heavy it could be, and how it is lit.

### Which walls should stay solid for art?
The walls that should stay solid for art are the ones the main sightlines land on: the wall you face as you come in, the end of a long hall, and the wall opposite the main seating. When I start on a space, I survey it and its sightlines and define the main wall from them. On a plan, draw the line from each door and each seat, and mark the wall it meets.
Keep those walls clear of openings, vents, switches and access panels, and label them as art walls on the plan and the elevation. Tall and double height walls need an early choice of one tall work or a sequence, because the light follows from it (see large wall art ideas). In an older house under renovation, the same test applies before the walls are patched (see art for a Brooklyn brownstone).
 

### What to decide while the drawings are open
While the drawings are open, decide the art walls, the structure behind them, the light and power around them, and the way in, each at the phase where it is still a line on a drawing.
 

### Blocking and structure for heavy works and sculpture
A heavy work needs blocking inside the wall, and a large sculpture may need a reinforced floor or a built base; both are the structural engineer's decision. Draw the art zone on the elevation: the band the art will occupy above the finished floor. Its middle is the hanging height: I work at 57 to 60 inches (145 to 152 cm) for the center of a work, lower where people sit (see how to hang pictures).
Draw the blocking band across the whole art zone, not as a single line, because the final frame size and fixing point are often settled after the wall is closed. Photograph the blocking before it is covered. For sculpture, give the engineer the size of the base and the weight. Loads and fixings are confirmed by your structural engineer, never taken from a rule of thumb.
 

### Where should picture lights go in the drawings?
Picture lights and adjustable spots go into the drawings at design development, placed from the art walls and the sizes of the works, not from the ceiling grid. Plan the lighting before the hanging. Set each spot so the light falls evenly across the work and any reflection in the glazing drops to the floor; the lighting designer confirms positions, beams and fittings. A hardwired picture light needs a recessed box above the art zone. The aim, the setback per ceiling height and the bulb are in how to light art.
Give the art its own light on a separate control, so the work still reads when the rest of the space is dimmed.
 

### Power for lit and digital works
Lit works, light boxes and screens need power, and sometimes data, behind the work: a recessed outlet inside the art zone, with its control on the switch plan, never a cord down the finished wall.

### What should an artwork schedule include?
An artwork schedule lists every work in the project, one row per work, with what the other consultants need to draw around it: where it hangs, how big and heavy it is, how it is fixed, lit and powered, and how it gets in.
 Put the schedule in the set as its own sheet, keyed to the plans and elevations. For a work not yet chosen, record the largest size and weight the wall should carry: the drawing needs an envelope, not a title.
 

### Commissions and lead times
A commission usually has to start while the building is going up if it is to arrive with the finishes, so decide at design development which walls need a work made for them. I work directly with artists on commissions from initial concept to final execution, and I manage production, framing and installation within defined timelines and approved budgets.
For a sea view villa in Caesarea, I commissioned a 3.5 meter triptych from an Italian artist. A work at that scale asks every question here at once: a wall long and solid enough for three panels, structure behind them, light across the full width, a route in for each panel. How long a commission takes depends on the artist, the scale and the technique, so fix the timeline at the start and record its stage in the schedule (see commissioning art for a new home).
 

### The delivery route and installation
Draw the route a large work takes from the street to its wall, and check every door, turn, stair and elevator on the way against the crated size, which is larger than the framed size. Where a work cannot pass, decide now: a wider opening, a section left open until the art is in, or a work made in parts.
Hold the installation window until floors, paint and furniture are in, so heights suit how the space is used. I have my own installation team, and I carry insurance with a certificate that can name the landlord or managing agent on request. The full chain is in framing and installing large scale art.
 

### Working with a curator from the plans
A curator can join from the plans alone, before anyone visits the site; the earlier, the more of this checklist is settled on paper. While design development is open, ask whoever takes the art scope for the art walls marked from the sightlines, sizes and weights for the schedule, and the walls that need a commission. How I work with studios is on my page for designers and architects. For an office fit-out, the six steps a corporate art consultant follows show where these drawings sit, from choosing the art to installing it.
Budget planning is one of the seven steps of my art advisory process, so give the art its own line in the budget early, before the finishes spend it. Homeowners can read their side in art for a new build and working with your interior designer on art.
I am based in Tenafly, New Jersey; I work in person across New Jersey and New York City, and from your plans on projects anywhere. Studios can start on the page for designers and architects.

Questions:

Q: I'm an architect. How do I bring art into a residential project early?
A: An architect brings art into a residential project early by giving it a place in the drawings from schematic design: mark the art walls from the main sightlines, keep them solid, and add blocking, lighting positions and power at design development. Bring in a curator or art consultant while the set is still open, so sizes, weights and commissions reach the drawings in time. I can start from your plans alone, and I work alongside architects, not around them.

Q: Should art be planned during construction drawings (lighting, blocking, wall space)?
A: Yes, art should be planned during construction drawings, because lighting, blocking and wall space are built into the walls and ceilings and cost least to change on paper. The final works do not need to be chosen yet: an artwork schedule with the largest size and weight each art wall should carry is enough to draw the blocking band, the picture light positions and the outlets. The works can then be chosen for walls already made for them.

Q: Is art part of the FF&E budget or the construction budget?
A: Art sits in both budgets, split by who builds or buys each part. The works, their framing and their installation usually belong in the FF&E budget or a separate art budget. What is built into the walls and ceilings for them, blocking, circuits, recessed boxes and outlets, belongs in the construction budget, because the contractor builds it. Give each its own line early; I set the art budget per wall, not per piece, and give most of it to the wall people see first.

Q: Who confirms the blocking for a heavy artwork or sculpture?
A: The structural engineer confirms the blocking for a heavy artwork or sculpture, and the contractor builds it to that detail. The curator or art consultant supplies what the engineer needs: each work's framed size, framed weight, position on the elevation and fixing method, and for sculpture, the size of the base and the weight on the floor. Where no work is chosen yet, give the engineer the largest size and weight the wall should carry, and photograph the blocking before the wall is closed.

### Restaurant wall decor ideas: art that works through a full service

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/restaurant-wall-decor/

Restaurant wall decor is the art and wall treatment that carries a restaurant's concept to every table, chosen to read under evening light and to survive steam, grease and cleaning. The feature wall matters most, because most diners see it and many photograph it. Below are restaurant decor ideas by type, how to place art for the tables, what holds up through service, and how to time the art with an opening date.

Most decor photos show a restaurant empty, in daylight. Your guests see it full, from a seat, after dark, and they came for the food. Add steam, grease and nightly cleaning, and a restaurant wall has a harder life than almost any wall in a home. I have spent more than 15 years in the art world, and my hospitality work includes collections built while collaborating with luxury hospitality leaders. Here is how I would approach your walls.

### What does restaurant wall decor have to do?
Restaurant wall art has three jobs, in this order:

- Tell the concept. I start where you started: the concept, the cuisine, the neighborhood and the people you cook for. Every piece needs a reason, so nothing reads as a prop.
- Read from the tables. Guests see the walls seated, in low light. Strong shapes and clear contrast carry; fine detail is lost after dark.
- Survive service. Medium, glazing and hardware are part of the choice, not an afterthought.
Through all three, the art never competes with the plate.

### Restaurant decor ideas by type: fine dining, bistro, cafe and bar
Let the type of service set the wall strategy, not the theme on the menu.
 Restaurant decorations bought by the yard, one theme on every surface, age fastest. Wall art for cafes that open early has to read in daylight as well as at night. Bars and restaurants inside a hotel follow the property's wider program; see hotel artwork.
 

### The feature wall and the sightlines from the tables
Choose the one wall most tables can see, and spend there first: often the wall facing the banquette, behind the host stand or behind the bar. I survey the sightlines from the door and from the seating: what guests face, not what looks best on the plan.
2/3of a banquette section's width, for the work above it8 to 10infrom the banquette back to the frame (20 to 25 cm)57 to 60incenter height where guests stand (145 to 152 cm)Above a short banquette, or one section of a long one, treat the seat back like a sofa: a work about two thirds of its width, 8 to 10 inches above it. Guests lean back, so it hangs on two points, never one wire.
 Where guests stand, the usual height in how high to hang pictures holds; where they sit, the center can come down a little. A large bare wall wants one work sized for it (see large wall art ideas). A long banquette wall suits a series or a gallery wall with one steady gap.
 

### Lighting, steam and cleaning: what art survives service?
Art survives when medium, glazing and position are chosen for the room in use.

- Daylight. The Northeast Document Conservation Center calls light damage cumulative and irreversible, and advises keeping framed color photographs and watercolors away from direct sunlight and spotlights, behind UV-blocking glazing. The risk is the window table at lunch, not dinner.
- Evening light. Low, warm light flattens pale works, so the main work needs its own dimmable light.
- Steam and grease. Keep art clear of the kitchen pass, the espresso machine and the grill, and check anything near an open kitchen against your local fire code.
- Glare. Glass facing a window or backlit bottles becomes a mirror; use anti-reflective glazing there.
- Cleaning and crowds. Works on paper and photographs go behind glazing staff can wipe, on secure fixings out of reach of chairs and trays.
 I plan framing and installation with the choice of the work, not after it.

### Restaurant wall design trends: what to follow and what to skip
Follow the trends with a local reason. My test: will you still want it at the next refit?

- Follow: local artists. Work from your city, or your cuisine's region, gives the walls a reason no catalog can, and your staff a true story to tell.
- Follow: one commission. A work made for the feature wall and about your story is the piece guests remember.
- Follow with care: murals. A mural fills a wall no frame can, but it is as permanent as the paint.
- Skip: the selfie wall. A neon slogan built for phone pictures dates fast.
- Skip: art by the yard. Mass-produced canvases bought to fill a wall look like exactly that.

### Wall color and art together
Let the concept and the designer set the palette, then choose art that answers it.

- Contrast. A busy work needs a quiet wall; a light work reads best on a deeper one.
- Night color. Warm evening light shifts every color, so I check the palette on the wall itself, in daylight and under the evening lighting.
- Dark walls. Deep green, blue or charcoal makes a lit work glow and swallows an unlit one.
At home the conditions are gentler; dining room art covers sizing a work over a table.

### Sourcing: local artists, commissions, prints and rotating shows
There are four routes, and many restaurants mix them:

- Commissions. Made for your wall and story; the longest lead time, set by the artist's schedule.
- Originals by local artists. Bought outright, they stay as long as you want them.
- Prints and editions. Right for volume: a banquette series, a second dining room, a corridor.
- Rotating shows. Local artists show work for sale on your walls. Works leave when they sell; agree in writing who insures, who hangs, how long works stay and how a sale is handled.
Where you buy matters too. In most cases, buying through a private curator costs less than buying at a large auction, where bidders push the price up, or through a gallery, which has to cover its venue, its inventory and its staff in its prices. I carry none of those costs. The price you pay through me includes a private consultation for your restaurant and my work with you until the art is on the wall. And I represent you, not a roster of artists, so I can reach out to any artist in the world. More on what buying through a curator costs and on art for restaurants.

### When should art be planned for an opening?
Plan the art with the design, before the lighting is fixed, so a picture light lands where the picture will be. I work against the build: commissions start first, framing follows, and the works arrive when the walls are ready. My own installation team hangs them between the last coat of paint and the first service. If you are already open, I install after hours, and when your building asks for a certificate of insurance, I provide one, naming the landlord or managing agent on request.
I am based in Tenafly, in Bergen County, New Jersey, and work with restaurants in New York City, New Jersey and California, and online with clients anywhere. Send me the plans and the opening date, and see how I work with restaurants.

Questions:

Q: What is trending in restaurant wall design?
A: The restaurant wall design trends worth following are the ones with a local reason: originals by artists from the restaurant's own city, one commission made for the feature wall, and murals on walls no frame can fill. The ideas that date fastest are neon slogans built for phone pictures and mass-produced canvases bought to fill a wall. My test for any trend is whether you will still want it on the wall at the next refit.

Q: What are some good ways to decorate a restaurant?
A: A good way to decorate a restaurant is to start from the concept and work in the order guests see the walls. Give the one wall most tables face the strongest work, ideally an original or a commission. Give the long walls a quieter rhythm, such as a series of photographs. Choose materials for service: glazing staff can wipe, nothing near steam or direct sun, secure fixings. Then light the main work so it still reads at night.

Q: What color should restaurant walls be?
A: Restaurant walls should be the color the concept and the designer set, chosen together with the art rather than before it. A quiet wall lets a busy work read. Deep green, blue or charcoal makes a lit work glow at night but swallows an unlit one. Warm evening light shifts every color, so test the paint sample and the art together under the lighting you will actually use at dinner.

Q: How do restaurants get artwork?
A: Restaurants get artwork in four main ways: they commission it, buy originals, buy prints and editions, or show local artists' work for sale in rotation. Many mix them, with a commission on the feature wall and editions on the long walls. Buying through a private curator like me is, in most cases, more affordable than a large auction or a gallery. The price includes a private consultation and my work with you until the art is on the wall, and I represent you, not a roster of artists.

### Ten questions to answer before you buy your first serious artwork

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/guide/ten-questions-before-you-buy-your-first-serious-artwork/

Before you buy your first serious artwork, answer ten questions about the wall, the light, the life of the room, provenance, condition, framing, the full budget, resale, your designer and your advisor. I ask every new client these before I show a single work; here they are, with my answers from real homes.

I ask every new client these ten questions before I show them a single work. They are the difference between a purchase that looks right in the gallery and one that still feels right on your wall in ten years. Answer them on paper and half of the market noise falls away.

### 1. What does the wall actually measure, and what is around it?

Measure the wall, the ceiling height, and the distance from which you will usually see the work. A painting that fills a gallery wall can disappear in a double height living room, and a work that is perfect at two meters can overwhelm a corridor you pass at arm's length.

In a Caesarea sea view villa, the answer to this question was a 3.5 meter triptych commissioned from an Italian artist, three storks at its center, made for that wall and no other. In a Hod Hasharon villa it was a single large scale figurative digital work, chosen to define the emotional center of an open, light saturated home. Scale is decided by the room, never by the catalogue.

### 2. Where does the light come from, and when?

Note the windows, the direction they face, and the hours you are actually in the room. Direct sun fades works on paper and some pigments, and glass or glossy surfaces facing a window turn into mirrors at exactly the hour you want to look at them.

In a Herzliya Pituach apartment I positioned a large painting by Yigal Ozeri, an aged and textured window, near the entrance so it speaks to the sea facing windows rather than competing with them. In a Tel Aviv Bauhaus residence the central work is a hyper collage printed on glossy anti reflective acrylic: the depth of gloss without the mirror, which is the answer to this question.

### 3. What life is lived in this space?

Be specific. Is this where you read alone, where the children do homework, where you host thirty people on a Friday night? The work has to belong to the life of the room, not to the idea of the room.

For a Manhattan client who loves to entertain, the anchor of the apartment became a large format digital collage above the custom bar, drawing on the visual language of glamorous social gatherings and referencing Manet's "Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère". For a Ramat Gan client, the answer came out of a trip to Korea that changed them: a large format photograph by a Korean artist, two figures in ceremonial dress, at the heart of the living space. "It gives it memory." For a Tel Aviv client who loved the intimate imagery of the series Shtisel, I commissioned the artist whose paintings appear in it: a mother caressing her baby, rendered with quiet warmth.

### 4. Where has the work been?

Provenance is the documented history of the work: who made it, who has owned it, where it was shown, and how it reached the seller. For a living artist that is often a direct relationship and a signed certificate. For a work that has changed hands, it is a chain of invoices and exhibition records that should be complete and legible. When I commission a work directly from the artist, the chain is one link long and it starts with you.

Gaps are not always a problem, but unexplained gaps are. When I sourced large scale works from France for a private collector's estate in Caesarea, I worked through a leading gallery, negotiated the prices and aligned every choice with the collector's taste and long term investment goals. Documentation sits inside that conversation, not after it. Buying from a gallery on your own? Read how to buy from a gallery without overpaying.

### 5. What condition is it in, and who says so?

Ask for a condition report and read it. Ask who wrote it, when, and whether they are independent of the sale. Photographs flatter; raking light and a close look at edges, corners and the back of the work do not.

With works on paper, photographs and digital prints, condition also means the print process and the substrate. I work with expert printmakers, and both are chosen for longevity before anything is printed.

### 6. How will it be framed, and who decides?

Framing is not decoration. It protects the work, sets its scale on the wall, and either agrees with the architecture or argues with it. Decide before you buy, because the frame changes the finished size and the budget.

In a Caesarea garden villa, two richly textured portraits of women facing the front door got slim contemporary framing. I manage framing and installation end to end with expert framers and installers, within the agreed timeline and budget. More in framing and installing large scale art.

### 7. What is the real budget, including everything after the price?

Write down the number you are comfortable with, then add what follows the purchase: shipping, insurance in transit, framing, installation, and sometimes lighting. Buyers who skip this step end up with a work they love and a frame they compromised on.

Where you buy belongs in the same column. At a large auction, many bidders push the price of the same work up, and a gallery prices with big margins to cover its venue, its inventory and its gallerists. I carry none of those costs, so in most cases the same work costs less bought through me, and the price includes my help until it is on your wall. The detail is in what an art advisor costs.

### 8. Are you buying to live with it, or to sell it?

Both are legitimate. Pretending one is the other is where people get hurt. Most art is not liquid, resale through auction or a gallery carries its own costs, and a rising name today is not a guarantee of anything.

For the Caesarea collector, long term investment value was a stated goal, so the selection and the negotiation were aligned with it from the start. When a client simply wants to wake up next to something that moves them, that is a complete reason too. The mistake is buying for the second reason and telling yourself it was the first.

### 9. Is your designer part of this conversation?

If you are working with an interior designer or architect, bring them in before the purchase, not after. My role is to bridge art history, the market now, and the creative vision of your architect or designer, so all three arrive at the wall as one decision.

In a newly built residence in Closter, New Jersey, I curated a collection that brings depth to the interior design, working with leading New York City galleries from the start and placing Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices. The result is a house where art and architecture speak the same language. I work with designers, not around them; here is how.

### 10. Who is advising you, and what do they gain from your choice?

Ask whom the person guiding you represents: you, or the artists they sell. Ask what they do when they think you are about to buy the wrong work. An advisor who sits on your side of the table can walk away from a piece, assess its market value, negotiate on your behalf, and answer the questions above honestly.

That is the role I take. More than 15 years in the art world, an M.A. in art history from Ben-Gurion University, curatorial work in museums, managing a gallery in Tel Aviv, collections for private homes across New York, New Jersey and Israel, and art concepts for hotels and cruise lines abroad, among them Waldorf Astoria Chengdu, St. Regis Amman and Holland America Line. The work is not complete until the piece is installed and you are fully satisfied.

### Before you buy
