Put your ten answers on a single page and keep it with you when you look at work. To talk through your answers with me, write to stav@stavtheodor.com. Also worth reading: how my advisory process works, how to start an art collection and, for a company's first purchase, how a corporate art consultant works.

Questions:

Q: What questions should I ask before buying my first serious artwork?
A: Ten: what the wall measures and what surrounds it, where the light comes from and when, what life is lived in the room, where the work has been (its provenance), what condition it is in and who says so, how it will be framed, what the full budget is after the price, whether you are buying to live with it or to sell it, whether your designer is in the conversation, and who is advising you and what they gain from your choice.

Q: How much should I spend on my first piece of art?
A: Start from the number you are comfortable with, not the number a gallery suggests, then add shipping, insurance in transit, framing, installation and sometimes lighting, because those follow every purchase. Where you buy matters too: in most cases the same work costs less bought through me than at a large auction or in a gallery, because I carry none of their costs, and the price includes my help until it is hung.

Q: What is provenance in art, and why does it matter for a first purchase?
A: Provenance is the documented history of an artwork: who made it, who has owned it, where it was exhibited, and how it reached the seller. For a living artist it is usually a direct relationship and a signed certificate. For a work that has changed hands, it is a chain of invoices and exhibition records that should be complete and legible. Gaps are not always a problem; unexplained gaps are, because they affect authenticity, resale and insurance.

Q: Do I need an art advisor to buy my first artwork?
A: No. Many people buy a first work on their own and are glad they did. An advisor earns her place when the purchase is large enough that a wrong choice would hurt: she brings access to artists and galleries, assesses market value, negotiates on your behalf, and manages framing and installation. Ask whom she represents, you or a roster of artists, and what she does when she thinks you are about to buy the wrong work.

Q: How do I know what size artwork is right for my wall?
A: Measure three things: the wall, the ceiling height, and the distance from which you will usually see the work. A painting that fills a gallery wall can disappear in a double height living room, and a work that is perfect at two meters can overwhelm a corridor you pass at arm's length. Decide on framing before you buy, since the frame changes the finished size. Scale is decided by the room, never by the catalogue.

## Projects

### Caesarea, Garden Villa

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/caesarea-garden-villa/

In the foyer of a garden villa in Caesarea I placed two large scale portraits of women, painted with rich layered texture, facing the front door so they are the first thing anyone sees on entering. Slim contemporary framing keeps the attention on the paint, not the edges.

### The space and the person
A garden villa in Caesarea, bright and clean lined: a long foyer with pale floors, a black front door, an open staircase, a mirrored wall, a bench. The house had been finished with restraint and the entrance was still bare. Whatever went there would be seen by everyone who came through the door, for a second or two at most, and it would set the tone for the whole house.

### What it asked for
Presence, fast. A foyer does not give a work time to be studied; it is read on the way in and remembered on the way out. The scale had to match the height of the walls. The framing had to be quiet, so the work read as part of the architecture and not as pictures hung on it. And the entrance needed to greet people with warmth and color, in a house that is otherwise white, grey and wood.

### What answered it
Two large scale portraits of women, tall and narrow, painted with rich, layered texture. One is built in greens with a crown of pink; the other in deep blues with a flare of orange; both carry small passages of gold. From the door they read as presence and color. Up close they read as paint, built up in layers you want to touch. I placed them facing the front door, so the first exchange in the house is between the person arriving and the two women who meet them.
 

### What it took
Choosing a pair rather than a single work, and choosing two that share a language: same scale, same texture, same framing, so they become one statement about the house. Slim contemporary framing in black, specified to protect the edge and then get out of the way. Placement, scale and framing were decided together, not one after the other, which is why the foyer feels settled rather than decorated. Then logistics and installation, finished only when both portraits were up and the owners were happy walking in.
 If the first thing people see in your home is still an empty wall, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Caesarea, Luxury Residence, Home Office

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/caesarea-luxury-residence-home-office/

For the home office of a luxury residence in Caesarea I brought in two artworks that reflect the client's two loves, horses and music, by artists living and working in the client's country of origin. One was an existing painting I acquired; the second I commissioned from the same artist for this room.

### The space and the person
A luxury residence in Caesarea, and within it a home office: a desk with two screens, a seating corner against a wall of warm wood panelling, guitars hung on the wall, a track of lights overhead. A home office is the most personal room in a house, because it is built for one person. The client has two loves, horses and music, and wanted the room to hold both, in work by artists living in the client's country of origin.

### What it asked for
Two works, not one, and a reason for them to belong together. One for the wall above the desk, seen all day. One for the seating corner, seen when the work is done. The art had to come from artists living and working in the client's country of origin, because the way a painter handles a horse or a musician carries the place they come from, and the client would feel that at once. And the two pieces had to share a voice, so the room read as one idea rather than two purchases.

### What answered it
Above the desk, a painting of horses in motion, greys and whites, all energy and restraint. On the wood panelled wall of the seating corner, a musician at the piano in saturated color, blues and reds against the timber. The first was an existing painting I acquired for the client. The second did not exist yet. I commissioned it from the same artist, so the two works share a hand and belong to each other across the room. A commission made for a specific room and a specific person carries a meaning a purchased work cannot fully match.

### What it took
Defining the two themes with the client before looking at a single work. Research among artists in the client's country of origin, then the acquisition of the first painting and the commission of the second from the same artist. Then logistics, framing and installation in the office, finished only when both works were up and the client was satisfied.
If there is a room in your home that should feel like yours alone, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Caesarea, Private Estate

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/caesarea-private-estate/

For a private collector's estate in Caesarea I sourced large scale artworks from France, layered pigments with 18k gold detailing, in close collaboration with a leading gallery. I negotiated the prices and guided the choices to fit both the collector's taste and long term investment goals.

### The space and the person
A private estate in Caesarea: a double height hall, a wall of pale stone rising above the fireplace, wrought iron along the gallery, brass sconces. The owner is a collector, and that changes the conversation. A home owner asks whether a work belongs on this wall. A collector also asks whether it belongs in the collection, and what it will be worth in the years to come.

### What it asked for
Works with enough scale and material presence to hold a stone wall of that height, and enough quality to justify their place in a serious collection. Both questions had to be answered at once: taste and long term value, together. And the acquisition had to be handled the way a collector expects, with discretion, a clear view of market value, and someone on their side of the table in the negotiation.

### What answered it
Large scale artworks sourced from France, built from layered pigments with 18k gold detailing. Gold takes light differently from pigment, so the surface changes as the daylight in the hall moves and again under the sconces at night. Against the stone the work reads as both contemporary and permanent. Above the fireplace it holds the whole hall.
 

### What it took
Close collaboration with a leading gallery to secure the works, price negotiations on the collector's behalf, and guidance aligned with the collector's taste and long term investment goals. Before the negotiation I assessed market value, so the price we settled on was argued from evidence, not from wanting the work. When an advisor represents the collector, the conversation with a gallery changes: I know what a work should cost and what is reasonable to ask, and my relationships are direct, which brings the price down without damaging the relationship for the next acquisition. Then logistics and installation on a stone wall at height, finished only when the work was up and the collector was satisfied.
If you are building a collection and want someone on your side of the table, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Caesarea sea view villa: a 3.5 meter triptych of storks

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/caesarea-sea-view-villa-triptych/

For this sea view villa in Caesarea I commissioned a 3.5 meter triptych from an Italian artist, three storks at its center. They stand for homecoming, strength and belonging: the homeowner's own journey as a new immigrant, and the storks that migrate through Israel every season.

The homeowner had just made Israel home. The villa faces the sea. The wall needed a work at real scale: 3.5 meters. Those three facts decided the project before a single artist was named.

### Why storks
Every season, storks pass through Israel on their migration. Anyone who lives on this coast has watched them. For a person who has just moved their whole life to a new country, the image needs no explanation: three storks at the center of the work stand for homecoming, strength and belonging. The composition is the homeowner's own story, told in a language the neighbors read too.

### Why a commission, not a purchase
A 3.5 meter work is almost never waiting in a gallery, and if it is, it was made for someone else's wall. Commissioning meant the scale, the palette and the subject were decided for this house, so the work belongs here and nowhere else. A work made for a specific space and identity carries deeper meaning, greater value, and a presence that cannot be replicated. That is the case for a commission in one sentence.
The artist is Italian. I choose the hand for the story, not the story for the hand, and this story needed a painter who could give three birds presence and lightness across three panels. Working directly with the artist is also how I keep a commission at this scale competitively priced.

### Three panels, one wall
From across the room the three panels read as one composition. Up close they are three moments, and the eye travels with the birds. In a house whose windows face the sea, that movement belongs.
 

### What I handle on a commission

- Concept and creative direction with the artist, from the first idea to the finished work.
- Scale, palette and timeline, agreed with the client and the artist.
- Price, negotiated on the client's behalf through my direct relationship with the artist.
- Logistics and installation, within the approved budget and timeline.
Work is not complete until the artwork is installed and the client is fully satisfied. On this wall, that meant three panels hung as one.
If you have a wall that deserves a story of its own, write to me. Read how I approach commissioning art for a new home, and if you are moving to Israel from abroad, art for a home in Israel from abroad. Another Caesarea project: the private estate collection, with works sourced from France.

### Closter, New Jersey: a collection for a newly built house

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/closter-new-jersey-new-construction/

For a newly built private residence in Closter, New Jersey, I was commissioned to curate a collection that gives the architecture more character and the interior design more depth. I worked closely with leading New York City galleries, and the collection brings works by Jewish and Israeli artists together with other contemporary voices.

### A finished house, with nothing on the walls
The house was complete when I came in: white walls, wide plank oak floors, a beamed ceiling, black framed glass doors opening onto trees and snow. Every finish had been decided and every finish was right. What it did not yet have was a point of view, and that is the one thing you cannot order from a builder.

### The problem with new construction
A new build is coherent by design, and coherence can read as quiet, even anonymous, until art gives the rooms someone to belong to. The brief was to bring depth to the interior design and raise the architectural character of the house, not to decorate it. The collection was to include works by Jewish and Israeli artists alongside other contemporary voices, and the two had to read as one collection with one sensibility, never as a category and its exceptions.

### Room by room
I built the collection with leading New York City galleries, to amplify a house that was already built and designed. In the dining room, three small paintings in blues, pinks and violets hang in a row above the oak table, close in scale and palette, so the wall reads as one gesture under the two black pendants. In the office, a single large canvas in greens and yellows carries the room by itself, opposite the desk. In the hall, a large framed work in gold and violet sits above a bench and a bonsai at the foot of the stair, where everyone passes it several times a day. Each work was chosen for its wall, and each wall for what it could hold.
The result transforms a well designed house into a space with soul, where art and architecture speak the same language.

### What I managed
Viewings and shortlists with the galleries, negotiation, shipping. Framing where a work needed it, then installation, with every piece hung at the height and spacing its room asked for. I handle this end to end on every project, from the first plan to the last hook, and I consider it finished only when the clients walk through and the house feels like theirs.
If you are building or finishing a home in Bergen County or New York and want the art planned with the same care as the architecture, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Creating Hope: 27 Israeli artists, from billboards to the United Nations in Geneva

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/creating-hope-exhibition-un-geneva/

Creating Hope is an exhibition I curated of works by 27 Israeli artists, each interpreting the word "hope". It traveled across Israel, was shown on billboards in public space, and was presented at the United Nations Offices in Geneva, Switzerland, in June 2024.

Most of my work is private: one family, one wall, one conversation. Creating Hope was the opposite. One word, 27 artists, and audiences who never chose to visit a gallery.

### The brief: one word
Each of the 27 Israeli artists was asked to interpret the word hope. That is a generous brief and a hard one. There is no subject to hide behind and no client to satisfy. What came back was 27 different answers, and my job as curator was to bring them together so that the differences spoke to each other rather than cancelling out.
 

### Three settings, three ways of seeing

- Across Israel. The exhibition traveled, so the same works were seen in different cities and different rooms. Every new venue is a new hang, and every hang is a fresh set of curatorial decisions.
- On billboards. The works were shown in public space, at the scale of advertising, to people on their way somewhere else. Art on a billboard has a few seconds to land.
- At the United Nations Offices in Geneva. Presented in Switzerland in June 2024, to an international audience in a diplomatic setting. The same works, read in a very different room.
 

### Why this matters if you are a private client
Curating is the same discipline whether the room is a foyer in Caesarea or a room at the United Nations Offices in Geneva. You look at the work, you look at the space, you look at who will stand in front of it, and you decide what goes where and why. I learned that discipline through curatorial work in established museums and by managing an art gallery in Tel Aviv. Creating Hope asked for it at every scale at once, for audiences I could not brief in advance.
It also reflects how closely I work with Israeli artists, emerging and established. Knowing an artist's studio and pace from the inside is what lets me bring the right artist, on the right terms, into a private home.
To see how that plays out in a residence, look at the Caesarea sea view villa or the hospitality collections. To talk about a work by one of the artists, or about a commission, write to me.

### Herzliya Pituach, Sea View Apartment

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/herzliya-pituach-sea-view-apartment/

Near the entrance of this sea view apartment in Herzliya Pituach I placed a large scale painting by Yigal Ozeri of an aged, textured window, so that it speaks to the real windows facing the sea. Sculptural elements and organic textures carry that conversation through the rest of the home.

### The space and the person
An apartment on the Herzliya Pituach shoreline, with a curved living room and a run of windows that open straight onto the Mediterranean. Pale stone floors, cream sofas, a low table with cushions around it. The sea is the strongest thing in every room, so the art could not compete with it. It had to answer it.

### What it asked for
An answer to the view rather than a rival to it. A work near the entrance that would set the tone on arrival, before the sea appears. And a material language running through the whole apartment, so that the rooms felt connected by texture rather than by matching colors. A home by the sea needs weight somewhere, otherwise the light washes everything out.

### What answered it
A large scale painting by Yigal Ozeri depicting an aged, textured window: worn paint, old glass, the memory of a wall. I positioned it near the entrance, so the first window you see in the apartment is painted, and the next ones, as you walk in, are real and full of sea. Time on one side, light on the other, in quiet dialogue. Beside it stand two tall pieces of driftwood on steel bases, and sculptural elements and organic textures continue into the living room, where a tall bronze toned form rises between the sea facing windows.
 

### What it took
Reading the apartment from its strongest feature and building the concept from there. Selecting the Ozeri painting and deciding its exact position near the entrance, then choosing the sculptural pieces and textures for the other rooms so that everything spoke the same language. Logistics and installation of a large scale canvas and freestanding sculpture, handled end to end, and finished only when the last piece was standing and the owners were satisfied.
If you have a view and are not sure what belongs beside it, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. Read about framing and installing large scale art, see a photograph placed at the heart of a home in Ramat Gan, or how the art advisory process works.

### Hod Hasharon private villa: one work as the emotional center of the house

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/hod-hasharon-private-villa/

For a private villa in Hod Hasharon, an open, light saturated home where concrete and nature meet, I chose a single large scale figurative digital artwork to define the emotional center of the space. One work, on the one wall the whole room turns toward.

### A house where the garden is the main picture
The living space runs the full width of the house under one dark timber beam, with sliding glass along the garden side and the pool and the trees a few steps from the sofa. Concrete floor, one concrete wall, a checked rug, wishbone chairs at the dining table. Light comes in from everywhere. Homes like this are easy to love and hard to hang art in, because the view is already doing the work a painting usually does.

### Not a collection. A center.
This was never a project for many works. The house needed an emotional center: one place where the eye lands and rests, strong enough to stand beside the garden without competing with it. The concrete wall beside the sofa, under the track lights, was the obvious wall. The open questions were what belonged on it, at what scale, and in what palette against all that grey and green.

### The work
A single large scale figurative digital artwork: a woman's face in profile, dissolving into a cloud of red roses on a pale blue ground, in a thin black frame. Against the concrete it is the only saturated color in the room, and it needed to be. The figure gives the space a person, the red gives it a pulse, and the scale lets it hold the whole open plan, from the dining table at the far end to the sofa beneath it. One work, and the house has a center.

### Restraint, and the practical part
The temptation in a large open home is to fill it. The discipline is to find the one piece that can carry the room and get its scale and palette right for that wall, which on every project I check in the room itself, in daylight and under the evening lighting, before anything is produced. Then production at full size, framing, and installation on concrete with the lights set to the work. Concept, selection, logistics and installation, handled end to end, and finished only when the work was up and the clients were happy with it.
If your home has one wall that everything else depends on, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Hotels and hospitality collections: Waldorf Astoria, St. Regis, cruise lines

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/hotels-and-hospitality-collections/

For years I designed art concepts and built tailor made contemporary art collections for luxury hospitality groups: premium hotels, exclusive resorts and large cruise ships. The projects on this page are Waldorf Astoria Chengdu, St. Regis Amman, Holland America Line and Costa Cruises.

Hospitality taught me to work at scale without losing the individual work. A hotel collection runs across lobbies, bars, guest rooms and residences, against an opening date and an approved budget. Every piece still has to be right for its wall.

### Waldorf Astoria Chengdu, China
Sculptural works for the lobby. A lobby is the first thing a guest sees and the one space every guest passes through. Work there has to hold a large volume and read from a distance, and sculpture does that in a way flat work rarely can.

### St. Regis Amman, Jordan
A bar with a horse mosaic, the guest rooms, and the residences. Three different briefs in one property. A bar wants one memorable gesture. Guest rooms want consistency across many similar walls. Residences want the feeling of a private collection.
 

### Holland America Line and Costa Cruises
Restaurant and stateroom art for Holland America Line ships, and work for Costa Cruises. A ship is a hotel that moves. The art has to be planned for motion and for a constant turnover of guests, and still feel considered in every restaurant and every stateroom.
 

### Other clients and partners
Clients and partners also include Four Seasons, Rosewood Hotels and Resorts, The Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection, Accor, Carnival, Guesty, Eagle Hills and Hotels of the Mandarin group.

### What this means for a private client

- I have built collections for entire properties. A home with ten walls is not a stretch.
- I know how to hold a budget and a date. In hospitality both are fixed before the first artwork is chosen, and every stage is managed within defined timelines and approved budgets.
- I bring the same network of artists, printmakers, framers and installers to private residences.
If you are a hotel or hospitality group, or a designer working for one, write to me with the property and the timeline, or read art for hotels and hospitality, boutique hotel art and art for restaurants. ### Manhattan skyline residence: a collage that quotes Manet above the bar

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/manhattan-skyline-residence/

For this Manhattan skyline apartment I selected one large format digital collage to anchor the custom bar. The client's love of entertaining guided the choice: the work draws on the visual language of glamorous social gatherings and references Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère by Édouard Manet (1882).

### One wall, built for one work
The bar is the social center of this apartment: a marble counter, backlit shelves of bottles and glassware on either side, a brass rail at the foot, and in the middle a panel that was clearly built to hold a single picture. The client loves to entertain. That was the whole brief, and it is the kind I prefer, because how a person hosts tells me what the wall should say.

### What the wall needed
One piece, not a group. Large enough to hold the center of the bar wall between the shelves, and with the energy of a room full of guests, so the mood is set before anyone has poured a drink. It also had to sit inside a restrained interior: dark stools, grey stone, city light through the windows. Playful, but not loud.

### The collage
A large format digital collage that draws on the visual language of glamorous social gatherings: a woman in an evening dress at a laid table, a man in a dinner jacket leaning in, glasses in hand, the figures cut and repeated across vertical panels so the scene reads like a party caught in a mirror. The work references Un Bar aux Folies-Bergère, painted by Édouard Manet in 1882: the barmaid behind her marble counter, and the crowd that appears only in the mirror behind her. A work that quotes Manet above a private bar gives the room a lineage. Guests feel the reference before they place it, and the client has a work that says, in one glance, what the apartment is for.
 

### How the choice was made
I started with the client, not with the art: how they host, who comes, what the room should feel like late at night. From there I narrowed to work that carried that feeling and could be produced at the size the panel required. Then the practical part I manage on every project: production at the right scale, framing, and installation above a bar, where lit shelves and marble put reflections everywhere and the hanging height has to be set for people standing, not sitting. The project was finished when the piece was up and the client was happy standing in front of it.
If you are furnishing a New York apartment and want one work chosen with this kind of attention, write to stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Ramat Gan, Private Home

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/ramat-gan-private-home/

For a private home in Ramat Gan I placed a large format photograph by a Korean artist, two figures in ceremonial dress, at the heart of the living space. The client had come back from a trip to Korea that changed them, and the work gives the room that memory.

### The space and the person
A private home in Ramat Gan: pale oak cabinetry, a deep white sofa, terracotta vessels along a low oak shelf, daylight from the terrace. Between the two runs of cabinets, at the center of the living space, one wall was waiting. The client had come back from Korea, and the trip had changed them. That was what the house needed to hold. Not a souvenir. Something with the weight of what they had felt there.

### What it asked for
A brief like this is about a person, not a palette. I listened for what exactly had changed: a sense of ritual, of stillness, of ceremony done properly. The work had to carry that feeling to a guest who had never been to Korea, and it had to sit at the heart of the room without turning the living space into a themed one. Scale mattered. Too small and it becomes a postcard on a shelf. Too loud and the room loses its calm.

### What answered it
A large format photograph by a Korean artist: two figures in ceremonial dress, quiet, formal, full of presence. I placed it at the heart of the living space, on the wall the room already turns toward, with the oak shelf and the terracotta beneath it. The soft green and pink of the dress meet the oak and the terracotta as if they had been chosen together. The best description I have of what it does is three words: "It gives it memory." I have not found a better one for what art does in a home.

### What it took
Listening first, before I proposed a single image. Then research and sourcing through my network of artists and makers, a decision on scale against the wall, framing, and installation. Concept, selection, logistics and hanging, handled end to end. The work was done only when the photograph was up and the client was satisfied with it.
If there is a chapter of your life your home does not yet reflect, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Tel Aviv Bauhaus residence: a hyper collage on anti reflective acrylic

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/tel-aviv-bauhaus-residence/

The focal point of this Bauhaus residence in Tel Aviv is a hyper collage digital artwork printed on glossy anti reflective acrylic. The medium was chosen as carefully as the image: a dense, layered picture needs a surface that stays legible in a room full of light.

A Bauhaus home gives you clean walls and a lot of light. Both are gifts, and both make demands. The wall wanted one strong image. The light meant that whatever went there had to be seen clearly from every angle, at every hour, without glare.

### The image: a hyper collage
A hyper collage is a digital work built from many layered fragments, dense enough to reward a second and a third look. In a residence where the architecture is quiet, that density is the point. The eye has one place to go, and it keeps finding more when it gets there.

### The medium: glossy anti reflective acrylic
Printing on acrylic gives a digital image depth and saturation that paper cannot match. The colors sit inside the surface rather than on top of it. Glossy acrylic has one weakness: in a bright room it mirrors the windows. Anti reflective acrylic keeps the depth and the shine and loses the reflection, so the work reads as one clear image at midday and from across the room.
On a piece like this, the print and the mount are half the work. I manage production through expert printmakers, framers and art installers, within a defined timeline and an approved budget. A weak print on the right acrylic is still a weak print, so the printmaker matters as much as the material.

### Why one focal point

- A Bauhaus interior is already a composition. One work respects it; many works argue with it.
- A central focal point gives the room a center and lets the furniture arrange itself around it.
- One well produced piece is easier to live with over time than several that need to be balanced against each other.

### Two Bauhaus homes, two answers
In a renovated Bauhaus home in Tel Aviv, the focal point was a work chosen for color and texture in a monochromatic space. Here it is a digital image chosen for depth and legibility. The architecture set the same question. The people gave different answers, which is how it should be.
If your walls are clean and your rooms are bright, the choice of medium matters as much as the choice of image. Send me a photo of the wall and I will tell you what I would put there, and on what. For production and installation in detail, read framing and installing large scale art, or how the process works.

### Tel Aviv, home of Roni Daloomi: three works, two artists, visual candy

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/tel-aviv-home-of-roni-daloomi/

For the Tel Aviv home of singer and actress Roni Daloomi, I selected three artworks by two contemporary Israeli artists: joyful, minimalist pieces that reflect her optimistic spirit. Visual candy, in two words.

### A home that is lived in out loud
Roni Daloomi is a singer and actress, and her Tel Aviv home looks like her: sheer curtains that let the light through, plants on the balcony, a keyboard by the window with a stool for practice, a kitchen with a pink banquette and a black island. Nothing in it is formal. Art for a home like this cannot be solemn, and it cannot be decoration either. It has to have the same energy as the person.

### What I was looking for
Works that match her optimism without turning the apartment into a gallery. Joyful, light on their feet, minimal enough to leave the rooms breathing, and immediate enough to be understood without a wall text. Nothing heavy, nothing that needs explaining to a guest.

### The three works
Three artworks by two contemporary Israeli artists. Two of them share a language: tiny figures scattered across a pale, almost empty ground, sunbathers and swimmers seen from above, and one of them hangs beside the keyboard where she practices. The third, near the kitchen, is the opposite in density: a building facade broken into bright patches of color, all geometry and sun. Together they are what I call visual candy: sweet, immediate, impossible to walk past without smiling. They reflect her, which is the whole point of putting art in a home.

### How it came together
A conversation about who she is and how she lives, then a short list of artists whose work carries that lightness. I make the final choice in the home itself, where the light does the last edit, and that is true on every project. Framing and installation followed, with each work placed where it is seen every day rather than saved for guests. That is the order I work in on every home: person first, then artist, then wall.
If you want art that sounds like you rather than like a showroom, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. ### Tel Aviv private residence: a painting commissioned from the Shtisel artist

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/tel-aviv-private-residence-shtisel-commission/

For a private residence in Tel Aviv, I commissioned a painting from the artist whose paintings appeared in the Israeli series Shtisel, in response to the client's love for the show's intimate imagery. The result is a mother caressing her baby, rendered with quiet warmth, hung on the concrete column between the sea and the city.

### Between the sea and the city
The living room has the Mediterranean on one side and the Tel Aviv skyline on the other: two walls of glass, a polished concrete floor, and between the windows a single concrete column with a spotlight above it. The beach and the promenade are directly below. It is a bright, hard, beautiful room, and everything in it looks outward. The client loved the Israeli series Shtisel, and specifically the paintings inside it, the still, intimate images at the heart of the story.

### Why a commission, not a purchase
The column was the only wall that mattered, and it is seen from every point in the room. Whatever went on it had to hold its own against the sea and give the space the one thing the windows cannot: interiority. The client's attachment was to that hand and that quietness, so instead of buying, I went to the artist whose paintings appeared in Shtisel and commissioned a work in response.

### The painting
A mother caressing her baby: seated on a plain red chair, wrapped in blue, against a dark ground, rendered with quiet warmth. On the column, lit from above, it does what the brief hoped. The windows pull the eye out to the water and the towers; the painting pulls it back into the room. The client has the story behind it and never has to tell it for the work to hold.

### What commissioning involves
Commissioning is different from buying, and I manage it the same way on every project: I approach the artist, translate the client's wish into terms an artist can work with, and agree the subject, scale and timeline before any work begins, so neither side is surprised. Then delivery and installation, here on a concrete surface with the light set to the painting. The work is finished when it is hung and the client is standing in front of it, quiet.
If there is an image you love and want made for your home rather than bought off a wall, write to me at stav@stavtheodor.com or use the contact details at the end of this page. Read how I commission an artwork for a home, see another Tel Aviv home, that of Roni Daloomi, or a very different answer above a Manhattan bar.

### Tel Aviv renovated Bauhaus home: one artwork as the focal point

URL: https://stavtheodor.com/projects/tel-aviv-renovated-bauhaus-home/

In this renovated Bauhaus home in Tel Aviv, one artwork is the focal point, injecting color and texture into a monochromatic space. A minimalist home does not need more objects, it needs one decision made well.

The renovation had already done the hard work: clean lines, a restrained palette, nothing on the walls that did not need to be there. The question I was asked is the one I hear most from people who live in minimalist homes. How do you add art without undoing the calm?

### One work, not a collection
In a monochromatic room, color and texture carry more weight than anywhere else. One work that has both becomes the focal point of the whole space. Two or three would compete with each other and with the architecture. Filling the walls would have been a mistake. Leaving them empty would have made the home feel unfinished rather than restrained. So the answer was one artwork, and the work went into choosing it.
I do not make that choice for a client, I make it with them: a short list, each work considered against this wall and this light, until one is clearly right. The others are usually good works in the wrong room.

### What the artwork does here

- It brings color into a palette that has none, so the room reads as chosen rather than unfinished.
- It adds texture, which matters in a renovated home where most surfaces are smooth and new.
- It gives the space a center. The furniture and the openings now sit in relation to it.

### With the architecture, not against it
A Bauhaus home has a strong character of its own, and a renovation that respects it has already made a set of decisions. I work alongside architects and interior designers, not around them, and here that meant one work that completes the room instead of decorating it.
Art is not an accessory. It is a meeting point between a person and a space. In a home with this much restraint, that meeting point has to be exact.

### Same city, different answer
Another Bauhaus residence in Tel Aviv asked the same question and got a different answer: a hyper collage digital work printed on glossy anti reflective acrylic. Same architectural language, two focal points, because the people were different.
If you live in a minimalist home and are not sure how to add art without breaking it, send me one photo of the wall. For how I work from the first conversation to installation, read how the art advisory process works. If a designer is already involved, read working with your interior designer on art.
